item.title: I slept incredibly well last night
item.description:
I slept incredibly well last night. I didn't do the work of remembering what I dreamt (I tried to), but I made it into the morning early enough to say that I love waking up early. The first few hours of the day will always feel freer than the others: they are normally outside the territory of any authority, and they feel unusually liberated from the demands of productivity and capitalism.
It's maybe for this reason that these are the hours I treasure most for creativity. My mind is free to wander and be "unproductive," glancing off one thought or another on its course toward or through the reading I've done for the morning. I often feel much more license to explore my thoughts, because there is no one demanding that I put them in service of their work.

When I think about what this means, I generally land on the assessment that I have a little demon in my head threatening me with a hammer any time I start thinking about relaxing. The little demon threatens me with the knowledge that any free time not utilized as a vehicle for productive capital is somehow wasted time. I find that even on the days when I have a very legitimate excuse for not being productive (vacations, illness, days when I "just can't"), the little demon with the hammer is even worse, hopping from foot to foot with an impish smile on their face, knowing that I should not by any means expect a moment of rest.

Yesterday was one of those days. The night before, I'd slept horribly due to the unexpected consumption of a caffeinated tea at 9 p.m., and I was up until 3:30 in the morning reading as a result. I finished two books in direct succession. It was delightful! And I paid for it all day yesterday, as the little purple imp in my brain demanded I produce something of value in response to the productive late-night hours of reading. One of the books I read was Perfection by Vincenzo Latronico. It sent me into a spiral, and that spiral is what forced me to finish Lindsay Hill's Sea of Hooks, which has a cathartic-while-tragic ending that made its strange micro-chapter structure utterly worthwhile.

Naturally, when I woke up yesterday, I was incredibly motivated to write about either. What does it even mean to read a book if you are not somehow turning your enjoyment into some material insight that you can then place in front of others as an indication of personal legitimacy?

However, my need for proper rest had other plans. I am 36, practically middle-aged, which means that not getting my structured 7–9 hours of sleep leaves me an absolute pile of grey [slurry?] the next day, and nothing meaningful will happen with the day. Part of getting older has meant accepting this fact and creating room for it, which meant that, as a formerly over-employed ex-tech worker without any meaningful job prospects or vision for my future against the incoming job apocalypse, I could "allow myself to relax" and "do less with my day."

Which absolutely did not work. Being utterly exhausted, I resigned myself to thinking that maybe I could simply pick up another book to read, but since my well-rested self tends to over-aspire as to the literature I intend to consume, my pile of to-be-read books is filled with only challenging, vaguely [illegible: two words] books. My brain couldn't do it. [So be it?]

I had some accounting to do, and that didn't work either. The moment I sat down to pile my receipts on my desk, my motivation evaporated and I ended up in the kitchen, peering across the shelves of the fridge. (Come to think of it, this is what happens every time I try to do any accounting. I struggle, we struggle.)

At this point I resigned myself to free-writing in my notebook to see if I could tease some sort of insight out of my restlessness, thinking that maybe somewhere in this [illegible] would be a set of reflections on Latronico's Perfection. They never came, and besides, what Rosie Spinks had to say on the book is more insightful than anything I'd have had to say anyway (you can and should read it here; in fact, read all of her articles, she's brilliant). When the Brilliant Thoughts failed to arrive, I felt it: the panic of not knowing why you can't be productive. Mind you, this came after the rationalization that I could "relax" that day, and I had attempted to fight the notion anyway with a string of tasks.

That panic is infuriating to look back on. It doesn't demonstrate some virtue; rather, it indicates that part of the death drive our society instills in us is the inability to take a fucking break. I'll admit openly that upon realizing I had no cognitive capacity available for the day, I turned even to social media, and the work I have done to wrest myself free of consumption addiction proved itself useful here: Instagram, even, was deeply unsatisfying. Eventually I gave up and stared at the wall instead, my emotions [still?] racing through my chest, and by the time I'd actually checked in with my body, I realized I was incredibly, deeply tired. I fell asleep on the couch within ten minutes.

And you know what? It helped. I didn't wake up and suddenly have the energy to write a panegyric essay on Hill's Sea of Hooks, but I felt calmer. I had more clarity. I was better able to accept that the day was not going to mean anything, and I went out on a walk with my dog instead.

Line edits worth checking

Beyond typos, punctuation and italicized titles:

  • Timeline. The page anchors on "yesterday" but later says "the entire next day," "when I woke up the next day" and "today I could relax," which read as three different days. Changed to "all day yesterday," "when I woke up yesterday," and "I could 'relax' that day."
  • "turning one's enjoyment into some material insight that one can" → "your … you can," to agree with the sentence's "you."
  • "my ability to need proper rest" → "my need for proper rest."
  • "not getting my 7–9 hours … means that I am an absolute pile" → "leaves me an absolute pile" (removes the doubled "means that").
  • "wrest myself of" → "wrest myself free of."
  • "glancing off of … on the course toward or through" → "glancing off … on its course toward or through."
  • Kept as written: "their face" for the demon, "Instagram, even," "Brilliant Thoughts" capitalized, and "a fucking break."

Readings to check against the page

Page As transcribed Alternatives / note
1 (fragment) in a [illegible] way Top line partly cut off by the frame
1 (margin) Dan [Mirant?] Could be "Marant" or "Morant"
1 ~~a sense of deep pride at the way~~ Struck; "deep" could be "sleepy". Dropped from the edit either way
2 the little purple imp Could be "little people imp"
2 grey [slurry?] Could be "sludge"
3 formerly [overemployed?] First letters unclear
3 vaguely [illegible: two words] books Possibly "dense, dreary" or "dopey, dyspeptic"
3 [So be it?] Page reads closer to "So to it."
3 somewhere in this [illegible] Reads roughly "dummy"; could be "dreaming" or "doodling"
4 my emotions [still?] racing

Links added (per the AI notes)

  • "here" → Rosie Spinks, "Does where you live matter? An obituary for a millennial lifestyle fantasy," What Do We Do Now That We're Here? (Substack). https://rojospinks.substack.com/p/does-where-you-live-matter. Confirmed as her post on Perfection (2026-10-29).
  • "brilliant" → What Do We Do Now That We're Here?, Rosie Spinks's Substack. https://rojospinks.substack.com/>)

item.title: I often begin aging myself in advance
item.description:
I find that I often begin aging myself in advance of my next birthday by about four months. It could be that this is a function of aging, and I simply don't care anymore; the notion of needing celebrate a given day feels less important when in the wake of accumulated years this single day feels like one among many.
Yes this year, I celebrated by birthday with complete strangers. This is one of those behaviors I have earned and kept up with, not exclusive to birthdays, but to other celebrations I've had in life. I first did this by celebrating Thanksgiving with a Christian musician in Georgia in a field at night with two guitars and a plastic tub of chicken tenders we'd bought at Kroger. I celebrated Christmas with a thatch of drunk Chileans, Argentineans, English, French, and Germans on a beach in Ecuador after feasting on wild-caught fish in a local's backyard. The bonfire we build was so high that it seemed to lick the fabric of the night sky with its flames, and in the search for more downed wood my friend (she is still my friend) sat me down and told me to enjoy the night that we'd made. I spent of of those Easters cycling across Japan weith trhee men, and the day of may have been when I had to remove a tick from the skin of one friend's scrotum with a pair of tweezers while laying in a room full of other traveling strangers, having carried our bikes up over a thousand steps to get to where we lay. Another Thanksgiving was during an ice storm in Kansas, where trucks littered the highway median jack-knifed, and I ate a Sizzler at a Denny's where once we left, the rusting towbar of my truck came loose, throwing sparks across the highway, and I pulled over to swing the last bit until it broke off completely, and we slept at a rest stop that played a farmer's weather radio station on a muffled speaker all night until we woke up covered in snow.
It's not that I don't like celebrating occasions, it's that I'd rather use their marker as a way to remember something else. My sense is that a meal that acts the same as the same meal from the year before will be remembered that way. I won't forget my 36th birthday. I ran along Col de Fours with three men in a race and whooped as loud as I could with my lungs full of mountain air, and was chastised by a Frenchman stranger who said they don't do that here. I felt like an ignorant American despite my native roots, when we left that man behind, my new Bavarian friend told me that they did the same where he came from, so it was okay. People have different ways of responding to the mountains. I took a photo when we reached the pass with the three of them, and Benni sent me a message afterward, asking forgiveness that he'd placed it among his other memories as a way to mark the occasion. By nightfall that same day, the route I'd made had sent an Italian and an Englishman over a pass between France and Italy into Bardonecchia as the sun went down, and they said it was the scariest, hardest thing they'd ever done, but that they'd do it again in a heartbeat. My birthday ended with a shot from a bottle of Genepy on a folding table next to a brown Renault van at the top of Col de Vars, and the sad, smiling puppy of a Frenchman who'd marked the checkpoints of our race got me a sparkling pair of socks with 'Badass' written on the side as a gift.
There are better systems for making memories than those we're told to use. The unimportant things, I'm not as good at remembering, and as I get older I care less about trying to. I make stories from the things that are important, instead. They aid in granting gravity to the experiences with other than I want to share, and for months afterward, ticking into years, those memories work hard not to be filed away. The folders I could tuck them inside feel golden, and on the sorting desk of my mind I can't help but keep them there for a git longer. A bit of suffering, together. A laugh. The dark. Caipirinha or champagne on a beach on a sullen beach, with stranger. Frigate bird wings, ripping through the air like torn paper. Life is richer that way.
What I am saying is this: there are systems for memory, and there are good memories. We can make the choice to remembering things, however inane, or we can choose to make memories we will crave never to put away. Think of this. Fo the next time you celebrate the turning of a year, don't try and repeat what you have already done. Ask instead: what is the strangest, most brilliant thing I can do to ensure that it is worth remembering?

item.title: Will the mountain be reforged?
item.description:
On the OCC track today, watching runners filter by. It is 10 in the morning, they have run 23km so far, and there's much more to go. They are running through Trient, a blip of a town in Switzerland, and it's hard not to feel completely arrested by the landscape around us. All the while, I'm lookin up at a glacier that appears, more each year, to be merely holding on. The change is happening too slowly for anyone to witness directly, but it's happening faster than anyone is likely willing to admit. All the valleys around Montblanc are valleys of inspiration, and I cannot help but ask myself how much longer it will remain inspiring.
It might also be the people who will keep this inspiration in motion. These are people who will continue to show up to these races even after the glacier is gone, either out of a desire to continue testing themselves, or (hopefully) out of respect for what the mountain is meant to be. Mont Blanc. The white mountain.
This week, however, a dam burst on another glacier and a wall of water careened down the same kind of scenic valley. The footage is terrifying. None of it looks real, conjured out of an imaginarium of inescapable calamity. Every video I have seen of it is filled with people who I know, instantly, are dead. That part of Nepal is ruined. Their mountain gave way, and now the valley has been scraped clean - much in the same way that glaciers tend to, but much more violently, gathering all that remains before it in one miasma.
In Trient, I'm leaning on a bench with my feet up in the sunlight as we wait for our friend to show up. It is balmy today. She is the one running OCC - a sports influencer with a heart of gold. She is the one who shows me the first video of Nepal, the night just before she wakes up to run.
I watch a woman rush up behind a runner in her cycling cleats, and shouts encouragement after him - Allez Jerôme!, and the calls are more desperate as he gets further from her, Allez Jerôme!, harboring hope and fear at once. The choice to engage in endurance is a test, yes, and particularly one filled with fear of not knowing how we will return. The desperation in the woman's voice is one we all know well - we didn't know how we'll come back any time we have tried; a little changed, very tired, well-tested against conditions.
And so if the mountain shrugs of itself its cap of snow - should the name change? Or will it be hardened, when all the water is gone and rock is all we see, will its name be a memory of what it had once been?
There is no mystery to me. Already all the great footraces of the world against which athletes bash their bones to divine their futures are measured under the forbearance of this mountain's name. The 'MB' will one day remain a contraction, and nothing more, and we will continue to run circles around the mountain, forgetting that there was a time where we couldn't, because the white of that glacier's cap came so far down that the route wasn't there to take. This is not an indictment. Why would I? It's human. Thousands just died in Nepal, and people will still go back to the mountains to make themselves feel big. I probably will too.
Respect does not necessarily come with service in hand, nor rather it is only veneration when no service comes with what we've chosen to call respect. Running through this place is not respecting it. It's worship without supplication. We do nothing for the mountains.
All the same I sense a turning, I think, A sickening guilt of not leaving anything for whomever comes next, abject fear of realizing that the bite we have taken is too large and we must yet swallow it, with the friction of its mass grating its way down our throats. Damn the future. Whose it is anyway?
I am still proud of my friends and the efforts we undertake. I think of them sometimes as a form of thanks, but in the way an ant can thank us for not crushing them below our heel. Partially I can enjoy this remove and show up to these events because I know at some point we will learn our lesson. I'm not expressing a fear that the future will turn out terribly. It already is. We don't even tally the numbers of the dead anymore.
I think when we have vomited fprth the build of having destroyed most beautiful things, we'll see that guilt transform us. I think about katharsis and its literal meanings - contrary to what the Czech writer Milan Kundera had to say about vomiting, I invite us all to purge. I think it is necessary.
This year, the trophies for the winners of UTMB received 40 trophies across races made by Andy Parkin. They are all made out of trash. The base is scorched wood from when the second floor of the 300-year-old mill he call his studio burned down the first time. the landscape over which the runners traverse in his trophy are tin cans left behind by the melting glacier, or aluminum that smelted into slag and fell into the basement, or aluminum and copper sheeting from roofs and storms across the valley that he'd gone out to find. Maybe the trash the glaciers of Montblanc pushes to the surface are a form of vomiting, and when the bite we have taken has risen, it is heaving with only blood like phytobacteria left before bone. Maybe when the snow is gone, it will finally feel clean, changed. Reforged.
When Andy Parkin fell climbing, he decided he'd keep living. He said that he came back likely stronger than he was before he fell. He is his own artwork, a continuous trying that resulted in the person I got to meet. His paintings evolved. I like his dark period, but no one in ultrarunning knows who his is, or who he was to climbing.

  • I think my issue with this essay is that it's good, thematically, but it's not focused on what actually needs telling:
    • we are running around a dying mountain like ants confused by their own pheromones
    • Andy Parkin makes art out of the glacier's trash.
  • Revolution?
    • ca ira

I cannot divorce endurance and revolution because from either we experience the same. I do not think that running is revolutionary, but I do think that what it teaches can be.

Structure:

Who do I really want to be?
I seem to want to work in ultra-endurance on the one front, which is great, but I also specifically want to tell stories. I feel as though there's not a holistic interpretation of how these races matter to people, much less in the same sense that the Mountain Races in China hold an incredible appeal to me.
I think it's also important to tell stories about endurance in general - beyond the question of athleticism.
How do I line them up?

item.title: Under the Aiguille du Midi
item.description:
I'm sitting under the Aguille de Midi in Chamonix at the great generotiy of a frirend who is running of of URMB's races this Thursday. In treturn, I'll be supporting her at checkpoint and readying her for each leg - taking in the athletic atmostphere and contracting it, emotionally, to the experiences of the last week. UMB is a professional-level race, and with the trail-running boom in full swing, the running world's many eyes are fixed on the ALps this qeek. By contrast, only a scret few know the names Ilooked gortward to seeing in te mountains between here and Marseille.
The Speed Project (TSP) is well-known in running culture, but not as much in the professional running scene. Those in the pro scene who do know about it fall under two camps - those who know it but think of it mostly as being silly, and those who understand that the popularity of running is not merely rooted in athleticism. This is not to say, necessarily, that TSP has in any way directed what we call running 'culture', but it certainly has done so in the past. Those who have done so across the years have been a tight collection of brands and race programs - a small crowd somehow penetrating beyond the fabric of locality into a globally-recognized phenomenon.
For my part, I've always thought that the current wave of 'running cool' owes a through-line to some of the first unsanctioned races that were popularized through Orchard Street Runners, with Joe DiNoto's Tuesday night runs out of New York City's Lower East Side having set the tone for the grit of 'urban running', whose aesthetic has reverberated over the last fourteen-or-so years. 2013 OSR was perfect for the Instagram era - grainy black-and-white images of athletes darting through traffic late at night - athletes covered in tattoos who gave off a recklessness built for admiration. At the time, the demographic of these runners skewed toward one group - the majority of those represented on social feed were white men putting themselves up against the risk factor of the concrete wilds. Joe, to massive credit, recognized this and worked to bring attention not only to the women who showed up, but as well the wider (non-white) breadth of runners who were willing to put themselves to the test. For a while, the critique of Joe's races was that while it liked to cast itself as 'urban running' - the permission of who got to call themselves 'urban runners' was open to debate; does urban mean white tattoed guy? Who else runs in these cities?
Again, to Joe's credit, he worked on changing this representation, any by the time of his final OSR Midnight Half in 2018, the field was as diverse as one might hope from a race that based itself in New York City.
For a while, OSR was in high demand from brands as a crucible for New York running culture. Adidas dangled the possibility of greater growth over everyone who contributed to OSR for years until Joe finally got fed up and shifted his attention to a bigger, more lenient brand in Nike, who continues to back his efforts today.
However

item.title: Nightshift radio: a broadcast from the TSP deathmarch hour
item.description:
Running down mountain paases from Val-d'isere
Altitude sickness

Welcome to nightshift radio, the unofficial radio station for all your deathmarch hour needs
We're the radio station that won't play anything at all and gives you nothing back for free, located in dark little Villar-saint-pancrace somewhere along the edge of France and italy
Tonight we'll be playing you the pattering of rain, the snoring of a teammate, and the anxiety of not knowing when the other guys show up.
Follow along as we narrate the panting of the midnight hour as a company for that red-bull you never thought you'd drink and well make that sweet sweet sensation of not knowing if it's rain or sweat dripping down your back seem normal, sleep well, just not on your feet
That's all for now, make us proud, or don't, that's fine, just don't get lost, and we'll see you in that little house down by the sea before long, or we won't, I guess we'll see you at the end of this TSP

There is a type of running that feels like purgatory

A good idea for a trip with Rachael would be to go to the reaching of the Alps that we went and stay in the refuges that are up here.

-

item.title: You're not on Sabbatical
item.description:
A few weeks ago, I attended a writer’s workshop with Olive Tree Writing Club (highly recommend if you’re in NYC and have the time). When we went around the room introducing ourselves, everyone described what they wrote about and what everyone did for work, and after three separate people said they planned to write about the ‘intersection of tech and philosophy’, it turned out that about 20% of the room claimed to be ‘taking a break’ or explicitly ‘on sabbatical from work’. I find the language being used here interesting. I can’t recall perfectly whether or not I’m right in saying this, but I’m almost certain all of them were ex (or current) tech workers. That tells me something. I think there’s really only one difference between being ‘on a sabbatical’ and being ‘unemployed’.

I certainly haven’t rested. During this imposed ‘sabbatical’ I have: applied to graduate school, trained for a marathon, run a marathon, run from one city to another through the desert, attempted to write a lengthy and ambitious work of fiction that is still in ambiguous progress, and trained for another marathon. I did not actually take any ‘time off’, and instead I have mostly treated this time as an extended performance of endurance and self-flagellation. This has culminated in my present state, where I am physically tired all the time, financially less for wear, but maybe having learned something, if anything, from the time I’ve spent riding the blinds toward whatever comes next.

What do you mean you want time off

The traditional definition of the sabbatical is an earned departure from a place of work coming from having ‘paid one’s dues’ in time and effort, with this period ending in a return to secure, normalized employment. A sabbatical is or has been most common in tenured academic environments, with Harvard being the first school to offer it in 1880. The sabbatical is meant to be a recognition of the amount of work that goes into being an intellectual and is presented as an opportunity to step away from one’s work, with some level of certitude that there is a job to come back to.

The academic standard set was that this time would be used ‘productively’, to either result in some personal body of work or simply as a way to recover from professional burnout. At some point in the last 50 or so years, the affordance was ported over to the traditional workforce, with sabbaticals usually ranging somewhere between 4-6 weeks of leave on the basis of having worked some set amount of years at a company, with some of these sabbaticals paid, partially paid, or unfunded, but always with the guarantee that there’s a job to come back to.

Security.

I said, what do you mean you want time off.

This is decidedly not the way that I have heard people in my life use the term. No one that I have known to say that they are ‘taking a break’ have been taking 4-6 weeks off as a result of working at a company for 10 years, because no one I know has worked at a company for 10 years. Those I have met who claim to be on sabbatical are doing so for up to a year, with the majority of these people saying that they are ‘figuring out what they want to do next’. It means that the people I know who are choosing to use the term are really just choosing not to work and conjuring the faith that on the other side of this period of ‘rest’ they remain employable and necessary to some work environment or other, thus allowing them to bank on this security. More power to them (and myself) for this.

It takes guts to think you’re worth that much.

The sabbatical is a structure put in place when the work environment was constructed around a relationship between a worker and the company or institution to which they belonged. A sabbatical, along with decent healthcare, childcare, a guaranteed pension or long term return, were included in the suggestion of work - you take care of your tools, your tools take care of you.

That structure has all but eroded - health care at most companies is a major expense that actively works against those who want to use it, no where provides anything for childcare save the embattled parental leave, and it seems impossible to imagine staying at a company long enough to imagine that they’d be willing to retire you, so whatever pithy pension was paid into after the good luck of a job that contributed to a 401k is all you have to live on, in the end. The only thing that matters anymore is how much you’re getting paid.

There’s wonder in not knowing what you were made for

There’s an expression in Spanish I sit with quite often. ¿A qué te dedicas? Most people would translate it directly to 'what do you do for a living,' but directly translated it means 'what are you dedicated to?'. I think at some point in the past it might have been possible to say that you are dedicated to a job that takes care of you for the work that you put into being there. Now, with that relationship gone, workers seek to remain dedicated to themselves, to find purpose outside of the false, wavering mission of a company that doesn’t make them feel valuable. Hence, those with the means take a break to figure out how to develop self-worth.

The thing is, I know a lot of people on sabbatical right now. More than one might expect, and I don’t know if it’s normal for this many people to be on sabbatical at the same time. Demographically those I have met who are claiming this privilege skew toward high-achieving people from corporate environments who found some level of status in their careers, and the general sense I get from them is that they are exhausted. I sure am. If you have some money set to the side, it feels a lot better to call unemployment a ‘sabbatical’, because that allows us to brush off the uncertainty to an unknown point in the future and (in theory) should allow us a degree of rest. Hopefully (for some) it gives us the time to also answer a question of ‘what the fuck do I actually want to do’ when the workforce lets you know it doesn’t really care whether or not you are a part of it.

The distinction is more obvious than I think we’re admitting to ourselves. Claiming that one is ‘on sabbatical’ belies an exhaustion at the prospect of re-entering the workforce and participating in the humiliation ritual that is the job search. It is the reason that among this population of those ‘at rest’ there is a pervading sense that maybe, just maybe, it is possible to remain in this state of self-directed regulation in our relationship to work.

The perfusion of the ‘portfolio career’ is exactly this ambient desire - a hope that there is a way to remain employable without ever really having to be directly employed - thus magically avoiding the insecurity, obligation, and lack of agency that comes from committing ourselves, our lives, our time, and our energy to a mechanism that works us to the bone until the day it suddenly decides that part of its body isn’t necessary anymore and lops it off, leaving all the muscles, nerves, and capability that existed in that limb twitching, amputated, unmoored and questioning its value as anything more than vestigial. Oracle fired 21,000 employees last week. I’m upset, clearly. Too many of my friends have been laid off from what they thought was their dream job.

Thus I can’t blame anyone claiming a sabbatical over their actual state - being unemployed is stressful. It confers a deep doubt that we know what we are doing or that we are even worth anything at all, and in a society that values employability above all else as a metric for measuring worth, it is difficult to feel this unmoored. If a person has the privilege of money to take a break, it is likely because they pursued a career so endlessly that they didn’t pursue anything that might have resulted in other responsibilities, such as children, mortgages, or other dependencies. I can’t imagine someone taking a modern sabbatical without money.

Sometimes the blinds swing shut and you realize you are in a cold, dark room, alone.

Those of us with the means to do so are all ‘on sabbatical’, but specifically the vertigo of the statement is ‘from work’. Implied here is that ‘work’ will simply take us back at some point.

But we’re really just unemployed.

If work is love made visible, then rest is the love you give to yourself in return for the effort of work. That is, ideally, what a sabbatical should offer.

The fine line between sabbatical and the sheer cliff of unemployment is mostly financial anxiety. I think people who have a ton of money to spare are far more likely to take their time in finding a new job, whether or not their period of unemployment is willful. That’s just sort of how it is. Congrats, if you’re there. I mean it. We worked way too hard, we don’t know how to rest, and we aren’t sure what if anything we can do next.

For my part, there was a shift when I got to the 100,000 word mark in my book, where I realized that all the work I’d put into it was not necessarily going to pay the bills. I’d taken enough of a break to constitute rest, all while rigorously sticking to a writing schedule that got all those words out in 4 months — but the book isn’t done. I had to change tactics. Which meant I had to reconsider my runway for getting it done.

I ran from LA to Las Vegas in April, and I came back feeling like everything had fallen apart - any aspiration that I had around the book lost steam and I began to wonder if it was worth working on. Up until that point, the sabbatical had a point: something to prove, more to myself than anyone else — and the moment that I doubted it, I shifted from sabbatical to unemployment. Now there’s pure uncertainty on the horizon with the desire for certainty in how I afford to keep going. That wasn’t there before when I felt like I had momentum. Any time you stop for too long, you start to wonder if you have the energy to keep going.

However what I learn from running in places like the Mojave at night always brings me back to the same knowledge; the future is a yawning abyss filled with monsters you never know if you’re going to meet, but even in that dark you have to keep putting each foot in front of the other. I’m not on sabbatical. I’m just running toward something different. Endurance requires that you keep going.

What are you dedicating that forward movement to?

item.title: In response to Mona Alsubei
item.description:
In response to Mona Alsubei's most recent Substack post

At that point, I was giving up the lighting industry. I knew it. It moved too fast. I didn’t know how long I’d be gone. But I knew the technology would change. The people would change. Everything would change.
[...]
Wonder dissolves age. Nobody is old in front of something they’ve never seen before.

Career changes are strange like this - the realization that you may have niched down onto the frontier of whatever vehicle is encouraging forward change, then realizing that it requires an enormous amount of emotional and constitutional energy to stay there.
It's no surprise that in the modern age we are seeing such an increase in burnout or sabbatical remove in the workforce; we have developed so many new frontiers that anyone who stays at the front of them often runs out of the energy to keep going. The moment that you stop moving with that momentum, it can feel as though you are being left behind.

What I truly love about this interview is the fact that you've tapped into the sense of fulfillment she has found in not keeping pace, but rather seeking out how the threads of a previous life might fit into whatever personal frontiers can be made instead, making, I think, for a far more fulfilling life.

Gibran once wrote, to the great discredit of those who called him a pop philosopher:

You have been told also that life is darkness, and in your weariness you echo what was said by the weary.
And I say that life is indeed darkness save when there is urge,
And all urge is blind save when there is knowledge,
And all knowledge is vain save when there is work,
And all work is empty save when there is love;
And when you work with love you bind yourself to yourself, and to one another, and to God.

Notebook Transcription:

There is a pain in knowing oneself — above specifically we leave behind both the judgement of others and their fixed awareness wholly alone in the experience we are having, carrying something that no one or so few can understand.
I think I'm getting there, in one sense — I'm beginning to rub up against the soft surface of my own potential and am astounded by what I can see. I don't especially know how that path plays out, but I will—
It's just really astounding to see that at 36, I am going to be more in shape than I have ever been in my life. I'm going to be able to do more than I ever have. At this point, I'm just trying to see if I can do it — whatever it is. Meaning myself.
I watched a video that said briefly that I am not unmotivated, but rather I need a reason. A reason why I want to pursue something. My immediate reaction is to resist — after all I seem to be getting along fine, but as well — I don't especially want to have to rationalize everything in order to pull it off. Sometimes you just want to do it.
I guess the question then is what I want to do, and I have spent months puzzling over this stupid question. I want not to agonize over the injustice of not having the world hand me my next step.
I think I do need a reason, but for the large part this reason needs to be something to which I am first internally aligned with. I think that's nature, somehow, but as well it's being outside, it's moving one's body, it's caring about things well beyond that which our society desires of us. That is to say, I want people to care about the world with me.
The impression I have is that we're better off chasing the ideas that make us excited about life than those we think we are meant to do because it's the sensible choice. I liked running the goalkeepers today because it made me feel like I am capable, and I'm not especially certain that many people can do what I can.
But I don't want to be doing that without a reason — I'm not about to throw everything behind merely just because I'm good at it. I don't want to end up taking it as a result.
The question is now of what I want on the balance — is it the pursuit of a wild step toward wilderness first, then a "career" second. Norway does seem in a way most like the place that would meet those desires, but I don't think I would be happy there.
My ideal scenario would be going to Trondheim to study renewable or hydroelectric power, then running my ass off in that place, then coming back together with her. It might mean a lot of time (years?) apart, but I could see it being the shape things take. It would be so wrong to force upon her to assume that she somehow would uproot her life and pursue something that only supports my dreams. And what of Leo? How would I survive the fact that he may not have that many more years yet? Is making decisions around him in my life the right call yet? What if I have to plan in spite of it?
On the face of it, what I want to do in the long term is navigate the complex politics of how to make a sustainable future more economically attractive than not doing so. I think we so far only get one earth and the massive challenge of figuring out how to oversee its limitation means that we need to be ready to navigate the work together. I do not yet know what it takes to truly unify humanity.

This week.
- Send Jahed message for PIQ energy
- Research other companies.
- Write a blogpost on energy independence in the Northwest & its relationship to Datacenters.
- Write ya damn dummy!

'reacts' video script

At the end of this video, I'm going to leave you with a question. Now, it would be easy for you to scrub forward, react, then move on to whatever you want to watch next, and honestly, that was a hook: it's a mechanism designed to get you to make the decision to stay here. However, that decision is the point of this video, so if you'll stick with me, maybe you'll have a good answer to the question I'm going to ask.

Move backward
We mainly use the internet to produce, consume, and interact with information.

The amount of information reaching people each day is notoriously difficult to measure. One researcher tried to measure this in 2012 at around 34gb per person per day, and increasing by 5% each year, but gigabytes aren't a great unit to measure information in. It's easier to measure it in decisions - and today we're constantly forced to make a choice as to whether or not we actually want to pay attention to something.

Five hundred years ago, a person's world was small enough that almost everything they encountered came from a few dozen known people and places in a day — nothing like the volume, or the novelty, we're asked to process now. It's too much to fully interact with, but that's what we're dealing with nowadays. It's no wonder we feel underwater.

With so much of human interaction brought into the information age and channeled the attention economy, this is even more difficult. How do we respond to such an increase in bids for attention?

In most contexts, we do it by reducing the complexity of our interactions - instead of actually sitting with our reaction and coming up with a good response to how it makes us feel, we respond with the simplest tool that we have on hand: the like, the heart, the thumbs up, or the emoji react, and sometimes the gif response.

The like, the heart, the emoji react isn't necessarily meaningless, but it's the only response we feel like is fast enough to survive at that volume. It's not as meaningFUL as saying something more.
Move toward camera
So, is a higher volume of overly simplified interaction actually better than less? What comes of those interactions? Does a like actually mean what you want it to mean? Are you developing a relationship between yourself and what you are consuming, and what are the results of those interactions?

When we flatten our interactions to a simple set of reactions that are offered to us, we don't actually get to express how something makes us feel - beyond 'liking' something, we don't ask ourselves what else comes to mind, so all the other emotions vanish under that simple response.

So having watched this video, I'll ask you the question: Having watched this video, what do you feel compelled to do? Do you 'like' this video and move on, or is your emotion more complicated than this?

Let me know, because that's what I'm actually interested in.

item.title: Slowness, Endurance, and the Arc of Sports Culture
item.description:
Life gives us coincidences as a way of making sure we are paying attention. Probably, anyway. Only if you're paying attention.
Náko has a great bench outside front of the place - it doesn't shift when someone sits down to share its length with you, which means that if you're in the middle of writing a sentence by hand, there's little risk of their sitting down messing with your handwriting. I got back from Seattle on Saturday on another redeye, and because it took me all weekend to recover from the bad decision of thinking I can replace sleep with travel, I only got to my usual coffee spot in the neighborhood today.
Three people sat down next to me today, but one stood out because I thought I knew him -- I don't say anything at first because I was in the midst of writing, but glancing over his shoulder while writing a sentence (as one does) I see that his email signature matched his hat, and it confirms for me likely we'd met in another life. I tell him so as he got up to leave.
The person who sat down next to me turns out to be Ben of Attaquer. After trying to figure out the overlap, we confirm that he lived in Brooklyn around the same time that the cycling boom happened.
Ben and I talk, briefly, about the rhythm of change and what is expected of people when they take part in sports, then how they defy the odds. I realize while speaking that what humans want are human experiences, and that money flows where people want to go, not when people are told they should. I get the sense that cycling somewhat died off when the sport evolved toward the inspirational instead of aspirational; when cycling athletes pushed the limits of the sport, the sport began to feel less accessible, and less people aspired to be a part of it. Attaquer was founded in 2012 in Sydney, and I must have met Ben when he lived Brooklyn. It's not clear either of us really remembered one another, but we were both here for that particular period of time where New York City was the epicentre of the cycling world, so there was common ground to chat over.
I invite him into my thoughts; he tells me that more than a few people he knows who moved from cycling to the running world are rotating back to two wheels. He's seen cycling change, he ran marathons since it did, and now cycling seems to be coming back. There was a time before running was the sport du jour, and I've been meaning to talk, a little, about what it looked like when everyone collectively moved through that trend, as well why it is that running is going through the same arc right now. I really don't want it to, but it's likely the way of trends.
A few years ago, I ran the White River 50km ultra outside of Tacoma, WA with a close friend. At one point in the run, we stopped on a ridge with Rainier standing up ahead, and others passed, asking us if something was wrong. "There's a mountain!" I exclaimed, pointing at the looming presence of the thing. "Oh, yeah," many of them said. I suspect many of them were from Washington or the surrounding states, where it is normal to see massive quantities of stone and earth protruding into the sky. It is something I tell myself I would take for granted if I lived there, even while I'd hope I wouldn't. Everything becomes normal after a while.
However, I tell myself that this is what I am learning from running: that if I learn to stay strong, I can also learn to endure the longer effort, and I can enjoy it for longer. The journey is sweeter specifically because with endurance, it becomes easier to enjoy the sights along the way rather than barreling headlong into the effort and then looking back with the broken sense that you don't remember any of it.
I don't know if the same can be said for careers. My immediate sense is that others take on the ambition of careening toward the completion of an effort — they miss a lot. Attaquer celebrated a 10-year run as a brand a few years ago, according to a quick google, which means that the brand survived the bust of trend popularity that followed cycling. Maybe they end up happy,--I don't know. I just don't want to get to whatever the next stage is and realize I didn't pay enough attention to how I got there. I don't know if it's the same for careers, but I do think that those who take a long, slow, meandering path through the woods are probably those who know it better than anyone else, and they are probably happier in the end for it — they saw the moss growing on a fallen tree that will one day become soil; they paid attention to the ferns that grow from the upturned roots — they can see the mountain and so much more in the midst of moving forward. People who stick with a single job without the need to rush ahead and get to the very top of it all do indeed seem to sustain their appreciation for what they are doing.
I also think there are a lot of ways to frame a 'career' - we have careers that make us money, but then we have careers that act more like vocations. There's an expression in spanish I sit with quite often. A que te dedicas? Most people would translate it directly to say that it means it's own translation: what do you do for a living, but I like to sit on the edges of the definition, because directly translated it means 'what are you dedicated to'?
Maybe the reason running is like meditation stems from this fact: compelled by forward movement in a steady rhythm, we find ourselves able to sit within our thoughts. For a long time I envied people who said they would think when they ran. I often said that it was when I thought the least. Now I realize I had never tried to. Running, paradoxically, has given me the tools to slow down. Now, and only now, years into the practice, do I have some of the tools necessary to pay attention and sift through what is at the center of what I'm thinking. For a long time, what dictated what happened was only whether I was moving, not whether or not I was actually doing what I intended to. The conscientiousness of running only comes under the expectation that the movement is the point, and certainly not at the velocities expected of this world.
I wonder aloud if it's just because they want to be outside again. It's the same reason rock climbing will once again have its moment, and I wonder if this happens because we do actually know what we need most. What I want for either of these sports is the sense that people will actually respect the world that gives them so much. I've been seeing a lot more of Ultraromance lately, probably for this reason. Ronnie Romance, or 'Ultraromance' as he was initially made popular through the instagram cycling era, is a cyclist who has always focused on 'anti-Fred' culture. People want to romanticize the experience of enjoying something, and when this is sapped from the experience itself. I think people can tell. A small, optimistic part of me wants to believe that maybe this time it will be different, and people will remember that it is the outdoor they are after — that they will pause for a moment to actually see the mountains in front of them. Maybe this time they'll remember that the air we breathe was paid for by the trees they run or they walk past.

notes:
- I note that there are two threads here:
- One in which I'm writing about how running culture is following a similar arc to cycling culture
- The other in which I'm talking about slowness and the desire to actually enjoy what you are doing
- Which in some way talks about my ultrarun in Seattle?
- Maybe we remove the personal element here
- I think the connection between these is that both sports followed a similar 'speed' trend - it all became about going faster, further, harder, and that shook people off
- it was inspirational af, but it was not exactly accessible
- What ensures the longevity of any one trend is remaining accessible
- The issue is that trends change - which isn't avoidable. Nothing can stay interesting forever.
- However, what does make sense is finding an audience. Attaquer is still around, I'm glad to see. If anything it seems to be doing better than it was when it started
-

item.title: Badwater under a full moon
item.description:
running through the desert under a full moon
badwater is a place
tell me where I got lost
made of something
maybe salt
not white
baked brown by the sun
you aren't special

To run through the desert in March is one thing. To run through the desert in the middle of the night, under the light of a full moon, to turn off your headlamp and let that light guide you, to think that you've died and you're in that middle space, waiting to understand where you need to go next, that is another.
You hear lies from people about which direction you should be headed, but they aren't lies, or rather they aren't meant in bad faith; they become lies because you're tired, because you're in a different state of mind, because you're accusing the desert of taking something from you that you offered, that you gave up. You stand at the edge of Badwater thinking that there was something you could have done different, and where everyone else runs left, you turn right, and then you're alone, except for the few who follow you, who frame the experience in exactly the same terms and sense of self-respect, and you all watch the sun fall and the stars rise and you get lost in it. The roof of the car is a temple. You don't hear a soul headed toward you.
Somewhere on the route south a bolt shakes loose and you see panic on the face of every other runner with you, the feeling of being so far into something that you don't know what you can do but keep going. You trade out teams, you ask one another if you need a break. You look at one another, dogged eyes staring back. No, I want those miles, those are my miles. And so you rotate, and right when you're headed uphill, the night comes.
I didn't get lost in that desert. Not exactly. I tore something out of me that was afraid of getting lost and there was a moment where we came over the ridge and the moon was already there, waiting for us, but the road we came down was so dark it felt like a jagged edge had been pulled away from the sky. We saw one other car, and we never saw their runners, and the hill was steady, and in my miles the car dropped off the horizon, so I was left with a straight line in the dark headed east.
It felt like I'd died. What I mean by this is that there was a moment where exhaustion, the amount of sugars and absorption-optimized carbohydrates in my blood met the fraying wires of electrolytic expenditure in my brain, and I made up shadows following me. I turned off my headlamp all the same. It feels good to die. That's the reason it's so enticing. I wish I didn't feel that way.
I remember in the middle of two miles churned out at a flat pace without a headlight or a soul to see thinking that if purgatory is real, it does feel like this: terrifying, but wondrous at once. Dying while you're doing your favorite thing has its costs. I thanked the moon above like it was a mother reminding me that the heat from the sun is something I take for granted, but with the cool air of the night there was something else there, and I pulled forward, firing on every cylinder. We rarely have that feeling. I no longer felt

I no longer felt like a person. This is what it's like to di, and I feared it, because that cloud of fog to my left didn't look real, and the sound of the frogs didn't feel real because the desert meant they weren't, because the movement of shadows as I churned forward in a single, unstoppable line meant not to choose death.
By the time you meet up with your friends again you'll remember the same thing, and you'll get to them at the exact moment you need them to remind you that you haven't died. I turned to Steve when I took his hand and I said I wanted to run a mile with him because I was afraid. I'm not usually. But he said sure and we kept going until we got to the RV, and they were all ready, and they took off, and we went to sleep, 50 more miles through the desert at 3 am again and again past people who didn't expect us to be there, spirits or apparitions that didn't trust themselves to exist. We didn't exist. We don't. I did. I'm glad I'm alive, and whatever I threw at the desert was thrown back, that fear turned into a zeal for life. That lie we were told was just a misunderstanding. We're in the right place, at the right time, and that moon, heavy over head, shining light down like a beacon or a gift, well, it never saw us to start with, kid. you're not that special anymore.

item.title: The effort to be made
item.description:
The effort to be made, the effort to be made, the effort to be made. I do not need to get up at 5 in the morning to write, then grind away my life. I'm not really interested in being the sort of person who needs to show everyone else what I do and how I do. June is the ninth month, it is the halfway point, and it is the point at which it's all going to turn around. I'm not sure what will happen over the next 6 months, but I think I can make it good.

The question I keep asking myself is what I want to play. I have not focused on this question enough — I do not seem to know what the end character looks like, to start with.

She is strong. I know this much. Her time at the gym is about having the best body she can, on her terms of life. She does not worry about money — not because she makes tons and tons of it, but because she has her finances managed to a point that there isn't much to worry about — things like big dinners might raise an issue here and there, but the baseline will always be safe. She dresses well every single day because it is important to give people the impression that she takes care of herself and that impression's effect on others. People come to her for advice, and it's part of her job — the work of being someone who lifts others up, making them into the best version of themselves. She is not tied to any one thing, but she is very good at what she does.

Now in first person: I will direct people on policy contribution. I'll be an expert in the sector because it is crucial, and because it is an area I can talk about for a long time. I will write about this. I will talk about this. I will work on this.

I will also be a writer. Not just opinions on, for instance, energy policy, but art and fiction, or on subject matter and its relevance. I will work on contracts, and I will have to travel to examine facilities and how they function in line with expectation broadly set.
My intellect makes my abilities, and I will do the work of translating for others what they do not know or understand.

I find fulfillment in the work because it makes me feel that we are driving toward a better future for everyone at hand. I will match this energy. I'll take charge of conversations because I am the sort who knows how to navigate them. I like control. I want to do more of it. It is a problem I have: how to work on, and a problem I want to be in there for. I know myself in this way.

In the mean time, in my life, I am still writing. I am doing it differently than I used to; now I work in a way that suits my love of the discipline, rather than fleeting as though I have to perform for those that are overly focused on numbers and on impressing others. My sense still continues to be that the direction of athleticism is in the direction of adventure. People want embodiment — and while we are moving in the direction of embodiment — we will praise those who do the work to make the pursuits remarkable — who push beyond the expected.

This means I write about two things: endurance, and energy. I can write about either under the other, and part of the reason that I do has less to do with the environments I am a part of: I know these things because I am already doing these things. I am a part of them because I am a part of them, just as I will be in the future. This is an invigorating fact.

The version of myself that exhibits these qualities already exists: I am her. I haven't found a way to be in the position I need to be yet, where what I do is what I will be doing, but I feel a certainty for something I need to try: there is something there I want to explore.

The person I am is known because I do not mince words and because I am an advocate. I know what I am talking about when given the chance to speak, and I speak confidently. I am the difference between a leader and a boss — someone who inspires, but not someone who requires themselves to manage people on anything more than a mentorship level. I do not put myself in such a position, but others want me there, more often than not.

Let's summarize, then: I make probably around $300K a year, but I do not all come from one place. I dress well every single day, without fail, because it is how I want people to perceive me. My personal brand is affable, confident, connected, and attentive. I care about everything that surrounds me. I am determined. The work that I do takes me to exciting places because that is where the work needs to be done, but also because I want to be there. People want me there because my being there means something to what is happening. My presence will mean to the people involved that they are working on the right thing.

The question then becomes — how do I take where I am right now and position myself so that I get to be this person? What story do I need to tell about this in order to become her?

My career is not confusing. The throughline is essentially obvious: it is energy, and it has always been energy. My fascination with the world is factually rooted in this knowledge, and I don't need to doubt this fact. It is the foundation I am and have been building on.

The Ambiguist - Unapocalyptic

  • "the ambiguist is not just a science fiction writer with a wacky idea. They stand in a directly adversarial relationship to Artificial Intelligence. They oppose our natural human cognitive tendencies toward premature closure."
  • "The ambiguist has to exist as a specific kind of person, who draws a visible line in the sand declaring that we will not prematurely decide what some things are.
    • five candidates emerge:
      • Academics
      • artists
      • diplomats / translators
      • Poets
      • Indigenous Knowledge Keepers
    • abeyance is the act of not immediately drawing a conclusion, and ambiguists are well-suited to being the people who maintain a position of skepticism around subject matter in order to critically examine how something fits into society

OPEN

  • something really exciting is happening in running, want to talk about it
  • but to get there: how trends rise and fall
  • credentials: Park, 14 years NYC running scene, anthropology degree, started as photographer w/ OSR, shifted to participation

THE BOOM

  • running blew up out of COVID — 27 million new/returning runners 2020-2022
  • run clubs everywhere
  • people wanted to be runners — brands and institutions figured that out
  • Marathon Majors proof point: original five in 2006, Tokyo added 2013 (seven years), then Sydney AND Cape Town in just the last two years, ninth on the way
  • that's not about the sport needing more marathons — that's profit

THE VIBE SHIFT

  • you're feeling it, I'm feeling it
  • two forces hollowing it out:
  • commodification (top-down): community is why running works → companies/institutions stripped that for promotion and money → races got too expensive → people asking what's the point
  • dilution (bottom-up): the thing that felt special when it was yours and your crew's starts to feel like everyone's, then no one's
  • the sport was never the problem — the culture got hollowed out

THE PIVOT — ULTRA-ENDURANCE

  • huge shift away from talking about training for the majors
  • attention moving to adventure-style ultra-endurance
  • Dowdle: 306 miles, 73 hours, G1M Ultra — 4.2-mile loop every hour until everyone else sat down
  • people are drawn to efforts they can't easily imagine themselves doing
  • marathon boom = participation ("you can do this too"), this = aspiration ("how far can this go")
  • can't commodify a hundred-mile race through the mountains

THE CRESCENDO — WOMEN

  • who's leading this shift? women.
  • Dauwalter: just ran Cocodona at 41
  • Entrekin: won Cocodona outright — 56 hours, 19 min of sleep, overall course record. "I feel fine."
  • Western States this week: deepest women's field ever. Abby Hall back. Molly Seidel's first 100-miler. Jenn Lichter's Black Canyon course record. International field. Men's defending champ and runner-up both declined to return. The women's story IS the story.
  • Vol State 2018: I watched Rhoda Smoker come in second overall across 314 miles — eight years ago. The gap has been closing. People are just now noticing.

CLOSE

  • running isn't dying, it's correcting
  • the culture is shifting from "can you do this?" to "how far can this go?"
  • land on women + this moment

--->)

item.title: On wandering attention
item.description:
Constantly I am urged to solve my wandering attention with some panacea — all I need is a system. All I need is a one-shot solution to solve it all.
I'll admit — the prospect is enticing. My inclination is and has been a burden my entire adult life, and I am constantly fighting the foraging action that pulls me off task, only to find myself suddenly (I swear to god this has happened) suddenly playing a violin in my bedroom, the intent to get on with it utterly and blissfully forgotten.
As a result, one-shot solutions like keeping a stack of lists, or putting up sticky notes — or whatever else is offered in my direction — are all enticing. I have not staying on task. The number of times in my life where I have been reduced to the indirect realization that I have, once again, been forced to pay the "ADHD tax" is a number so large I wish it was my bank account balance itself. What is worse is the certainty that I am not alone in this journey, and that my experience with four has been long-established enough to recognize that in the flurry of "systems" I have sought to implement in order to change one of my afflictions, there really isn't a convenient solution. To some sure
Everything about trying to remember and to struggle through the toil of keeping on is difficult. I say this knowing intimately that I have failed myself so many times as to wince at the thought.
Despite this, I have seen success in my life: I was a successful photographer for around 8 years. I have done more than most people might think of doing in several lifetimes, and for a brief period of time, I was a tech CEO. All "impressive" things by most measures, but I am here to say, in explicit detail, I struggled through all of it. It is easy for this to be called "high-functioning ADHD" — or whatever name we want to offer it — but the truth is that I really did struggle. Half the time that I have been "succeeding" at anything, I have been white-knuckling my way through the work in pursuit of its completion. There is a reason that this has worked for me, but it is not a one shot solution.
The reason that I've been able to do any of this is that I am stubborn. That's it. It is the reason I have been able to develop discipline and have plunged into the hard work of anything: to do it all not in spite of myself.
If we take a step back, we can get a slightly better picture of what exactly this means. I often see (very inspiring) videos about people's journeys toward success, and usually among the barriers to success are framed as being in the hands of other people: they always mention, never identify first "haters." What baffles me just a bit when I see these videos is that I'm often caught wondering who exactly these "haters" are, — who has the level of anti-capital within them so pronounced as to rise in the face of those who struggle toward success and to tell them that they won't.
My greatest error is that I don't think "haters" actually exist — or rather they themselves, I do think wondering who these "haters" are confuses me greatly because I know my greatest hater: me. I inevitably believe that I can't do something. It could be that this is some survival function in my brain trying to protect me from harm, but being that the things this part of my brain says to me are so harsh as to outpace anything anyone could ever dream up, it's difficult to manage worse haters. This is why I have I am a struggle: no amount of barriers put up by someone else are worse or more powerful than those I impose upon myself.
It would be really easy after this to devolve into a hackneyed, grit-and-determination parable on struggle and particularly struggles with our own afflictions, set of values. That isn't what I am trying to do here. I'm not even sure I am offering advice, rather thinking my way around the reality of my experience to explore why necessity is a heat that I keep stoking up. It is just perspective, which is all we really have in this life. The reason I have been able to keep going despite the difficulty and the mosquito-like whine in my ear to stop is because I am stubborn — I show up entirely in spite of myself.
It's a bit of a reaction often to the fact that I have my hard days where I am exhausted and find it incredibly hard to get up, and then am peppered by a world that truly does think that each person's system or perspective somehow can resolve for another. I really do hope that the bullet journals and routines and exercise and psychiatric drugs do work for everyone who tries them. I they do work.c
But only if you stubbornly keep showing up to decide that they do.

item.title: Évanouir, épanouir
item.description:
As you watch gold leave
From the crown of the trees
On something street
Through the skylight of our car
Three things will come to mind:
You will watch two birds, one airplane, a crow
A fly
The pink of long lightbeams in
The clouds beyond
Two words in french;
Evanouir: to grow faint, to pass out, to vanish
And epanouir: to flourish, to grow, into something more
And I turn to you

-
