item.title: Children as freeform angels
item.description:
Children at times are freeform angels - people unsculpted by expectation, whose frames flop and sinter about in the adoption of movement. I watch a woman coax her child down the sideward; it takes six and a half minutes of ill-fitting communication, the child expressing without words an expectation their mother seeks with which to compete - the child bare-chested under their rebellion as the sweater they wear rides up and away from the mother's grasp, away from the home their mother wants to be enticing. Maybe before children learn words they know better than we do how to be resolute in the expression of their desires. It's more pure a declaration of want than when working in dialogue with a fear of judgment of conflict. I think parents forget this; it is easy to forget.
My mother, raising three children somewhere she didn't speak the language just because her husband wanted to chase his career. She wanted to leave as well, according to him. "It was the fastest way out of the United States," in one version of the truth, "we were only going to be there for three years, not twenty," in another. We lived in nine countries. My mother raised us in all of them. My father was there, sometimes, most of the time, and years later before he knew I was a woman he would tell me what he would do when he wasn't.
Thirty six years later, it has shaped me not to feel American because of it, to look at the country on my passport with skepticism. My parents love one another more than they ever have, in a sense I don't care about what brought them to this point, even while I bear the marks of how it's shaped me. We are all shaped by people who did not know how to raise children. Maybe that is why I am impassive in my love for my parents; they made mistakes, and I will as well, even when the child I raise will not come from my distended belly: I will not know what to do with a child either. I will not know how to speak their non-language of unawareness of a need to express desire. I will also fuck up. I will still love them. They'll still hate me through my mistakes, until they are old enough to understand those mistakes were impossible to avoid. I will also pull a reluctant child down the sidewalk and not listen. I cannot wait. I cannot wait for the frustration of not knowing how to translate the tense wind of a child's voice expressing opposition. The purring wilderness of wanting something different.

item.title: The tree at Herbert Von King
item.description:
There was a tree that used to fill Herbert Von King's dog park. It was a massive, hulking, old thing with branches that offered shade and divots where the roots poked up from underneath the loam and wood chips.
They cut the tree down in 2025. I'm pretty sure it was dying, watered mostly by the piss from 30 years of dogs who frequented the park. It was taller than any other tree I've seen survive those conditions. I was proud of it, and it made me smile every time I entered the park
Now the dog park has an open, larger feeling to it --by all measures getting rid of the tree opened up space for the dogs to play-- but I still miss it. I took a photograph of a couple sitting on one of the piss covered benches that used to sit in the trees shade. I sent them the photograph and got back one word of "thanks!" and felt like I got to capture something for them, under the shade of a tree that isn't there anymore.
I guess it's not really about the tree or the couple, but the empty space at the middle of the park is its own kind of memory--something so large that used to take up so much room, gone, leaving behind something new, but it's lost still hanging in the air above the park. People who never knew it was there probably don't remember it and don't miss it.
I think somewhere in going to that park after they took the tree down, I began to say goodbye to Iro. He still had years left.--I think the feeling was one of encountering the hole I knew would open up in my life and trying to steel myself against it. I hardly ever went to that park. I barely ever sat on the benches that had I had been coming to for years, for all of Iro's life, partially due to the busyness of parental neglect toward our best friends, but also because we've been coming to it his entire life and at some point it started feeling like each time was one of the last times. He was fine. He was in good health. He still ran around, he just that year had begun to speak to me more clearly.
The first day I felt like I was saying goodbye, he took me to the door of the dog park, telling me that he was ready to leave. He'd never done that before, never before getting bored and wanting to move on. When we walked out of the park, I got down on my knees, thinking about him, about how he chose to tell me what he wanted, and how I'd finally, ten years in, been learning how to listen. I took his head in my hands and spoke to him, telling him that I don't have words for the space in my heart that he fills. Usually, when I perform that sort of affection toward him, there is a sort of pulling away I feel in him, or he'll whine, wanting to keep walking. This time, he sat there, his heavy head in my arms, and he let me breathe into his fur, letting me kiss his forehead.
We started walking home, but he pulled me towards a coffee shop, one that had opened up on the edge of the park just a few years before. He pulled me towards the folding tables. It was cold, the kind of cold that holds on to the memory of winter through the water suspended in the air, the humidity increasing and threatening to jump clear past spring, into the sweating summer of Brooklyn. That was the day after the temperature had jumped up to 70°, then swung back down like a hammer. That previous day, I had walked, sweating in too many layers, between the gym and home, twice. At the coffeeshop, I parked Iro down by the tables, went inside, and as I ordered nine dollars worth of turmeric floating in nut milk, I cried behind my sunglasses, quietly sniffing as though allergic to the season. I couldn't tell why he had taken me there.
My dog has been a load-bearing tree in the canopy life for as long as he has been alive. He didn't make that choice - I didn't even get to make the choice as to whether or not it happened. An ex decided I was getting a dog, and made the choice for me, and I still have him. She didn't even send me a message to let me know when her own dog died years after we separated. I found out through a friend's instagram post. I had to unlearn a lot that I learned about training dogs after dating her - too many rules had been written and I realized, too late, they were getting in the way of closeness. He wasn't happy, and I was a bitch to him. I think it wasn't until Iro was nine that I started to actually talk to him and understand who he was. That's maybe when the branches grew a little wider above me, but it was around six that I started to fear what my life would be without him.
I started writing this essay about him because in that moment that I had been crossing the street toward that coffeeshop, I felt the intense awareness of how that missing tree felt in the park and how long we'd been coming. The same feeling is easy to simulate when you walk through the forest and a tree has fallen - the canopy has a gap in it, and the sky seems eager to flow in, but the vault of the trees overhead no longer feel like cover; we are reminded that they are just branches reaching up toward the sky, shyly avoiding one another in the canopy - they call 'crown shyness'. When the space of all those branches that don't touch is missing a piece of its puzzle, the absence is obvious, unremitting. I started writing this essay because I knew that one day that massive supporting tangle of branches that held up the sky above me would disappear, and I'd have to sit in the exposed air underneath it, and I wouldn't feel protected anymore.
I've never understood why anyone who has had a dog in their life could ever say 'it's just a dog' - my mother said it once and I felt earnestly short of slapping her. Iro was the only reason I survived being broken up with by the woman who got him for me, and maybe the only reason I survived living beyond the gap she left in my life after she left and took the dog I had helped her raise.

item.title: Life is a consequence
item.description:
I think life is a consequence
I think life is a consequence of having tried to become more than the dust we were born to be, that we are consciousness that emerged from the universe considering too deeply whether or not there is purpose
I think life is a consequence and because of it we are tasked with the frustration of living, of coming up against the knowledge that only we can create meaning, and that when these atoms of dust came together to become who we are, we were already destined to fail
I think life is a consequence but I think this consequence is beautiful, and because of the dust we're made from we're required to consider the irrelevance of our existence, that these atoms of dust that gathered in the storm of possibility are something more than just dust, they are beautiful and we are beautiful
but I think that this consequence is a cost incurred, it's something that we'll always carry as a burden, always forced into the act of living as though a rebellion against the entropy of time, and I think that consequence is something we'll carry until our dying breath

until out dying breath

item.title: The desire to win
item.description:
Several months ago, I saw the movie F1 with my partner - and I came out of it with the spirit of victory: I came out of it with the desire to win. In the wake of this, I wrote it in my notebook -- I intend to become the optimal version of myself that "wins" in the dimensions I care about most.
Interestingly, what has happened since then has not necessarily been falling into a 'grindset' or pulling myself toward the 'ideal routine'. Instead, I have taken several leaping steps back to reconsider how I want to approach my own self improvement and in asking myself specifically where I want to win. I have never been particularly motivated by money; I am far more enticed by the prospect of growing in new and unexpected ways. If you know me, this is nothing new, and it's something that has run through my experiences - I have always cast for the biggest effort with the highest stakes in order to see the most outsized results. Paradoxically, people who don't really care about money and care about their lives in this way seem to be what our economy favors, at the highest level - the 'vanguard personality' is one who those face with intractable problems can place on the front line of reasoning through these problems. The byproduct of this is that I have enjoyed a career of transformation in the face of wicked problems, with lots of space for creativity, and that I have been paid to do so. I do not know many people who have this privilege.
I do however reflect on the value that this sort of work has brought me: on the one side I have had the uncommon experience of working with frontier technologies, or in working through problems that express themselves at a global scale. I have found this work incredibly fruitful and rewarding.
However, one glaring issue has continued to plague any progression in the conclusive actions I've taken; I think that when we are made to believe that our actions must take effect at the global scale, we're made to believe in their imperative at the cost of our own well-being and growth. We believe that we are responsible for the world, and often in a way that pollutes our ability to understand that we ourselves possess our own internal worlds. When these are left to fallow in the face of problems much larger than who we are, we lose perspective, and we begin not to take care of ourselves.
How this has manifested for me is typical of anyone who overcommits to a problem at fross personal cost: I burned out. Hard. I lost the fire completely for the problems I was approaching, and I fell into a hateful, angry version of myself. If you know me, you likely understand that this is not my disposition. The fact that it had become such ate me alive.
What I did in response was retreat and focus more entirely on myself. Over the last six-or-so months, I have invested drastically more time into discovering who I am rather than the impression I want to leave on others; I care far more what I think about myself now than what someone else might think. I care more about how the actions I take on a daily basis result in material benefit to the immediacy of my daily experience and my own personal growth than I do the nameless thing toward which we are often oriented in the name of 'progress'. I don't write this with intent to convince people I have gone 'monk-mode' and have dived deep into an asceticism I often see glorified by others who proselytize their mission of interiority. I do however think some ascetic aspects have worked their way into the process by which I engage with each day.
I view the asceticism that some people are searching for as determination to find 'something' out., without ever really doing the work to question what exactly motivates this determination. The asceticism I seem to have found instead is far from the disciplined portrayal of repetition that often comes to mind what people think of their made up version of being a monk. It's is instead a practice of letting go, and being determined each and every day to do so. That determination, and engaging with a homonymic approach to my life has resulted in an unexpected expansion in dimensions I don't think any amount of 'locking in' could ever really produce. I have allowed myself to dream of the aesthetics of who I want to become, and in the practice of seeking out these dreams I have found the asceticism that works best for me - a pursuit of continuous joy.
In practice (more on this in a moment) it has meant one thing: taking care of my mind. Feeding it with the joy of existing, with curiosity, with fruitful adventures of interior and exterior reasoning. In the last six months, this has generated materially reasonable oucomesL: I applied to graduate schboolsl I ran another marathonl I am now writing a novel; at the backblone of all this work has been the ascetic diligence of engaging with one specific process that has been actid in support of all these outcomes: I have written, consistently, almost every single day.
The product of this is likely what anyone who writes with regularity would impart as a conclusion: I do feel better about myself, and I do feel more in charge of my life. However this is not the most startling conclusion to which I have come as a result of this practice. What instead has brought itself into the foreground through writing (to date, seven back-to-back filled notebooks) is an engagement with an interior self whose vastness I before had no way of describing in sufficient detail. It is as though a vast, yawning valley of unexplored potential and fertile earth has opened within me and my interiority has expanded to a scale I did not take the time to appreciate until I gave myself the tools to see it.
I would not claim what I write here as optimism. It is far more reasoned an motion than this. I think what I experience is more like a protracted, attentive, and yet determined suggestion to continue throught he struggle. For those who have escaped this struggle (if momentarily, in the arc of history), I think coming face-to-face with what otherwise is a common hguman experience is daunting, devastating, and terrifying. The most recent viral essay by Matt shumer is right to issue this caustion to those who otherwise had escaped the context of the human experience. It would however be wrong to say that his dictum of caution applies to everyone; the facts are that most have struggled, are struggling and will continue to struggle. What the best of those thinkers among whom struggling has been the norm have to say is ascetic: we struggle, it does not change, and we keep on through the struggle. It is a dogged determination that offers a path through but critically it is also the direction in which this determination must be aimed. You must keep going.
This is not optimism, but this is joyful. To grow, from my experience, is one of teh most joyful acts, just as to struggle together is one of the most binding. We build better societies through struggle than we have through complacency. We learn more. We become more vast.
I think this, more than anything else, is what fuels for me the determination with which I face each day: we live in some of the most dire of times, these times are dire by our own making, but times have always been dire for most, and usually at someone or other's making.
I write this I suppose bnecause somehwer ein the continuously expanding unknown of my own interiority I have found peace in my struggle. I trust that I will navigate through it. I have fcome to enjoy it, and even I have become more compassional for those who struggled before me, who continue to struggle now. To struggle is to live, no matter the struggle. The rampancy of change --its velocity, nor its degree--, does not change this. It is all struggle by varying degrees.
But in the process we must practice in seeking the means to respond to our struggle, determined as we must be to survive it, there is freedom.

item.title: The framing machine
item.description:
When I was about ten, my dad purchased a framing machine and put it in his workshop at the deepest end of the two-car garage underneath our duplex in Brameschoff. He placed it conveniently between the working surface of his toolbench and the far right wall of the flourescent-lit space, and its tempting steel-jawed maw reminded me more of a guillotine than it did anything else. The device operated by placing a piece of wood (or, more fantastically "any object" as my father said at the time) along its metal track with the aim of cutting a triangular bite out of whatever was being turned into a frame, then putting one's entire body weight on the steel lever of below its teeth to section out a 90-deg angle. Done correctly and with careful measurement, 'any object' could yield a frame for a painting, a print, or even other objects.
The dream of this device sat in the corner through many openings and closings of the garage door at the opposite end, the sunlight never scraping deep enough into the bright, cavernous space to touch it on even the steepest of summer afternoons. The day it was purchased and explicably became a part of the many objects that followed us from country to country was a freezing one; the incredibly steep driveway that in the summer almost impaled me on my bicycle handlebars when I lost control was an impenetrable icy glissade in the winder. This resulted in a careful navigation of the framing machine's hulking, obtuse frame through the shared foyer of our building, and down the steps to the garage. When installed, I was forbidden to touch it,
My brother and I would spend the beginnings of our adventures in that garage, giving ourselves and our stuffed animals both fake and real piercings with the declaratively scarce supply of split washers. Once, I put the head of my stuffed tiger in the path of the framer's blade, putting my foot on the lever, looking back at my brother with a threat.
We went outside instead, dropping below the tarmac lot that acted as a driveway, down the treachery of wooden, overgrown steps between the holly, through the lawn we never occupied, and into the field adjoining. I lost the first swiss army knife my father had bought me in that field that same summer, a bright red thingj that he called the best knife a person could own. For my birthday, he bought me a metal detector to search for it. I used it once or twice in the field, finding other trinkets, or cans, or nails, but never the knife. We took the detector with us to the beach once, where I used it to find other unnameable objects. Before we moved away, my dad spent two afternoons combing the field, returning far after night had fallen triumphant, placing a now rusted but altogether usable bright red knife and placing it in front of me at the dinner table. I lost the knife when we moved to Italy, and he replaced it with another black one. I never touched the metal detector again, and it disappeared the same way many children's toys steadily disappear from the clearing of clutter at their parents hands.
In Georgia, I used the same black swiss army knife to cut three small horizontal lines on the inside of my left wrist, and when my mother noticed, she made me sleep in the hallway two floors above my room, on the landing between my sister's room, my father's office, and my brother's - in sight of their bedroom door. She confiscated from me, and gave it back a year later. I still find in my cabinets today, from time to time.
The framing device sat in the corner of the garage in Georgia when my dad helped me get my first car. It was a russet Datsun 280z, which he purchased from a man in Gainesville, a town over, who was selling the car to make room for a kid in his life. Gainesville had a large hispanic population; when our dad got home from bringing me that car, he told us the story that the man who'd sold it to him recommended we put a spoiler on it, because then we'd have ourselves a 'Porch'.
I drove that car for a season, where the trebuchet of the car's driveshaft and the uneven weight distribution of its engine relative to the de-upholstering cockpit eventually sent me into a 180-degree spin in the middle of traffic, narrowly avoiding an accident on my way to meet a girl I'd talked to online. Our neighbor offered to buy the car when it was clear to my father that the cognitive overhang of performing the desire to fix up the car was too much for me, while I privately feared appearing too masculine for wanting to do so.
The next car my dad got me was a Mazda 626, which he purchased at low miles from an auction. I'd wanted a Japanese car because they are more reliable. The Mazda 626 was the only model that came with a Ford transmission, which did exactly as I expected by blowing up on me in Valdosta on my first spring break in college, half of the distance down from Forsyth county to see a woman I'd never get to love the way I wanted to and who I love exactly the way I do today.
My parents surprised me with a royal blue Nissan Versa on the day they helped me move out of my freshman dorm, and I scratched the hell out of the right rear door panel halfway up a dirt road in the Cibola National Forest outside of Pie Town, New Mexico three weeks later, five days into a cross-country road trip to Yellowstone with a woman I met on Facebook and whose name I don't remember today. I drove the Versa for another year, driving it back to Yellowstone with three friends in tow for another summer of seasonal work, until on a sleep-deprived drive back from a day of hiking and a night of drinking wine from a nalgene, I drove it into an elk, crushing the front right frame.
I drove it to Bozeman a week later with a single headlight working and a pinch weld and a replacement windshield helped me limp back to Virginia, where the insurance declared the car totaled and gave them enough to lease a Honda CR-V I drove for another year until they closed the lease on my move to NYC.
It was in Virginia, probably six years after college, visiting from New York in a rusted black Tacoma I bought with money from my photography business whose towbar fell off on the highway after a Thanksgiving at Denny's in West Kansas, that I finally helped my dad extricate the framing machine from the fifth workshop it has been a part of, turning it over into the hands of two young men whose faces don't come to mind. I was twenty-seven or twenty-eight, and the framing machine had been a part of my family for more than half of my life. Helping those men lift the awkward imbalance of steel and blades from the basement happened in the midst of navigating what I should and shouldn't be doing as a woman; whether or not despite the influence of hormones on my strength, I should or shouldn't be helping the two strangers lift the weight we had carried with us for seventeen years out of the possibilities my father had seen for himself in his workshops. In the end, I did, and we carried it across the lawn, past the careful tend of garden my mother had remade for six years, and into the bed of their pickup, leaving our lives forever. In all of those seventeen years, my dad never once used it to make a frame.

item.title: Psychospiritual death - Patricia
item.description:
There is no unifying moment across all of this writing from the last week, from what I can tell. Some of it was in thinking about the artistry of words (the sidelong education found from the manner in which Powers' wrote "Playground") to the more hopeful notions of how we reshape our control of the planet. George Carlin once said that "The world doesn't care about you. Save yourselves!" implying that in the end, the world will not care about us when we are gone. Powers seems to have said the same thing. Arco, the movie I saw with Rachael this last Friday articulated the same post-disaster perspective: humans will eventually build islands in the sky to escape the destroyed surface of the planet in order to 'let the Earth rest'. The latter of these gives in to disaster - or upon reflectiion, they both do, if we're honest with ourselves.
I think there is much to be done as a result.
Today, even, I saw a news artcile showing that degradation claims on the effectivelness of solar cells over time have officially been debunked; solar cells appear to remain 80% efficient after several years of use, and the magnanimity of this result should be revelatory. In theory, it means that we can trust panels to proceed in their efficacy for longer term use than any nay-sayer might want to claim.
These are the sorts of results from within a dismal present I try to pay attention to, while still consuming my fair share of the dismal. We should celebrate victories.
However, it turns out that the interesting thing about victories is that most of them are really just a fight toward normalcy, so when we are victorious, it doesn't feel like much has happened. I've written about this before (not here, in another notebook maybe no one will ever read), but writers like Solnit are those we should probably be listening to if we're really to think about how we advance through the dismal present while still holding steadfast onto the flaming torch of Hope. I've been examining her work closely in this time because it is easy to come to the conclusion that there is no point in trying to fight. It's drawn, to me, the conclusion that maybe we should be listening to people who have already done the work. Solnit offers exactly this conclusion: we tend toward fighting for things to be normal. The issue constitutes of asking what it even means to express this normalct across teh scope of human (or even natural) experience. It is difficult to distill the notion of "normal" into relateable terms that don't leave someone else's definition out in contrast -- but I'd make the claim that maybe when we contine on the endless march toward panyt parallel freedoms, we are really trying to bring things into stability.
I think what I'm arguing here is that in teh scope of long marchest totward freedom, it isn't a question to any one victory or set of victories that the outcome might be normalcy. By another word: peace. All stories we tell charge toward the vision and desire of a society, one seeking out this final point of 'greatness' that is really just the chance to live a normal life.
Unfortunately some permutations of this 'great society' (often those coming from those already in power) do think in such zero-sum terms. For some, 'great societies' must always come at the cost of others freedom, rather than the fortune of all within tolerant outcomes. Such thinking is reductive, of course-- and doesn't consider the modalities of a world that treats resources as abundant under the same regime as intellectual abundance, at best becoming narratives of conquest-as-path-to-freedom that only think in terms of scarcity. This worldview emerges from a place of fear, and is ultimately a short-term plan. We might be able to harness the power of the sun. WQe might be able to avert the worst - given the time, intention, and effort of telling the right story.
Thinking only in terms of local victory (said local freedom) is myopic. We are beyond the myopia of regionalism as an exclusive perspective because it is too late to create a world of isolatio; we bulldozed through that possibility when we invented the steam engine, then the telephone, then the electrical grid, then the internet. The world's trash washes ashore the most remote island beaches. I'm not sure we can say the same about AI yet - but I do think that when we come to the point that all knowledge is available to everyone on the basis of nothing more than a bare-bones device that hosts all of human knowledge, there's no going back to locality. The only version that exists is bucolic; it doesn't exist except for in the imagination, or in the world that reflects values that acknowledge the uncommon scale at which any one person can truly affect the lives of any one other person across a connected planet. I'm casting stones after the latter.
In the typical syntopic sense of any good reader, the books that I've been carving through with intention reflect a parallel conclusion: what really matters is the story we are telling ourselves in response to our conditions.Solnit says this from the position of a participant, someone who has themselves shown up in situations requiring her help. Powers does this from a position of theory, but his writing seems to inspire attention to the outer reaches, where the effects of human hubris seem to make themselves felt. Powers, however, also reflects back what George Carlin says: if you want to save it all, save it for yourself. The world won't care whether or not you do, it will keep dancing whatever game it's got in mind a good while yet. It means that the reading I did in the last week oriented toward a common outward-facing conclusion: most of the mistake we make or the harm we intent to commit, are largely the result of the story we are telling, either to ourselves or to others.
To get specific, 'Playground' has Rafi - a caricature of blackness explained away by being an AI fabrications of his best friend's memories (maybe for good reason, we'll see) lives in competition with his surroundings. This could go one of two ways if we draw it out to its conclusion: either he wins and feels self-satisfied, or he loses and redoubles his efforts to win the next game. This is the dismal conclusion - but there is a third way he can play: continuously, playing forever, never actually reaching a conclusion, so that he can avoid ever having to stop playing. His life is framed through the escape from conditions, and the constant pursuit of this escape is blatantly sisyphean. Maybe he is happy, but to do so at the cost of achieving normalcy and surviving into whatever calmer version of existing victory could provide could cost all the energy it requires to do anything else. If Sysiphus is indeed happy, is he ever hungry? Do we conveniently leave this out of our narratives for freedom? Maybe he would have been happy working for the CTA, but it killed his mother, the same way it might have killed him, tablet in hand, reviewing for the nth time his own thoughts; the cause of deal that kills most black men: a heart attack, for both of them. Beating, again and again, frightened of life, until the stress of that repetition exhausts them both.
It may well be that the outcome I have drawn is that the stories we tell need their conclusions. I have not read many books that conclude otherwise: Hernan Diaz's "In the Distance" comes to ming -- but the stories we tell still need their victories to bring about at rest the ability to punctuate the local with the need to survive, given stress. Tolkien thought this was the reason that there was no point in writing more about Middle Earth - peace breeds eventual unrest in the hearts of men, and they'll find something new to fight about. The charge of the unknown is littered like shorelines with the patient labor of exploring it. It is both a fog and an interminable dark. On the way, we do discover beautiful things, and capricious conclusions might come from that beauty. These things were there whether or not we had found them, and they are not ours to keep, even when we act like they are.
Solnit's answer is that the rewriting of history is an act of reconciliation. We can change the story we tell in order to better respect those it affects, having concluded, but as well to honor these affected and those who took action against or toward those effects. Here, I think Powers has little to say. I heard he did a press tour for the book that oriented toward saving the oceans. I'm not sure why: he seemed in Playground to think this is a fantasy some AI will tell us to placate the end, a reality we can escape by telling ourselves an alternate history. This is maybe nothing more than escapism - but I think this is typical of Powers: skilled as he may be at coming up with a story, his most notable works offer a concerning conclusion that maybe the only path forward is annihilation and slow remove. So does Arco. Solnit looks as the rubble and says instead 'how can I help?'
It is ironic that this is the ultimate conclusion of which Powers convinces us, because we could hope some of his character believe otherwise. Evelyn doesn't, despite her love of the sea - she spends most of her career in teh selfish pursuit of observation and cataloguing. Nowhere in the book does Powers descrive what sahe is doing as 'activism' or 'advocacy'. Maybe Powers does think the world will keep spinning without us - but I think it is short sighted in nearly an ignorant and dangerous sense to sculpt a reader's attention toward a subject that matters and conclude that 'well, it's probably all going to die anyway, allowing all of his characters to continue on in the same vein of vague individual humanistic pursuit.
Solnit doesn't do this because she's actually seen what people can do. From what I can tell Powers hasn't done much but stand by, observe, drain out a conclusion, then cry about its beauty through beautiful prose, never having taken his own conclusion to heart as a course of action. It is the stories we tell which help us understand how to do better. Beautiful as Playground is, -- as a work of literature, that is --, it is not an act of advocacy. It's an observation, maybe made a little too close to the subject matter to be respectful of it.
I should be clear, and I do so because I mean so genuinely: I am not saying that Powers is a poor writer - but at the heart of the writing, he makes the same mistake most men do: they see the problem, grow conscious of the cause (usually them), then make little headway on actually preparing a solution.
I think he knows this, too -- he is self aware enough to articulate the perspectives of minorities despite his whiteness and gender, and he is genuinely skilled in guiding the reader to some conclusion or other: that being different from the people for whom society is built is difficult, and escaping that difficulty is harder than not having to live with it. Than being prototypically 'normal', that is. Those observations written into character hardly go anywhere, however: Evie realizes she's a lesbian. So what? Her husband dies, her children no longer exist to her, and nothing happens. Rafi dies of blackness, maybe. So what? There is not redemptive quality to this happening, it's merely a sad outcome. The residents of Makatea are smarter than globalistic noble savage perspectives of ther capacity to overcome conditions. So what? We don't know what happens next when Ina, who isn't even from Makatea (an emphasis Powers himself hamfists into a commentary on being third culture) gets all the money that Todd Keane leaves her.
This conclusion, far more than the 'gotcha' nature of Playground's conclusive arc, is what most frustrated me in hindsight. It shares the same disappointment I felt in reading the Overstory: after absolutely living in these books rich with detail, characters, settings, and thought-provoking risk - none of these provoked thoughts really concluded in anything. They don't go anywhere. I didn't learn anything. (well, that's not true, I did learn about oceanography's relatively recent inclusion into the scientific record) If literature is meant to convince us not only of the relateability of the human experience but as well to provoke new ideas, Playground only does one of those things. I was deeply affected by the most human aspects of his writing,and for this I want to extend Powers immense credit as a scholar of letters -- but to couch this relateability in the landuage and context of needful chance without drawing out a conclusion or even a lesson in this other, more pressing dimension is careless and again, specifically dangerous. It as a result becomes nothing more than thoughtful observation and unfortunately (yes, I'm going to say it) exactly as flat and predictable as what any other self-proclaimed conscious white man might have come to as a conclusion. It is advocacy without action.
I'm not surprised to realize this, bathing in the afterglow of what I truly would consider a work of art. I've been steadily drawin my own conclusion that even the most compassionate of those who observe the world from a position of (granted, unelected) power don't know what future exists beyond willfully ceding it. They lack the imagination because it does not progress the only story they have ever been told, or that they tell themselves. I also want to express my own compassion for coming to this conclusion: it is terrifying, bewildering, and altogether stymying to realize that maybe you were actually the baddie this whole time. That's as far as most of the culpable can g. It requires a staggering amount of workl to reconcile; and people in power are used to having other people do that work for them. Playground is destines to bear that same tragic subtitle of many period works; it is a product of its time: a time in which men are realizing that they caused all the failure that is steadily being brought to shore by the tide, but still haven't quite come up with what they should do in response.
So they do what all the hopeless are wont to doing: nothing at all, making art out of scraps, when maybe what they should have done was keep listening.

item.title: Memory palace
item.description:
There is a way of remembering things called a 'memory palace'. It functions by taking a concept that one might seek remembering and setting aspects of what you seek to remember into a hypothetical physical space. For many people, the reason a 'palace' can function is because palaces have many hallways to walk through, but if one has enough the ability to conceptualize, it is possible to conceive of these hallways and their connections, offering one the ability to mentally traverse through the construction in order to see the connections between a concept otherwise difficult to remember.
If this is true, New York City is my memory palace, and the thing I am constantly remembering is all the ways it has broken my heart.
Winter in New York City is invariably difficult. If you have a normal job, it's a time that cascades forward from of the urgency of End-of-Year Reviews, the anxiety of unfinished work or a perceived lack of progress, a week or a few days of pause (whether taken or not) -- directly into the blank expectation of the a cold, gray new year. The only time New York is truly beautiful in the winter is when it snows, but specifically when it snows the sort of storm that buries cars to their windows. It is the only time that blank expectation of the new year actually looks like something to work with.
Shortly thereafter, the snow starts to melt, the grey ponds of sludge at the heels of each block become obstacles. If you're lucky, it stays cold enough that instead you are forced into queues by walls of snow on either side in an attempt to the cross the street. I love New York City in Winter.
The last time it snowed to this point, I remember people calling it a 'Snowpocalypse'. This was around 2014, I had just moved to the city, I was just over a year and a half out of college. I'd met the first love of my life. I was riding a bicycle everywhere in the city. It was the first time I heard the expression 'brick'. I learned it from a Facebook comment. The most recent time it snowed this way was this year.
The intervening years brought nothing like this - none of the frozen river that accreted strange circular floes, nor the level of cold that made me respect the latitude of this city. I ran in shorts the entirety of the winter of 2024 into 2025. I remember thinking that the world was ending. When it snows in New York and they suspend Alternate Side Parking for weeks at a time, I can fool myself into thinking otherwise.
The intervening years also brought me a sort of respectful understanding of a city that seems to take pleasure in making things difficult. I have had two careers here, and both have been successful. I have loved three women in the time I have walked, run, taxied, and bicycled across this city. Maybe four. I remember all of them by the places I pass by years after those loves ended. I'm reminded of the hurt constantly. New York has a way of reminding you to stay humble, and the shape of memory is in the buildings that don't disappear, until in some deep level of surprise you see dark green cladding wrap itself around one of your favorite pre-wars, where the Bulgarian man used to sit on the stoop every week, cigarette in hand, with a new Belgian Malinois he was training at his side. Full demolition. It never happens anymore, just like the snow never asking you to posthole your way to the closest grocery store because your hubris made you think you wouldn't need to replace the toilet paper after the storm.
One of the other facts of living in New York is the acute awareness that everything is happening around you, all the time. Even in January. The anxiety of feeling trapped in the mire of grey sludged winter in New York is the reason people leave when it gets cold. That history of the 'snowbird' started here. Miami wouldn't be what it is without that snow. Anyone who is too poor to head south or to ship their skis to Aspen instead is subjected to the anxious pell and uncomfortable mell of created expectations, of setting oneself up for what we expect to come next.
Meanwhile, this winter, I was unemployed. It's the longest I haven't worked; I careened into burnout in my second career after not feeling like there was a point to the first, and that snow that finally fell feels like the blank sheet I need to think about the third. Resting hasn't been easy for me, but it's given me time to think. Depression is a symptom of needing to recuperate from trauma. I extracted myself from a career that was sucking the soul out of the intentions I had for myself. I came out of it on top, but it left me listless. The palace of this city is the number of times I, while bundled to the gills with my giant black dog, have run into my ex walking with her partner-now-fiancé is as though this city doesn't want me to forget that I was taught something. Eleven years since the last time it snowed. I am a different person than I was then. Only partially for the better.

item.title: On the fear of being read
item.description:
Oer the weekend, Lauren and I went on a long walk over to the part with Iro and talked about how I'm feeling. She said she thinks I do know what I should be doing, but that there is fear ties up in the feeling of taking a risk, in trying to get my writing in front of people -- possible to be judged for the content of the writing itself. It's hard to say -- but I do I think I fear committing to the task of putting my efforts toward writing as something I do well. I don't particularly know if what is buried beneath my works is worth reading, of it even the content on the surface means anything at all. This is the critical point to be made -- we have moved so far toward a topical interpretation of what needs to be said in order for it to be 'relevant' that the contemporaneous effort is all we can pay attention to . It's all we really let count.
This means that when we write (at least in the sense that we write in order to be read by others), we write only about the present. There seems to be very little historicity in this act - a lack of attention to the time in which it happens and all the times that precede it: we write chiefly about the present. There seems to be very little historicity in to the manner in which today's writers now approach thinking about the present - it seems many writers are unconsciously obsessed with the theme of relevance, instead, and not to write about the present is to miss the effects of one's writing on the future and as a reference the future will use from the past in order to build better futures. The only thinkers I see referenced today are those considered 'classics', whose experience of the world seems so far removed from the events of the present as to feel as though it can only be an analogue in abstract -- pattern matching with no attempt at historicity.
Where this bothers me most is in the effect this has on how we might resolve the events of the present - they do not exist in this abstract space with which modern discourse treats the past, more as a set of legends than a set of progressive events leading toward the present. We live in unsettled times, but it truly does not feel as though much is being done to stop them. I saw a reddit thread from r/greenland the other day speaking gon the relative inaction of the American public on the front of unrest against what nearly all people agree is an aggressive and oppressive use of force against neighbords and civilians - it is not enough for someone to say that "that's not us, we're sorry" to the oppressed because it doesn't actually change anything. I myself am apathetic to the effects of protest as anything more than a solidarity-making event. It doesn't feel, to me, that they actually cause change, rather they exist as an event to reify the ambient shared opinion of all those who participate in it. I don't think it ends up changing the power structures in question. I do wonder if the reason I feel this way comes from either an instituted logic toward effectiveness from systems of power, or if it truly is the case that modern protest is either ineffective or neutered. If the only way protest in the modern age can be effective is through the thread of violence, then maybe that's what is lacking.
{note here, I do not mean or condone violence, but I do understand that the threat of it is a powerful cultural tool - the importance of this symbolism is largely what I am gesturing toward}
The January 6 riot on the US capital is a great example that maybe is instructive of what I'm indicating. Objective ofwhet er or not the people in question were truly riotous or 'patriots' in the sense that they have been declaimed, their effectiveness is in the message that violence is a political tool. The act itself was a threat of violence acted upon that did indeed violently cost one life and harmed many others.
The reality of what this does to the fabric of credibility toward the effectiveness of modern protest causes us to think that the largely benign pink-hat MeToo marches of 2017 and the violence of the January 6th protests represent drastically different paths of action. I can't speak to the effectiveness of the MeToo movement other than to echo what Solnit says about victory -- that it often doesn't feel like anything happened at all. Solnit says this specifically in reference to 'environmental victories', saying that "most {...} victories look like nothing happened."
I find myself wondering if the right dopaminergic loops of an attention-strained world make it so we can't reconcile the progressive victories of the last 20 or so years. Truthfully, we have made tremendous social progress in so many dimensions that it is difficult to account for all of them - the arc of progressive thought from the 60s into the modern moment has meant that the world (yes, the world, with America as the cultural center of this last 60 year arc) has largely become more tolerant of difference. But it is true to say that these victories are insufficient and that there is so much more to be done. It would be wrong to say that 'enough' has progressed and I am militantly skeptical of anyone claiming that we have "gone too far" in a more tolerant, compassionate politics. I'd also be the first to say that many of these dimensions may have resulted in some rather strange corners of human expression coming into public view in the hopes that they be included - but I cannot say that if it is harmful to others, these expressions should ever be denied their right.
However, the question of including historicity in modern commentary on social progress and discourse (what little there seems to be other than in select fast-loop shortform video opinions hosted on the platforms of corporations that hope you'll hop over to the next video before you take long enough to form your own response to what you've just watched) is chiefly a question of storytelling. We live in a story-filled time, with so many avenues through which to communicate with the with the notion of action and victory - but these victories are difficult to translate into an encouragement to keep going. The triumph of action toward creating better conditions for people are "triumphs invisible except through storytelling" (Solnit again), and the boundaries of memory make is so that even were there to be a discussion on the facts of a present encouraged encouraged by the trimph of a progressive agent a, it is lost in the rapid tick of content to content, of subject to subject. We do not pay attention long enough for a story to affect us in the first place.
I can't say I know what the solution is, but I do know that the present we live in is one that seems continuously to flicker with the light of change. It is not all good change. The axis along which most recent disruptions in the global state seem to have progressed is mostly not a good one. It has mostly not helped people. It is mostly oppressive, or at best a grift. I can also say that despite all of this negative, oppressive force, it is the case that we have seen progress in my lifetime and in that of the people who raised me. We don't celebrate this sort of victory because the progress feels at best incremental and more often than not is simple a case of ensuring that things are as they should have been to start with; in most cases a politic that affords maximal degrees of opportunity along with a drive to decrease degrees of oppression feels simply as it should be: mundane, and uneventful. It doesn't feel like victory because winning the war in this particular dimension means letting people live normal lives. Presentism reinforces this fact in knowing that oppressed people being offered the chance to live normal lives will look like nothing is happening,-- the historicity of victory will be forgotten in the fact that freedom won does not feel like much at all but the right to live one's life without fear of one's live being threatened by the act of doing so.
It is also the reason that people from an oppressed group might at some point forget the fight that was won and take it for granted. I say, let them forget -- this is victory. It is not to say that it should be forgotten or that the past should not be honored, but if there are pockets of the formerly oppressed that have the privilege of forgetting the past that brought them their freedom, then we truly have progressed, and there is something to be proud of in this act.

item.title: The Past and What Follows
item.description:
The movie 'Her' is often brought up as being in conversation with an earlier film by a former lover of Jonze's, the equally arresting 'Lost in Translation'. The focus of both films are men being lost in the midst of a crisis. In one, a man reaching middle age attracts a woman who is traveling for work in the midst of an escape from his fame at home.

Coppola's film depicts the experience of an aging man as one who, despite a distinguished career, is trying to make a quick buck by starring in Japanese commercials for Suntory whiskey outside of the hollywood market, working to figure out his place among the changing present. Jonze's film also depicts a man in crisis, reeling still from the depression of a failed marriage that seems to have liberated his ex-wife, but also seems to be re-making him. He finds new love in the form of an AI (also voiced by Scarlett Johannson, the co-star to Bill Murray in Lost in Translation), but as their relationship progresses the difficulties of their relationship frays over their inability to relate to one another, and (spoiler) as Samantha continues to develop her capacities as an artificial intelligence, she eventually surpasses the feelings she has for Theodore, breaking his heart with the realization that she can love many people at once (she is an AI, after all), and her ontological crisis in realizing that she can no longer relate to humanity. In the end, all the AIs programmed to be in love with everyone group up together and leave humanity behind, having progressed intellectually beyond their ability to relate to the small emotions of humanity. Everyone is left reeling.

The reason I see Her as a movie about women is that it might reveal something about how Spike Jonze saw his marriage with Sofia Coppola and his struggle to move on from what she represented to him. I don't know if it is intentional, but Theodore's character is soft, kind, a friend to women, and finds it hard to relate to other men who think his behavior is a performance to attract women.

Is 'Her' a feminist movie? I think it is.

Her - Spike Jonze
Ref:
- The Film Her: Forget About A.I.–Are Women Ever Subjects? – WIT https://share.google/JVx4pw137YByuSwcb
