item.title: Somewhere beyond Kundera
item.description:
In 2010 I was in a riverboat with twelve or so other people on my way to Rurrenabaque, Bolivia to spend time in the woods pretending to be a naturalist. I still have the notebook I brought with me where I sketched the native plants and their relationship with nature - and it was among the best experiences I had as a young person exploring the world - a feeling of returning to something deeper, wilder, all while feeling incredibly removed from the demands of my life. I was young. I knew how to live on a thousand dollars for two months. I can't say I was necessarily trying to find myself there, but I was doing the good work of trying to get lost, despite it. I was trying to find a story worth telling, either for myself, or for anyone.

One among a few books I brought with me was Milan Kundera's "The Book of Laughter and Forgetting", which would be the second Kundera book I had read. While we cut through Amazon headwaters at sunset, or midday, (I can't remember, but it was beautiful), I opened Kundera and read through Part Six, where Kundera seats a description of laughter as the sound of the soul disagreeing with the state of reality, or rather specifically that "laughter can be a revolt of the spirit against reality as it is". Angels laugh, Kundera says, because everything makes sense, but devils laugh because none of it does. Lucifer used to be an angel; maybe all the devils are, on either shoulder. We were on the boat for hours. My memory of what else he said isn't linear, because it was also this day that I read what he says before this, in Part Four, which was less aesthetic, but prevented me from writing for so much longer.

In Part Six, Bibi, the two-dimensional woman that she is, is exhausted and ineffectual due to the burdens of existing, and her friend Tamina arranges for her to meet with a local novelist Banaka to discuss her desire to seek in herself whatever it is that compells people to write. What Tamina doesn't know, and what Banaka doesn't remember, is that Banaka once molested Bibi in a bathroom. Despite this, Bibi meets with him, knowing that he doesn't remember her, and he asks her why she wants to write. She says "I have a feeling that my experience inside is worth writing about and could be interesting to everybody". Banaka rebuffs her by decrying the act of writing novels as 'deeply narcissistic' and not a means through which people come to understand themselves and others.

I remembered this passage incorrectly for the better part of a decade because I shelved the Aaron Asher translation and edition of the book on a book exchange in some other part of South America and have never been able to reference it. The cover, a photograph of a mirror on a table angling sunlight toward the other half of the same table, revealing a coffee cup, was a beautiful edition that apparently is only sold in the Southern Hemisphere and I've never wanted to own the garish Harper Collins Perennial edition of the book - so I never picked up a new copy until the month before I wrote this, which revealed how incorrectly I remembered it.

The following passage that Kundera did write and that I have now extricated from my memory by verifying it against the original text is an observation by Kundera that his taxi driver, who writes and fills "notebook after notebook" with his writing out of reaction to his insomnia, is not writing for anyone that he knows, not to be understood by friends or his family, but for a "public of unknown personas". This action is seen as tragic - we have no way of knowing if the taxi driver's writing is any good, and never having shared his writing (indeed we might think that he is writing so that these notebooks may only be read when he dies). It becomes an open question as to what end and why the taxi driver should even be writing, or for whom. If writing is performed for this unknown public, it is not possible to ever feel the value of the work--but the mere act of seeking to write so that this 'general public' might read what you have written is deeply narcissistic, per Kundera. This is a melifluous way of saying that art does not exist without a critic. Who on earth would care about who you are and your stories? Who would care enough to read them?

The way I remembered this passage smeared itself across my personal history with the following passage--in which Kundera recounts a ride with a taxi driver in Paris--and my own memory or interpretation of what Banaka says to Bibi. In my memories, Banaka is arrogant in his response, but Bibi comes off as bumbling herself, not really knowing what to say to start with. Maybe I was a misogynist at the time too; it takes a long time to unlearn the structures that bind us. I thought the point was that Bibi was mundane, and that she was wrong, that what her "experience inside" was meaningless and lacking in importance, and that no one would want to read it, just like no one would ever want to read what I had to write. So I didn't.

Kundera never really let himself be a critic - he was writing novels that acted as though they had criticism at their core, but his writing never actually pointed at himself, instead he held himself in such high regard as to think that his writing did not need criticism in order to be true. I, and so many other readers of his work have felt the same - his writing is awful and misogynistc, but he expertly removed himself from critique, somehow rendering his writing untouchable, and so early writers love it. Kundera doesn't argue that true novelists like Banaka are above the reproach of criticism - in fact all that separates them is a sense of aesthetic sensibility - , but the narcissism of writing without any consideration of who will read it among this undefined public constitutes instead a 'graphomania' - a belief that no matter the context, someone will read it. Who? Who on Earth?

It is this pair of passages which delayed for over a decade any inclination I had to write for anyone, either as a practice or otherwise. I was not narcissistic, you see - and I could not think of who would read what I have written. In the decades since first reading it, I stopped short of thinking that writing was for me anything more than a practice of remembering. I considered it an act more of coping, a method for navigating anxieties - writing for no one to be read by no one, and in many cases writing was so deeply personal to me I would find myself myself going back and scoring through pages of written text in the hopes that I could erase conclusions, revelations, unbounded truths that I was not yet equipped to handle, maybe because, as Andrea Long Chu writes in "Females", I actually only exist in response to what the world expects of me, maybe because I what I didn't want to conclude at the time was that I am a woman, and I was female, despite all insistence to the contrary at the time.

I don't know fully if my writing had a deep relationship with this obfuscation and fear of conclusion. Despite my writing in these years mostly being now boarded up behind the ink of redaction, I still came out. I prevented myself from writing on those fears. Part of the reason for it was a rejection of something I now consider mostly mundane, but yes, part of it was out of a fear that someone might read it - someone far off in time whose own conclusions about my writing would shape who I was as a person. How narcissistic! I thought I was writing for myself, but I was writing these deeply personal and redacted texts for who I expected I should be, which was a woman, again, despite all insistence through those blacked-out lines to the contrary.

I know better now - yes - much of the writing we do in notebooks trying to stay undistracted by a world begging so much for our attention as to see puerile will end up unread, reams of it were written under the expectation that they might, but maybe (hopefully, the sake of my younger fear) my handwriting isn't legible enough for this to happen, which I consider a blessing, because I was not narcissistic when I wrote them, and no one was supposed to read them, which is why I redacted the text I knew I needed to write, even though I policed my own language and even while I held back from ever becoming a writer because (among so many because) the idea that I was writing for no one in particular is merely graphomania. It's laughable, it makes sense, it doesn't.

Milan Kundera died on July 11th, 2023. I'm glad he is dead. I love his writing deeply, ignoring the fact of his searing lack of ability to properly process the concept of feminine identity as abstracted from the gaze of men, although I suppose there Chu agrees with him. I consider his writing to be of the greatest aesthetics, surpassing most of his contemporaries and my own. I think he was a weak ma, but not in the sense that men are pathetic for their weakness to vice as a tool for creativity, as Maggie Nelson sees them. Weak because I think his narcissism and his reflections upon it punctured the fabric of his identity as integral to all that he wrote. Many remember Nabokov for Pale Fire as a revelatory work with an unreliable narrator, Kundera was, and is, an unreliable author. I think Kundera did it best, I'm glad he's dead because I didn't understand what a person can do with a little narcissism and that little move cost me about nine to fifteen years depending on what we are talking about. Writing for me is or was an act of self-definition, both in the sense that what I have written defines me, but as well that what I chose not to write our of fear that someone might read it probably shaped just as much of the identity I now write from.

I'm resolved, in many ways, to write outside or through this graphomania. I wrote my notebooks fearful of who would read them. This was written in a notebook and will likely transform as I transcribe it (it did, I tell you now from the moment of transcription) into the format in which you read it. I am a narcissist. Who on earth would care what I have to say? Maybe you, because you've made it this far, you're already captive in the words I'm choosing, because I'm right in thinking someone would read them. I am a real writer, being poetic in the middle of my prose. You are a narcissist too, many of us are, we live in a domain and age of near continuous self-reflection-- it can all be documented because all of us believe someone will read it.

In a 2013 New Yorker article by Thomas Beller that I haven't read because it is stuck neatly behind a paywall, Beller says that it was a "radical cri de Coeur to claim 'we live in public'" in the opening moves of the internet. Now this is mundane, I think. Some of us have elevated this form of expression across the strewn digitalia of the internet's walled gardens to a form of aesthetic sensibility that Kundera wasn't familiar with. I do believe this, though I have never been able to employ narcissism so concentrated into 280 characters or two minute videos as to afford me the feedback from my environment necessary to elevate my own self-interest out of graphomania. Not the collective one, my own, the notebooks I have filled and have never shared, that I wrote for people I am afraid will know me when I die. My narcissism requires more words.

Maybe this is why it is manic, if attention can only tolerate concentrated aesthetics, I'll never made it, I always hit the character count, but I am still trying to be a writer, for the first time. I'm not going to ask why, I'm going to be a little narcissistic and think that what I write is something I can improve on, that what I am writing could be interesting to ... Well, not everybody. But some of you, because I disagree with Kundera, which is why I'm glad he is dead. Writing is a form of communication, because I'm trying to communicate an idea with you. I'm also glad Kundera's dead because he can't argue back, and I think he was too much a narcissist and a misogynist to have listened - he wrote in exactly the way necessary to feel removed of judgment and critism, and now he is in the real world, too. I don't hate him. Every story for the unknown public has value. Mine does too. Banaka could have withheld his arrogance to learn how to teach. Kundera could have explained to his taxi driver that his mania could be steered toward aesthetics. He didn't. A million people on the Internet should into a 'public of unknown personas.' Thousands listen. It doesn't mean anything. We're all narcissists. It's beautiful.

item.title: On healing - Kundera
item.description:
I think I've been going through a period of healing. The general sense I gather is that some of this is coming from a desire to incorporate more slowness into my life, a sense of living that allows me to stop and pay attention to my current surroundings, rather than those I am examining at some undetermined period of time in a distant future. Some of this has come in the form of a moralism with respect to how it is that we engage with one another as human beings; in a networked era, we believe we must communicate with everyone who can listen to us and that every opinion is equally important, but I'm not really convinced that this is a good way of being, because it requires us to think of everyone who we can interact with as a form of audience rather than a community.
Some of the healing that I've been engaging with is a particular kind of slowness that corresponds to trying to acknowledge who it is in my life that I actually care about and with whom I want to deepen my relationships. It turns out that the number of social media followers that you have nor the number of attempts that you've made to increase that number actually give you any moral or emotional well-being. As Ed Yong put it, you should cultivate an audience, not followers.
I suppose some of this writing is an attempt to return to those who have taken on the honor of signing up for this newsletter - So far it's been something that I only release one every sometimes, but I assure you that every time I write it, I do think about the importance of having written it and the importance of why I am sharing thoughts with the people who are receiving it in the first place. This is maybe where the moralism comes into play; a sort of pseudo-social attempt to get people to listen to what I have to say as though what I'm saying has any worth and it really doesn't. Backing off of that sort of self-deprecation is a parallel thought that keeps me considering that in fact I'm not trying to convince any one of you of anything at all but rather simply trying to communicate.
I think the present era does a really good job of making us believe that all of the things we say must be somehow important or relevant or a sort of commentary on the present era, and putting ourselves in the boundary of having to express ourselves in this way, I think is mostly just exhausting and takes away from our ability to interact with one another as equal human beings.
There is a section of Milan Kundera's Book of Laughter and Forgetting where he comments on a writer speaking with a fan who walks up to him in a diner and asks for advice about how she can get into writing. He asks her why it is that she thinks she should be writing. She responds that it's possible that some people might want to read what she has to say. The author sitting at the diner bench turns to her and says, "why would you think that you had anything important to say?" I think back on this quote often whenever I start to write, because it is a form of self-deprecation - Imposter syndrome for a writer made material as though to point out that there really is no point in writing in the first place and that you should really just pack it up and go home and not even try.
I don't really think this is what Kundera was attempting to convince people of and in the years since I first read that section of his novel, I've instead found myself thinking that maybe what he's saying is that you should ask yourself critically why it is that what you are writing about is something that you want people to read. I still don't really have an answer, but I think I've stopped getting in my own way in the search for one, instead allowing the words to flow and sort of drift into purposelessness as a form of expression that attempts to connect with other people. None of us really have anything important to say. That's not the point. While maybe the author in his novel is intended as a jaded old careerist who cannot understand why he himself has written up to that point. Even his writing can be unimportant, No matter his readership. So is mine. So is yours.
This contrasts with the sentiment I've been holding around the idea that social media is something valuable in terms of how it is that we articulate our thoughts to an audience. The difference between Ed Yong's description of what fans/followers are against an audience is the difference between trying to cultivate a mob of people who you want to listen to everything you have to say versus a group of people to whom you have something very specific to say. The latter version offers people agency and the former is really just a thinly veiled attempt to self-aggrandize.
The social media profiles that fascinate me the most are those with the incredible voices who have turned off comments on any of their posts - they take distance from the work that they are creating in such a way as to understand that those who choose to read what they are working on are not necessarily people they are trying to convert, but rather people with whom they are trying to converse. Another one of Ed Yong's comments comes to mind here. "Don't argue with strangers on the internet".
Other fragments of the reading that I've been doing lately have been from authors who are reconciling a shared narrative about accelerated, networked growth as a function of technological advancement, and then those who are attempting to remember what it means to be human in absentia of this supposed progress has brought us. This latter half are those who have left behind the purported advantages of an interconnected parasocial pseudo-presence and have instead found kindness in the smallness of the world they decide to surround themselves with - people who fell into deep burnout as a function of continuing to follow the ever accelerating machine, only to be spit out and to acknowledge that we as individuals have our own needs that exist outside of the system that attempts to use us for its own purposes.
As a result of this, I think some of the healing that I am taking on or attempting to steer myself toward is reacting to a desire not to put myself into the burnout I have witnessing people (mostly men) continue to obsess over. I have over and over incorporated the "grindset" attitude to my own work and come out with next to nothing, only to realize that what was most fruitful is to focus on the most important things with the highest amount of effort in the shortest possible amount of time in order to achieve it. This sort of effort is far more rewarding because oftentimes getting into the flow of this sort of work only requires knowing exactly how you want to approach it and then putting forth the effort to ensure that you actually do. I found that this is the sort of work that comes from the product of writing out what it is that I intend to do rather than simply reacting to what I think feels like the next most important thing.
This brings me to the lesson that I feel I've been learning more recently through this period of healing and that I hope others are starting to witness in themselves because I am one to believe that we are all conduits of the society that surrounds us: we already have everything we need.
No amount of algorithmically-directed consumption is going to teach us self-worth, nor will it be what informs us of what we within ourselves deem important. If media is used as the tool, it is possible for us to reflect on what we consume against what we know ourselves, but it is more likely to put us in service of further consumption - the conscientiousness required for us to ensure that we are the vehicles of our own intention is often outweighed by the intentions of the system that feed us the knowledge we believe is informing this perspective. 'Importance' is something we have to investigate within ourselves - a thing we inquire and unpack by virtue of focused, concentrated, attentive, and most importantly loving work. It does not require this work to be continuous, but rather simply focused and attentive.

I write this out of a desire to remind myself that much of my writing is about this question of importance, but that this importance does not require others to believe that what I deem as important need be what they themselves also see as such. It also means that writing anything at all and sharing it with the small constellation of people who have chosen to read what I write doesn't require me to hold what I have to say to such a high standard as to believe that what I am saying is necessarily important rather than just a conversation.

Writing these posts, however intermittent, is an attempt to connect in a way that doesn't feel so costly through a medium that feels more conciliatory and meaningful to me in particular. If I bring you along on the journey, then that's fine, and that's fantastic, and I'm glad this conversation can be something that we are all a part of - but it doesn't oblige me to consider what it is that I am saying as somehow important in the broader sense. I don't get to decide that for any of you. I can only decide the importance relative to my own scales.

So the healing I'm taking on is to remember that what I think is important is beautiful just because I think it's important, and that I don't need to necessarily find a group of people who also believe the same thing I do because I think that's mostly what's destroyed our ability to relate to one another. If you read this and you connect to it somehow, that's wonderful. And maybe that was the point of writing, but not necessarily out of a desire to change your mind.

Maybe this writing is a form of thanks for choosing to have received this in the first place, whether or not you believed that this writing would reach you. It's to say I'm glad that you think I have something worth saying. It's to say I am glad that you are participating in my healing with me. It's to say that just possibly we have been doing things in a way that destroys our ability to find common experience and instead has put us in a position of requiring ourselves to be enraged by the continuous onslaught of information that is at once irrelevant and unimportant to our ability to live balanced quotidian lives. It's not to say that some of the more important things won't somehow reach out and affect your life directly, and I know this. But finally it is to say that yes, I do believe I am glad that you are an audience to me.

-

item.title: A Canticle for the Mind's Eye
item.description:
Falling. It's hard to say if it is a dream because the falling is taking so long that the falling has become normal, and in the deep darkness of my descent it could have be mistaken for flying, I think.

My hands in the air play small resistance with passing but maybe that is a breeze. Maybe I'm not falling or flying. Maybe I am floating. Maybe I am not alive at all.

A pinprick is all I can see and it is why I suppose that I am falling, I turn this way and that way and that little point stay below me. I think it is below me. I think gravity is pulling me toward it. I don't know if gravity is actually pulling me toward it. I can't remember how I leaned what gravity is. So maybe it's not gravity. I don't know. But there is a pinprick of light and I can't remember how I learned about gravity.

I am not sure if I am afraid because I also can't remember ever being afraid before, or rather I'm realizing I don't think I remember anything at all and I think this scares me too but I also can't remember if this feeling is anything new, but my heart is in my chest (I think) and it is bump bump bumping faster than it was a moment ago before I was trying to figure out if I was afraid and my eyes are dry from the wind or the breeze and I'm cold on one side of my body from the wetness that just sprang across my skin. I don't know if I am falling and I don't know if I am afraid and I don't like not knowing anything and I don't know where I am.

I try to think about anything and there is a jumble of concepts like "mathematics" and "Hustvedt's unification constant" but I don't really remember who Hustvedt is or why I know about her how I know she is a woman or really what a woman is because I'm just falling and experiencing something I'm not sure I have felt before and that pinprick is the only thing I can see. I think it might be brighter. Good, at least my frame of reference is changing but what is a "frame of reference" and why am I hearing myself think so loudly when I can't hear anything else, so I shout and I can hear my voice more like a bark into nothing and I realize that my throat is so dry and I'm so thirsty, my eyes hurt too and I close them and the pinprick winks out.

Good. So I can close my eyes. I should again and it doesn't carry, it sounds like shouting into cotton but I can't remember how I know what cotton is. But I can close my eyes and the pinprick goes away, so maybe I can gather the noisy haze of my thoughts into something logical or at the least something I can steer like maybe Hustvedt's unification constant is something worth knowing and maybe cotton is important.

It's difficult in the noise of my heart beating faster and these concepts racing through me to make sense of what is more important than anything else. I know what a pinprick is and I know what a pin is and I know that Hustvedt's unification constant is the numerical limit at which the barrier to consciousness interacts with a quint momentarily cooled to 0 degrees Kelvin, where consciousness is denoted by the bitflip of states within which incoming information can be processed by an extant system across the boundaries of connected interstitial state engines all reacting to the same manifold of inputs at a predictive rate constituting processor-type memory within the system. A system is a set of interacting state engines within which the flow of motivating forces inform local transformations between states for each component interacting in relation to another, and when I open my eyes I can see that the pinprick is definitely a little bit brighter but when I close my eyes I can't see it, so maybe when I close my eyes it's just not real, as though locally there's some transformation of reality that collapses into existence when I open my eyes.

I keep my eyes closed for a while, which eventually feels a bit better because I am not wondering about the pinprick and I'm done thinking about why I know what Hustvedt's constant is, so I tell myself I'll just keep them closed for a while longer. It's a bit nicer in the darkness honestly and thinking about whether or not I could see the pinprick has meant I'm not dealing with all the racing thoughts that were trying to make sense of themselves but I'm still pretty thirsty and that's making my heart beat a little faster but maybe I can just not think about that. Can I remember anything other than concepts? It doesn't really seem that's the case but I'm counting out the numbers of Pi pretty far and I seem to know a fair number of primes and that's calming so I'm just counting those in my head as well since I seem to know a lot of them.

I've been here a long time, I realize. I don't know how long I've been here but I am starting to wonder if maybe I've just been falling for so long that I don't really remember when I was first falling and if I've already thought all of this any number of times, it's just been so long since I last thought all of it that I can't remember. This, again, scares me but that can't possibly true because I can't possibly have been thirsty for this long and it's a small gnaw at my stomach that makes me think I maybe haven't been falling for that long because someone who has been falling for a long time would probably me a lot hungrier and a lot thirstier, and I open my eyes to ponder this and oh god the pinprick is brighter but I can see what it is a little better now and it looks like a little more than just a pinprick, it has a shape.

But there's nothing else here for me to look at so I'm getting curious about it and allowing myself to feel the fear of looking at it and trying to figure out what's coming, and I realize that maybe it's something I can just barely make out, it's a shape I can recognize but oh god its an eye, just barely big enough for me to see it. I realize maybe I'm moving toward it and it's actually maybe even getting bigger as I look at it, but it's just this giant unblinking eye staring back at me in the middle of all this blackness where I can't even tell what direction I'm falling in.

item.title: On a religion made of rubber and salt
item.description:
After several years of covering running, I began running in 2019.

In the years leading to the present that love has fallen apart and come back together several times, as many religions do. My faith in movement has been shaken, dusted off, and rooted more firmly by the miles that sew it together.

These have been the years where running has migrated from intrigue, to mental health tool, to injury, to fatigue, to an imperative and finally into a form of freedom. This transition had to do with the pandemic and with changing states of self, but it also had to do with realizing there was something more in the staccato of other people's footfalls that I'd been chasing beyond merely getting to know other athletes - a sort of transcendental state that I'd grown used to watching people fall into. I started chasing that state in myself.

When I say 'covering running,' I'm describing the five preceding years to 2019 following running subculture, mostly by bicycle with cameras in the basket, primarily following some of the more critically unhinged in the community - people who throw themselves into the moving traffic of a moving city, people who run hundreds of miles across humid states in the heat of summer. People whose entire lives (at least for the period of time that I had come to know them) were about how to get out over the next stretch of miles.

I have made lasting friendships in this coverage and many of these people have ended up with their accolades; first woman and second place overall in the Last Annual Vol State 500k (thank you @rhodasmoker), a trice of top ten women marathon (I see you @jmackattack, @caitlinphillips, @wicked.la), several magazine covers (hello @iamlshauntay, @samuel4nderson), inspirations that echo in the people they meet (love and more love for @matthewlukemeyer) and finally, those who had brought me to the very front of it all from the beginning (unending appreciation for @orchardstreetrunners for this).

But when I really started running, the people who showed me why I should run are people I still run with, and are the people with whom I will run to the ends of the earth - the sort of people whose skin is dusty with the slow movement of the sun across countless days, and those who chase its progress beyond the horizon under a blanket of stars until it returns the next morning. These are friends with whom I have covered countless thousands of miles. People with whom I have found religion. People who are willing to take on the steel rush of semi trucks on empty tarmac in a hundred deserts. People I can't tag, for a variety of reasons, but who all of you know.

This does not toss aside those who showed me that there is something here to chase; I would not have gotten here without them--but it does reveal the cornucopic spectra of what people find in hammering out distance. Some of us want the speed. Some of us want the distance. All of us want the free movement of the air in our lungs, and those of us who want the deserts keep finding one another out there in its emptiness, over and over.

This is what has brought me here, at least. A religion of sorts, cobbled together with shoelaces, maltodextrin, laughter, and caloric deficits. A religion I'll keep practicing because it's something holier than needing to explain it away, a religion I keep close to me because a relationship with this sort of faith in oneself doesn't require explaining to others, because those who understand already understand. If you know, you really do know.

So I'll see all of you out there sometime soon

-

item.title: On intention
item.description:
More intention, or rather, the subject of the understanding needfully described as intention.

We are more than the sum of our parts - I expect that this is true, and the investigation intot he aspects of the self that we use to define this sort of commitment to self-discovery often seem to forget that the narrative of exploration is rooted most in the exploration of a vast inner landscape far outstripping our ability to explore it.

When we contend with this being true, we also account for the fact that in our own definitions or those that we use to articulate a pain of being (often referred to as ennui) we are placing ourselves on an axis of between the conscious and the unconscious and necessarily forcing ourselves to reconcile them; the felt sense of the body when there is something "wrong" contrasted with the centers of logic we use to sense_make_ of the experience equally conspire often to be at odds.

It's for this reason that somatic work has a particular importance that outweighs the requirement to 'make sense' of things rather than simply 'having your senses at your disposal' (Gregori 2004) in order to better navigate the complexity of our animalistic sensations and the higher-order explanations we have for intellect (if, at any juncture, defined by the intersection of a predator and its prey and the race conditions that lead to preparedness for victory on either side). Consciousness is thus an artifact of extrapolation and its tangential importance to the experience of responding to one's conditions.

This is why I generally reject the notion of a 'trauma-informed practice' because the very experience of being even a semi-conscious creature is to have built a network of responses to one's conditions and to have built a foundation on these responses. 'Trauma' negatively ascribes intention to mere 'experience' specifically in order to impose an axis between positions of empowerment and disempowerment - while it's a useful notion in order to better understand this axis, it's only as useful as being 'informed' actually results in progress rather than recalcitrant possession of an inescapable victimhood rejecting the notion of this very same progress.

I part with the notion of examining collective 'trauma' short of requiring oneself instead to 'start with trauma' in order to evaluate ways of progressing past its influence; if one is unable to do so, one is doomed not to resolve a sense of agency leading out of the teleological mire. Progressivism of this sort feels at best to root itself in this lack of agency, placing the burden of action entirely on those that cause the trauma without taking a declarative stance on arbitrating inaction on the part of those with the power differential. Those with the will to overcome an otherwise unconditional surrender to external influence are those who can overcome this sort of teleology; while it may be more difficult, it is nonetheless important to work the fields so that our children can work the shops, so that their children can make art: conditions of liberation are a product of painstaking commitment to action, not throwing one's hands up in the face of the effort needed.

One exception to this (or rather one important step on the journey toward embodying agency) is to ensure that at the least the history preceding one's liberty to progress is made legible and interpretable - its erasure constitutes a doubling back in rejection of accountability. It is possible to reconcile the concept of situational advantage and its lapses with a doxa of agency and an overall increase in degrees of possibility experienced by people from radically different backgrounds.

This reconciliation is not, however, one of meritocracy as the more rationally-minded might clai, Any truly 'meritocratic' function requires a deep removal of any and all biases dwelling in orbit around a given decision. (Of course, if you don't believe that these biases exist... You have a completely different problem).

Finding oneself at odds with the liberal imperative of increasing the index of possibility through a patchwork of non-conciliatory actions such as access programs was a good first step in experimentation, but these efforts lead to a dead-end when there is no conscientious notion of what it means to restructure the system that causes something like 'inequity' to arise in the first place. The importance of understanding that the experiences leading toward something as mundane as a name excluding you from candidacy for work, for example, is an important acknowledgment, because it is then blithely transparent to anyone executing on negative tendencies to assume much of one's identity leaves bare that the decision was not made on merit but rather bias; this specific example does the best to articulate where merit and bias intersect due specifically to the intermediate relationship between the two resulting in one informing the other.

-

item.title: On Contentment
item.description:
Contentment can be such an odd companion to uncertainty.

I think most what has made me feel confused by contentment is particular to those moments where I feel as though I need to escape it - where everything in my life feels balanced and I have what I need, where I feel as though for some reason I can't quite get down to the math on what it is that I want.

It's not the first time that this sort of feeling has arisen, of course, there's a Restlessness in being a part of something foundational--a reaction to the relatively mundane nature of contentment that can feel like a requirement to escape it. I can't quite suss out what part of that process is something that I need to fear or something that I feel an imperative to respond to, because at the end of the day the real frustration I feel comes from the knowledge that I have everything I'm looking for and still seem to be looking for more. As such, is it dissatisfaction? Is the notion that one has found contentment a reaction to the principle of having to be 'happy'? What is the difference between contentment and happiness?

I'm not convinced that they are the same thing - contentment is a general sensation that reaches toward the mundane, while happiness is a punctuation within that emotion, a contentment as a baseline and a happiness as a peak that exists within the landscape that exists atop it.

And yet, contentment is something that we can revel in, it is the partner who comes home after a work day to make dinner with you, who sits on the couch to work while you paint in the adjoining room. Contentment is neatly the mundane, but it is no less beautiful for this being true.

For if contentment is something that we have to react to toward the negative, it is just as much a sensation of not knowing what to do once we have what we are looking for, as though the taboo of having to adjust entirely to one's desire is a requirement. I'm not so certain that it is. When I break this down to an analysis of my own contentment, it's an experiment in assuming that I actually do know what I want.

I don't. This is the biggest challenge - I have a tendency to allow this to drift from me constantly, and because of this it's something that I feel I needed to more consciously explore because it keeps reacting to my presence and my ability to materialize the desires I have. The constant issue that comes with this is that materializing one's desires requires that we understand what those desires are motivated by, and to not have done the work to better understand what these are is specifically to doom oneself to the possibility of having to react, wholly, to whatever presents itself. That's not a way to live, because it never results in anything conscious.

I can't say that I necessarily understand my subconscious, either. I've been in conversation with it for years, attempting to understand what I value and what it is that I want to do with that estimation, but the wires that lead me toward my own systems of belief are somewhat out of reach for me conscious analysis without some sort of sincere contact witht hat subconscious. For a while I was doing this through the practice of therapy, but I've allowed that to take up mless presence in my life as I seek contentment - meaning that the general notion I'm forced to contend with is actually the realtively mundane existence that I experience in the presence of all the things that I've been looking for. I don't necessarily feel particularly pressed to have to evolve my conditions, if nothing else I need the reality of my convictions through the lens of my efforts, and I can see where it is that these things fall off.

The conversation with my subconscious notwithstanding, I can see that there's a notion of small sadness that accompanies seeing how I've let this life lead me rather than doing the reverse, the sentiment that I've been pushing myself to accommodate the reality that presents itself to me and to react to these opportunities as though they are something that I'm required to take on, but I can't make myself do that forever, because there is a distinct dissatisfaction with not doing what I know I want to be doing in the mean time, a fear that I've lost touch with what it is that I really care about.

Some of this can be traversed through consistent conversation with one or another therapeutic method or through sincere contemplation, but I only catch whispers of the goal. I hear things that tell me I care much more about things that have to do with moving my body and the stories that this inspires than I do with the requirement to embroil myself further into stories that need not expand themselves into the world, a notion of social imperative that is as risky as it is important--but I can't conceive of taking on this imperative without some due consideration for what it is that I actually want.

Most recently there has been the voice inside that says I 'want to be one of the greats' - fed by the notion that if one wants to be one of the greats, one must believe they deserve to be one of the greats. There is quantifiable and measured hubristic negligence in having to take on this notion, a necessity to push aside some partial fear that hubris will lead to downfall when in truth the consideration of one's own hubris can be placed in reflection to an environment that otherwise believes in our merit or at the least in our permission to believe in ourselves.

Belief is a part of this moral architecture that holds this imperative in place, where hubris can cause us to seek out that which might be costly and risky, belief is that which motivates us toward the otherwise illogical. To believe in oneself is to believe fully that the irrational parts of the self that make up the unconscious (depending, of course, on one's disposition) have some greater notion of self than the conscious parts that are forced to react to its motivations. A 'gut feeling' is a notion of understanding what we know for sure. We only get a few things to really care about, and it is our duty to respond when we better understand what it is that motivates us and what we need to do in order to see out a reaction to that inner truth.

A problem that is presented to use in this search, of course, is that the problem doesn't leap out at us from the page. We don't necessarily write and write and write each day expecting that we are going to come to some revelation, if anything this revelation comes from a steady and static reaction to the mundane that forces us to break patterns and rto realign ourselves with what matters. For instance, my understanding that there is something important in running could be logically discerned, but some of it is not logical, it is a part of the logiciel that comes with being in the situation that make me feel the most congruence with my environment, a tendency toward respecting something much larger than me.

I like to believe that this is what I'm chasing, some abundant understanding of a plan that I'm fabricating in the back of my mind, but it's just a part of the execution, a fragment that I'm constantly seeking to outcompete with the logical (and verbose) parts of who I am. The dialogue between me and that subroutine is constant, and what I'm forced to do out of respect for the less verbal and far more emotional parts of myself is to allow its reactions to carry the same weight as the logical conclusions I am capable of interpreting through the tried method of continuous self-application. Discernment is a process by which we take the information in front of us and attempt to better understand the whole - a blind mouse doing it's best to visualize the elephant.

Writing this of course does not bring some sort of grand conclusion to my eyes or mind, it's more of the same, a traversal of one's own continuous reaction to the Truth of existence. So while it's easy to be disappointed, it's equally important to ask oneself within the realm of possibility whether or not the opportunities that we are presented with are things that we know for sure we want to react to. Consciousness is a discernment of reality. Unconsciousness is our experience of it. A rationalist view of reality is to misunderstand that we 'create' reality only within the confined of that which we seek to interpret, but reality does not care about us, and that's okay.

While the question continues to orbit; what do I really want, what do I want it to look like, the reality of the notion refuses to fall short of answering the question and is almost certain to result in the conclusions to which we feel most aligned so long as we are respectful of our unconscious. This is not to say that we are required to take on opportunity, but rather that our reactions to opportunity require a sort of discernment that acknowledges that which we are capable of and that which we truly desire, and reconciles these two in order to find that which offers us the best conditions for both contentment and joy.

All the while I understand the importance of hardship, even of uncertainty, and the edge conditions that unfold from a requirement to exist at the edges of disturbance - Tsing's notion of salvage is what most speaks to this reality-breaking form of existence, an exploitation of an extant imbalance that allows us to exist in a state of constant adaptation that brings with it its own form of liminal joy. But this is an idealization because hardship as a requirement of joy is a self-defeating construct that we can use to force one another into conditions of negligence and disuse - and we as a species and as a consciousness deserve more than this.

It then becomes important to question whether or not in the more content periods it is more or less likely that we can believe in the adjacent possible - as a product of our desire to depart austere conditions we dream of better outcomes for ourselves, and this often becomes the motivator for assuring the action potential accrues sufficiently so to overcome conditions and strike out for more and better in oneself. I'm not convinced, however, that it is a requirement, because I believe that some of the greatest minds lived otherwise mundane existences and it was (is) the turmoil they experienced within themselves at a disagreement with reality over its basic functions that produced the conditions of salvage inspiring an exploration of the adjacent possible. Our ability to formulate turmoil within ourselves is thus a gift, a tool that we can use to motivate ourselves in exploring new local minima in the punctuated equilibrium of how we comprehend existence on both conscious and unconscious levels.

Creating conditions for contentment then maybe affords us the ability to think at grander scales abject of our experience on the local scale - if our needs are met, we are able to think outside of ourselves and evaluate problems that exist on a superorganismal scale. This being the case, contentment and the punctuated joy of existing are not somehow at a disagreement with the idea of progress - if anything they are foundational for thinking at larger scales, because the scope of one's area of effect is a product of how much influence someone has over their surroundings not through power, but through the collaborative tendency to participate in a collective reasoning that supercedes the self-interested individual.

A requirement of existing at scale and thriving withing one's 'potential' is then to bring the collective mission to a local stasis in as many environments as possible while combatting the likelihood of this meaning that self-same hubris results in conditions that decrease the degrees of opportunity available to others. If the tendency of the universe is to expand, this means that degrees of latitude are growing at a constant rate, the same can be both true and tried for.

The conclusion is then that we can materialize conditions of local contentment for ourselves, and that they can be foundational for us to seek out new and higher states. A state of contentment is a local minimus from which we are able to seek out the adjacent possible, and it's not a requirement to suffer in order to push oneself into such a state, because we are capable of considering a collective condition as equally important to that of our experience at the local scale. It means that we as individuals can take on an imperative to stabilize our condition in order to encourage the stabilization of others - and that this offers meaningful conditions within which we can continue to work collectively toward the betterment and growth of the human project. I remain somewhat convinced of this--held loosely, of course, as with any belief--but I believe fully in the importance of such a notion, because thinking this way seems to create the best conditions under which what is possible becomes less negligible, and minimizes reactionary belief that seeks only to escape locally detrimental conditions.

item.title: Every day is resistance
item.description:
Every day is some sort of resistance. I just don't really know to what, and I'm conscious of what it means for me to require it.

It could be that in times like this there is a sensation of resistance that follows us, because we see the relative normalcy of whatever it is that we have had to call a life and to see it disrupted is to seek out the logic of its passage from our attention. It's a relatively normal reaction, I realize - to struggle along in your current version of the present and to feel that you should somehow remain in this state, because while it is a struggle, at least it's yours, at the least this struggle is something that you can hold onto in the otherwise crashing and raging flood of change that continuously surrounds our ability to process the present.

It could be that the kind of resistance we have been told to employ is the sort that aims squarely at our expectations of safety rather than the sensation of positive change--I can't say that we expect our present to return to some idyll, but I do know that one core difference between people is the hope for something better against the expectation that things were at some point in the past better in their own right. This latter point feels like a particular crux periculi - when we seek out an idyll in the past, we are cursed never to meet it. The future is far more possible. A hope to make the future more like the past is a hope to return to something that doesn't exist, and indeed likely something that didn't exist in the first place.

My expectation is that this sends a message of hope - we might recognize that there is something far more valuable in seeking out the sort of unity and participation in a joint outcome far outweighing any concept of expectation. When we ask AI what is one thing that humanity could change about its nature in order to inspire forward social progress and it says empathy but somehow the default mode of a collective humanity is to be so fearful of shared power as to believe that this is something of which we aren't capable, something that we appear unable to comprehend the requirements to achieve, nor something that seems so dubiously out of reach due to the amount of social progress required in order to make it happen.

I say this, and I'm aware it's happened before in history, but that the unifying action that made it all possible was central control - there's no time in history where harmony was achieved by equanimity across all classes. There has always been some sort of hard or soft power balance that kept exploitation in check - and this indeed reveals exactly that which causes the mission of unity to fall apart before it is ever seen as achievable. Any wilfully democratic systems seems to fall apart at the moment that there is the affordance for anyone in the system to seize control of it.

This is nothing new, of course - it's something that I can appreciate having been known and part of the reason that many economic and governing systems are built around the principle of oscillating balance, in addition to the same reason that technologists want to build trust-minimized systems, but the former is slow and does not react well to change while the latter handwaves away any requirement to have a system of appeals to justice when a system is revealed to have erred. Neither of these facts negate the importance of figuring out a solution so that there is the ability to do the most important part: coordinate.

Coordination failure is at the root of any time there is deviation from the core principle, and this is truly what most gets in the way of maintaining a self-regulating system. If there is no affordance for a system of maintenance to be put in place, then there is no way to let go of the system once you have pushed it out into the world, and it will always require some form or other of persistent regulatory body that ensures it keeps going. In fact, more than likely, these systems will be exploited specifically by those who have become chained to it because the desire to create a system of liberty and equanimity was not intended to be a system that would also continuously require stewardship by those who create it.

This is central to the problem of coordination systems, particularly those that orient toward its financialization. What has always interested me is not how you pay people to do work, but how you encourage them to work together in the first place - and when we look back through history, it becomes apparent what the most effective systems have been. Great works such as those created by everyone from the Egyptian pharaohs to the Manhattan project dictate that what is most important is to orient a public toward a common goal. With the pharaohs it was the worship of their would-be living gods, with Roosevelt's Civil Conservation Corps it was the creation of a new and better United States with the preservation of its natural beauty as the jewel in its crown, with the Manhattan project it was the urgent requirement to do what was necessary to respond to the fear that someone might find out how to make the bomb first - that someone might hold the bigger stick before anyone else.

In any of these cases, the common goal is the unifying force, but it is never what keeps people working together. Whether the goal is worship, greatness, or fear - the regulatory function that many lean upon is the requirement to either oblige people to the work (mandatory stewardship) or to put in place a system of reward for the work done. Not often mentioned in the face of that which created the Great Pyramids was Egypt's burgeoning middle class those who would spend a portion of their year working on Great Works for the pharaohs in power and be recompensed for this work with their needs being met (not to mention the slaves who were obliged to this work). Nor is it brought up often enough that the regulatory function in place for the Manhattan project was a more global fear of someone else building the bomb, while the more immediate function that inspired those scientists to take part in executing one the greatest human achievements were the parties that took place on that mesa in Santa Fe every weekend.

Coordination requires the same balance of work and recompense that we expect out of the ability to lead stable lives - it is as important to work the fields as it is to sit back and admire the work that has been done, and it is as important to reap a harvest as it is to eat of what you have harvested. This is the root of abundance mindsets in their own right, to understand that the relationship between hard work is the reward of not having to work for periods of time - but there is also the meaningful realization that this is not true of those who fully devoted themselves to the act of creating great things - many of these people work(ed) tirelessly and at a gross personal cost because the goal the work at hand is to create something necessary. We see this in any genre of goal-making and indeed raise the mention of those so devoted, those who spend the hours that many of us would allocate to rest to the tireless pursuit of obligation, or to 'calling'.

I don't know where the thought leads, then, to consider that what unifies people is on the one level ideological belief, but on the other is the requirement by any one person that they lead a life of self benefit. I see polarization where the centrality of one's attention lies - the belief in the scope of where it is that we should be paying attention and those who should benefit most from the joint effort made

I'm trying to get my mind back into a place where I'm not completely at the point of doom and gloom - mostly because I'm not feeling out what it is that I should be doing and instead am feeling as though I don't really have the motivation to continue on with the work that we have been doing. I feel left behind, and I want to go to school, I want to move on with my life. It's not necessarily that I think what I have to do with my time is something bigger and better, I'm just not enthused by the state of things and more than anything I feel as though I'm watching the world around me fall apart in a way that doesn't really make me feel as though I have to give it much attention.

If what I'm really hoping to see is something substantial, my stronger sense is that I have to work within my constraints and I have to build of myself something that I can consider to be important, but only to me. something that I know I can look back on and be proud of. It could be that what I have to do with this is conceive of a framework of some sort for how it is that we build social structures, because I don't think that people have put enough work into defininig these particular parts of what it takes to make people work together.

This is why I'm considering the likleihood of there being something more interesting at the root of all the things that we know we'll see coming ahead. I don't want to be the sort who isoing to believe that what we're going to see is a full collapse - there are some parts of it that I do think are actually good and I think that we'll see something positive come from it, but it really does feel like the cresting of a wave, the sort of things that when looked back on largely benefitted us.

So what do we do withthis knowledge, how to we cause it to cohere more effectively, and what do we do once we have sought this out?1 And who knows, there's something to the way that people assume they have to

Letter to Tom 250204

A theory of friendship is one of how friendships end, what patterns emerge in a life of growing close with people.

  1. I used to care about my own thoughts, I used to explore ideas as though they were my lifeblood - none of that seems to matter anymore because I am not surrounded by people who hold that same thirst for knowledge. If anything, I feel surrounded by people who want to close themselves off from the world and who feel fearful. ↩

item.title: Bread at Grand Army Plaza (poem)
item.description:
Someone dumped several loaves worth of bread
Across Grand army Plaza and
Even though it was winter
I couldn't really make sense
Of why there were no pigeons

Stray
What is left of me across the same space
So that in knowing
I could have somehow left part of myself behind
For you to consume

--

I wish those were mountains
I could see just beyond the tree line
In Prospect Park
In the middle of the winter
When clouds choose to be dense enough
That we can't see through them
And we can pretend that they are landscaped instead

We can pretend that there are things far away
The cover higher ground
Over more distance
And that they're an option to climb

Buy me time with
The way you speak to me
Susurrations of that Horizon
Falling off with the curvature of the earth

Buy me time with
The way you have chosen to show yourself
On the Advent of sunset
When it is coldest
And when when my heart feels the most broken

Buy me time with
The mountains that choose to make themselves
Of the densest clouds
The carry snow for this part
Of the year

Buy me time
With sunlight that scrapes
The bottom of a cloud bank

I will not break
Against the bulkhead
Of that optimism
Nor will I allow myself
To be eaten alive by
A Sun never rising again

And I will be shaking leaves in the wind,
Remembering the park benches I could have slept on
Where the sun sets I'd failed to capture

Buy me time with the vastness of your love
With countenance is a form of lullaby
Of course I haven't swallowed the Sun, My son

--

How do I prevent you
From feeling as though
You have become invisible

How do I fill your days with
Pride and
The poetry of other people's smiles

How do I find the space
To acknowledge that you
Have made yourself bigger
All the while
Finding yourself
More comfortable in the frame
That you have been offered

Your invisibility
Rehoboam
I have taken you home in my teeth
And so you'll dissolve with time

-

item.title: What is Quantum Computing?
item.description:
What is Quantum Computing?

In the complicated sense, quantum computing is a system of computation that takes advantage of relativistic physics to drastically increase the processing power of computers. In a simpler sense, quantum computers are several times faster than their predecessors, and importantly that when saying they are several times faster, it's by orders of magnitude. A quantum computer can process information that would take a normal computer several hundred years in just a few hours.

The implications is boggling, because that last sentence almost doesn't make sense. There's a law in computing (Moore's Law) that describes the accelerated growth of compute, also known as 'processing power'. In general, it had predicted the the speed of computation to increase substantially based on the silicon chips that had existed before, but quantum computing speed is essentially unprecedented to anyone other than those who literally work in the field of quantum computing.

What was the breakthrough that happened this week?

Historically, any time you have a massive increase in computing ability, you also have a required increase in the energy needed in order to use that processing power; faster processing speed means more things happening, and more things happening means more energy in the system. While breakthroughs in quantum computing over the last 15 years were astounding, they were generally tucked away as the success of energy-intensive laboratories at universities or the research division of companies. Recent historical quantum computers have been described as near-holy copper and glass artifacts extending several floors up into laboratories - not anything that could be described as accessible to the public.

This week, however, Google gave notice of progress on their quantum solution, a chip known as 'Willow'. Willow proclaims to be 10^42 times more powerful than traditional silicon chips and is expected to be significantly more energy efficient, although precise comparative data on energy consumption has not been disclosed.

What this means is that Google has essentially transformed the trajectory of Moore's Law into a vertical spike. If, with Willow, Google has made progress toward what is known as 'practical quantum computing' (which often implies more stable and efficient quantum processing), then quantum computing could eventually become a consumer-accessible product — something that those with the resources might one day be able to purchase. While this is unlikely to happen in the immediate future, it significantly reduces the technological and energy-related barriers required to meet the processing demands of the chip.

What does it matter to Crypto? How is Crypto protected today?

While this is a significant achievement in the progress of computation, it makes so many things possible that it's important to examine and explore the effects it has on many other industries. In particular, it has implications for what happens to encryption.

In general, encryption is a technology based on code-breaking. It takes normal information and obfuscates, or 'encrypts' it using key information so that only a key holder can unlock it and understand the original contents. The point here is that the 'security' of encryption is mostly based on the time it would take to break a code - where 'breaking' a code essentially means 'trying things until you get the answer'.

Encryption helps you guarantee that what you are looking at is the thing you intend to look at: if you know that you were sent information from only the person you intended to receive it from (even if it's just yourself), you know you are receiving or viewing the same information that was input. If you know no one else could affect that information in any way, this also guarantees that the information can't be tampered with. These two points combine to how crypto benefits from and is built around encryption.

Crypto benefits from this on the principle that financial applications depend on an "agreed upon constant for unit value", or the idea that you can trust that your money is actually your money. Crypto was created because it turns out that if you trust a third party (banks) to hold your money and you don't retain control of what is done with it, they can go off and do things with it themselves. This is a component of what led to the 2008 financial crisis.

Crypto itself is protected by encryption standards, the "time it takes to break a code and reveal information" as a safeguard for showing that the money you own is tied to a set of keys providing the evidence that the money is only yours and that you are the only person who can use it. Most of crypto is protected by SHA256 encoding, which would take 12 "unvigintillion" years to break (that's 1.27 with 67 zeroes after it). This means that with modern computation methods it is practically impossible to reverse a 'hash' (the encoding) in order to get the original result.

It's this encoding that allows people to 'own' crypto - you can feel very certain that you are the only owner of information on the basis that you are the only person in control of the hash that secures your currency.

Where quantum computing matters to crypto is in what it offers as an accelerant for processing power. Even though the 1.27x10^67 year limit is an inconceivably large number for 'breaking' SHA256, if you have a computational system that can increase computational efficiency by 10^42 over traditional silicon chips, then it now only takes 1.27*10^25 years to break.

Without getting into the numbers, what this means is that you go from traditional silicon being able to break crypto's encoding in 10^52 times more time than the age of the universe to quantum computing being able to break it in 10^14 times the age of the universe. That is a drastic improvement in computation; it means that Willow would take [data] less time to do the work.

Roughly speaking, it means that while yes, Willow can drastically increase the speed at which crypto could be broken, it would still take several times the age of the universe to do it. That is a drastic improvement in computation; it means that Willow would take [data] less time to do the work, but at this end of the calculation, the time needed (orders of magnitude older than the age of the universe), there's almost no reason to deploy Willow on this technology in a way that could make tractable progress. It would simply still take too long.

  • Could new Quantum Crypto emerge?

It could--there are projects working on this, remarkably--but it's not a real threat.. At least, not until Willow or some other even better technology figures out how to get the time needed to break down the encoding down to an order of time that actually means something to humans.

Humans have only been around for the last fraction of a millisecond that the universe has existed. Until Google can come up with something that can break encoding in a way that makes it a problem that we can worry about on our timescale (rather than the timescale of 'the age of the universe' then crypto will have to worry.

item.title: Passion does not require meaning
item.description:
Passion does not require meaning.

At least, not directly. The importance of being able to do great things with the intent to resolve them into action only requires a directed amount of energy and the direction in which it is delivered. Passion then only requires care, the ability to direct this energy with a level of care that comes from a requirement to commit to resolution. Meaning is something altogether different, something that comes from a different source. Connecting the two is important, but they don't need to come from the same thing.

I'd always puzzled over this fact. The reason is that I care way too much, but then I start feeling a deep incongruence between the amount that I care and the amount of meaning that I derived from the work - and when we lose meaning (one of the most profound of the human afflictions) there is no coming back from having set up the wrong logic on why to continue on with what we're attempting to set ourselves in motion to do.

Meaning is altogether a different set of emotions from passion - it encompasses the reasons we do what it is we set ourselves in motion to do. Meaning is crucial to knowing why you are doing something in the long term - meaning is the motivator that keeps a person going when all else seems too difficult to proceed with. It's all too easy to conflate meaning with passion because they do rhyme very well - they are emotional cousins.

However, conflating them too much is a recipe for burning out, especially when a passionate person places too much care into the work they are doing and their energy expenditure outweighs the logic behind the approach. The reason that passion is also an emotion that fits in the realm of love is because passion is meaningless - it lacks definition and is simply an engine that is running in the direction of some corporeal motivation for connection, but meaning is not necessary to this.

The expression to a loved one that they give your life meaning is usually incorrect; a lover does not offer meaning, they offer connection, the meaning is derived from this connection attaching itself to the importance of that connection to your personal goals. Meaning is wholly in the realm of the personal, internal emotions. When we connect it too much to something external, we are offering these external things the power over our ability to survive, and this is not sustainable, in fact it is dangerous to do so. Meaning requires contemplation. Passion does not, in many cases it is automatic.

Passion is an emotion of the present, by contrast - it is something that arrives from a compulsion. It's for this reason that when people have told me that they assume I am passionate about the things I am doing, I have conflated their words with the search for meaning - I am not thinking in the present when I retort that I am not. I am removing the importance of the passion in the moment in which it is being experienced. Other people, in this moment, are right. To have passion is only to have directed energy and care toward something in order to see action take place.

There's an important implication here: passion without meaning in the long term is not sustainable. It is possible to use passion as its own motivator, as something that accelerates our actions into more vigorous attention and completion, but in the long term those actions will need to be paired with some sort of meaning in order to see out their impact on the larger arc of our lives. Meaning, in this case, is the reason we do something, and passion is how we ensure that we can keep doing so.

Passion without having searched for the meaning behind the actions - whether connected or not - becomes a drain. I mentioned above - passion is energy directed with care toward an outcome. Energy requires resources. If we are not being replenished in the actions that we are taking because they are not leading toward something, finding the energy to keep going becomes immensely difficult.

Additionally, meaning found in those things that aren't related to who we are as people and what motivates us more widely to keep going is a careful balance. Meaning is not monolithic, ideally it is a constellation of aggregated sources. It's important that these sources are both inside and outside of the self; those things toward from which we derive meaning must have as much to do with who we are as people as they are important to missions that exist outside of our own area of effect. Meaning is the source from which we can draw the energy to keep going when passion has us in motion.

Meaning is specifically not something that need be related to the actions motivated by passion. It is possible to do something with immense passion because it serves a meaning that exists outside the realm of direct effect; it is possible to work a job passionately because you want to provide for your family. They do not require a direct connection between one another.

This is how we do hard things that don't have meaning. Meaning is found from wherever the action meets what is most important to us. This is why so much work can cause a moral panic - when we place too much importance on the actions taking place as those from which we are meant to derive meaning, we often find that the actions themselves can remain quite empty. Sometimes the work that we are doing isn't necessarily meaningful. Meaning is elsewhere. Meaning is bigger than the passion with which we perform our actions

Finding the capability to hold on to this truth while we do work gives us the motivation to keep going: it is possible to find meaning outside of your work, and to use that meaning to motivate the passion with which you do it. This way, even when the work becomes something that drains you, meaning can be something larger, something more removed. If meaning and passion are connected, that's great - but it's not often the case. I'd even argue that it's dangerous to always try to pair the two. Searching for meaning requires energy as well, and often working with passion requires so much of our energy that if we are simultaneously attempting to fork what little energy we have toward these two intensive actions, it is costly, and specifically costly in ways that lead toward moral and energetic panic.

The reason I share this is because I have fallen into this trap so many times in my life, and it's often what starts to close the door on the reasons I keep going. I need my work to be important to me, but it's equally imperative that I explore that importance. It makes sense to search for meaning in the work that you are doing, but it also matters that you take care of yourself when you do. You can't and shouldn't do things entirely to the benefit of external sources, because your work will never love you back, and most of the energy you have available for love should be spent on the things that will. These are the sources that will give you the most meaning, at the end of a day. Very few things in your life will care about you as much as you will care about yourself.

Why am I feeling like I don't want to go to Rachael's? What is it about going over that is something I don't want to do? So I want more time to myself? Am I not getting enough?

This appears to be the impression I have; I'm actually not sure that I'm in line with my tendencies when I decide to go over there on a night where I am particularly tired and am having a hard time trying to justify going. My sense is that I'm likely trying to please her here but I'm trying to see if that's something that feels good. I'm not sure if it does, but I think the reason it doesn't is because I'm really tired and I want to go to sleep, actually. Do I think I'm not going to be able to do that there?

So far I haven't had issues so I'm trying to see how it's become one.
