item.title: The Speed Project, Atacama
item.description:
Maybe under a year later, you will need the rest from a busy mind that cares too much about too much, and you'll help another friend make his way through the driest desert instead, and you'll find yourself asking if what you are doing is something you want to threaten yourself with doing forever. Even as you work through the edges of these different deserts with the same name, through rocky outcroppings surrounded by the sand drifting into dunes that seem miles away, you won't be sure if you have a choice.

You'll find yourself wistful. It won't be that you don't want to do this forever but rather that you don't want to hate it. You won't ever want to force yourself into reenacting something you love over and over again until it's something you don't want to do, because this has already happened so many times. It will end up being something you don't want to promise because it needs feeling sweet and memorable, - and will lodge itself in your brain like an addiction.

The friends you make in the desert are special because anyone who chooses to be here couldn't possibly be a stranger after sharing this kind of experience. You think back on running along the beach in Iquique with Nils, and hearing his honesty, and feeling mildly enraged at the way people in your past have spoken about someone who has changed as much as this human has; this human, an untouchable force that seeks out more of this, just as you do, that seeks to play with the human spirit of risk just as you do. If you have been the subject of that same envy–turned–judgment, the question then becomes: for what? For choosing to do something that others demand that there be a point in doing? But life need not be made so inflexible.

It could be described as "vacationing in hardship". There's no denying this, but if there's no point to prove, then, there is no reason to justify it. Maybe there is some form of happiness found in knowing that you must live a life in acknowledgment of how your actions affect others, but this is a complex form of happiness. It's something that comes from a lifelong practice of adjusting and respecting asymmetries. Here two things are held in tension: we must acknowledge what privilege we have to go and do what we will do, but that acknowledging a privilege does not require us to deny oneself joy. But joy is found in simple things, and running in the desert is simple. Why deny that joy?

Nicki's words will ring in your ears instead, read over his shoulder on the walk back from our first dinner on the shoreline, What if? Why not? There is more to all of these stories than trying to prove a point, so much of it is just because it's there and we want to go and see it and we want to be excited by sharing the experience with one another, and so much of it isn't to tell a story as much as the yell at the back of an RV that you fucking love this shit, because this shit is unmatched. Nothing matches an experience like this, which is why you continue to seek it out. You ask yourself - is it that much of a threat to want to go and do what you would do and have others tell about it?

This sort of "vacation" teaches you something about yourself, and it happens over and over, and you continue to learn how much you can love others just for being there as you move through an experience, whether or not that experience was a choice. It's the sort of vacation that brings back a smile and memory just because it is that much more to relish and remember the chickpea and canned vegetable rice wrap that is more delicious than anything found at a restaurant, and that hug after 25 miles being "the best hug I have ever had". As we come up with road names that change and shift with the landscape around us, our insides are stirred by the exhaustion and emotion and anxiety of deciding that this was the planned from the start, but this was a choice. It was the decision to move into that next stage of ourselves, a movement between movements. It is all movement.

It is all movement in the staccato of our show, the rain, the engine idling, the exhales and changes that cannot unchange. It is all movement that turns us into something else, and 14,000 feet up we start remembering that we are 14,000 feet up, asking ourselves why the hell we're here, but "we've already won" just by being here at all.

The movement forces us to grow, and growth was always the plan, but there have never been rules on how to follow it – each story was just to keep ourselves, doing something new, something that earmarks the distance between who we were, and who we wish to b if the weather is right, we'll share that story, but there is no obligation. All of it is one about the joy of movement and living within one's body.

Sure, challenging yourself, without a good reason may seem foolish, but again, Nicki did already say it: what if you could do it? Why wouldn't you, if you could? Asi es que se hace and Y que, si se podria? Y si se podria, porque no?

item.title: Inspiration's mania - the fear of time
item.description:
It is so very strange to me how it is that we can be pulled from the energy that we had at one moment in time, directly into having completely been lost from the energy within us in order to write. Chiefly I find that inspiration does have a sort of mania to it - an excitement for what is touched upon, but with a loss accompanying the realization that there is finite time within which we as individuals are capable of utilizing the energy that we have at out disposal.

Rachael does point out very well that it seems my chief fear is time, that I am always trying to buy it back through one mean or other, because I don't wnat to run out of time to explore the thoughts that I want to engage. I can see that there's something true there. It's possible that the writing I want to do concerns itself with a fear of understanding that time is relative, but that we still age despite it, and that while a fear of death is something I believe we should all come to terms with, it's still a fear that the time you have is cut short or is badly used.

The memories we hold are those that will carry us the most into the futures we want to live - those that we have chosen to make important to us, those that we believe are something more than the sum of their parts and can be understood to matter to our constitution of self. If I remember the time I spent at that cabin in the woods so fondly, what is the reason? I didn't want to talk to Ruby at the time, but I did end up doing so several times, likely out of a desire to stave off the loneliness that crept up when I wasn't being attentive enough toward the solitude that I was seeking.

There are three inciting events that we can point to in that experience, that I was there to witness the eclipse, that I was there to be by myself and didn't get to enjoy this outcome when Henry showed up, and finally the missile silo with which I'm some what obsessed with wanting to explore, chiefly because the scale of the structure is so massive that I can't think of any reason not to want to explore it in its entirety (things hidden below the surface beg a sense of intrigue - I took photos on that day that I never did anything with, and I should change that). My sense is that if there is any story to be told here, its around the knowledge of the missile silo's implications and the complete awe with which I received the total solar eclipse - a contrast between that which is known and the terror of knowing this truth.

I sat down at a formica table in a trailer somewhere upstate, a place whose name I don't really remember and whose restaurants I didn't actually order food from, but I went there in the latter of half of winter on a search for enough inspiration to fold around the writing that I had driven up there to do. I don't know what voice should be employed to write about this, speaking about it in past tense feels a bit lost in the intention and I'm not sure that I want to that that approach, because I think there is likely far more that I need to explore in the writing. Maybe the way to approach it is in present tense rather than past - or even some sort of future imperfect, as though a reader is being pulled through the text that is being written.

I'm not sure how I could approach it, I'm struck by the fact that writing is something that comes naturally to me, but that it has never actually been focused into a form of effort that I can call comprehensive--there are satellites of ideas that float around execution, but never anything final--and these incomplete bodies make up a desire to create something bigger without ever actually getting to the core matter at hand, or a desire to encourage a reader through a body of work that anyone can call 'complete'. This is probably what I fear the most - that I've never put the concerted effort into finishing something so that there's actually something for people to hold on to.

I think this is why I want to get into the practice of actually creating writing that people consume and which they can offer feedback about - unless this is simply not how writing works.

Write a journal entry from the perspective of a character named "Echo," who is struggling to find her place in the world. Echo has always felt like she's been living in someone else's shadow, whether it's her parents' expectations or her best friend's accomplishments.

While Maura and I grew up together, it was around fifteen when I started to feel more frustration than not about how she was able to move through the world - the fact that she seemed to be able to engage people in a way that I always feared doing, something that I wasn't really equipped to do, or that she seemed far more capable than I was in just about every category of teenage achievement. I was always trailing behind her, whether following her in plans to the mall, planning her birthday parties, or acting as a neutral third party to the friendships-cum-relationships she seemed itinerant in avoiding.

In hindsight, it's obvious to anyone beyond the age of sixteen that insecurity is a core feature of young adulthood, and this was something that fueled Maura's spotlight - she thrived in being seen, but being seen was effortless. The flywheel of her visibility reverberated, but the anxiety that surrounded being seen and needing to keep up appearances always turned up in the conversations we held in my bedroom, her mother driving by later most evenings to pick her up. It was slow at first, but the envy that my association with her was causing me to seem less important drove a wedge between us, and I was the first to notice its presence; I needed time where I was allowed to take up room and be seen.

It's worse that her problems were so much more interesting than mine. She fell in love when she was sixteen with a nineteen-year-old who worked at a local pizza shop and we found so many reasons as a result to frequent the dusty formica and weathered red roof of a restaurant whose menu never changed, whose crusts were always as crispy as the first time, and whose root beer was always flat. The boy still seemed somehow oblivious to her advances; by most accounts she was more attractive than he was, but Maura wasn't a simpleton - her tendency toward introspection afforded an admirable sensitivity to character. Tolin was interesting - he liked science fiction novels and knew about cars, and often when he was the only one in the pizza shop, the three of us would sit for ours exploring the worlds he knew about - but Maura never seemed to be able to hint at him that she was actually interested in him beyond the friendship that we shared, and the duvet-cover debriefs that followed these nights often focused on how to overcome the issue, but never actually found resolution. I also never felt motivated to solve it for her.

I could see that over time I was starting to make myself smaller, that I wasn't growing from the process of being her friend. I was stunting myself. It was a difficult conversation to have when she finally came to me, concerned that I was distant because (finally turning her attention toward me) something was going on in my life.

There was, I had to explain to her. My life was happening. I was seeking to have one that existed outside of her, outside of a friendship that seemed otherwise all-consuming. I was glad for her achievements, but they were always hers, I and I needed my own. The crestfallen look on her face when I told her that I'd already arranged for my mother to speak with hers and ask that they come up with other after-school plans so as to free up my time for myself was a pivot - a moment where I realized my own self-conception and the spark of self-worth swelled inside of me at my own defense. I loved her dearly; I needed my own life.

item.title: There are times (poem)
item.description:
There are times i can feel it roaring

It is a notion to attend nor
Is the weight of it
Something that brings me to the closeness
I am earning

There are times where I have turned myself over
To the notion that
Things need not get better
there is something holy
made from knowing oneself
and confidently stripping away
the sea of worry

We have earned the keep,
the way of becoming
accompanying not having wavered
Atterizaje, a grounded tree
The same words uttered over and over,
In the feeling of my death echo
reverberating back through time toward me

Grace, I have known you
though those times
the hoary weight of time
I have feared those same things
that take harbor inside of me

Grace, I have known you
through those times
Hearing and respecting
In whatever caused me

Grace I have known you hearing me
In the best of those times
Not having thought that this was a place
That I would stop calling home

Grace
I did think that this time
this would be home
and so I stretched myself across it
as though it would be such a place
within which I would find
that safety

I bored into the landscape
With the desire to sink into it skin
And feel the moss veins of age it would offer

Now I am lucky to know something for sure
In exchange for what it gave me;
A family, estrangement
Telling me that I am loved
unwavering
known only by ocean
or by coastline

I think I heard far too late
that diminishing echo

So my reaction when it was made louder
By the canyon walls by which I was surrounded
It was not something to which I was ready to react

it enveloped me
and i heard it
And knew better then than I had before
That i am not home
And I am looking for it
and that it is not home that will find me

Grace, give me mention
for i spent the least time wandering
In places that offered me
unbridled joy
places into which I sank
Grace I know better where home is now but
I also know better that it is not a place i will find as i wander

Settled into my sorrow
I know I brought you here to let pass
the empty gravel of searching
ungraded and churning beneath my feet
The return to my roots
The emptying of bookcases and living rooms and
Meals and places
I wanted more of and
haven’t mentioned yet missing.

item.title: Insights
item.description:
And here we are, back to the same methods that we were using to keep ourselves on track - the same kind of logic that brought us to the same kinds of conclusions.

She pauses so that she can check the weather which, unrelenting, is rain that doesn't seem to want to stop, and means that she's going to have to go and run on the treadmill

Trying to align myself with the approaches that mean I'm going to actually stick to my ideals, the ways that I want to write and the ways that I want to force myself to write. The two-and-a-half pages that I want to force myself to write every day on paper but since there's no feedback mechanism, there really isn't a way for me to force myself into it. Constraint, the one thing that I don't seem capable of doing for myself.
The other part that stands out or that I make myself aware of is the face that in the entirety of my time working on the matter, there's not really anything that is making me pay the abundance of attention that I'd like to force myself into as a result of all of this work. I'm telling myself that there's a goal in mind, and I'm telling myself that I have to do what it necessary in order to force myself into the outcome, but I don't think I have ever known what discipline is, at least not in the context of what I'm actually capable of what what it is that I've sought out.

The insight that I've had from years of writing at this point is that most of it is in seeking catharsis, and that the 'warmup' of having had to think about what goes into the writing is what stands the most in my way - the realization that time is something that Id on't ahve a lot of control over until I do (because I do, and I realize that I do, and I forget that I do more often than I don't). Remembering that time is a function of novelty, and that what is most powerful about writing is that it is the constant generation of novelty. It's the ability to fabricate and connect the facts so that the information fits together in a way that creates outcomes more aligned with the spirit rather than the real - what is the spiritual versus the nihilist? What is the goal of thinking in the ways that we do, and what is it that creates this outcome?

the rain gets harder, as though to confirm that she shouldn't have been out there on the road, pounding pavement while being soaked to the bone, just having recovered from a 24-hour cold

And I think there's something to this, the idea that novelty is something that can be aspired to and broken apart, that there's a way to short-cut the human desire to get to what we expect of ourselves and the means through which we do so.

the lake is nearly invisible behind the sheet of rain between her and its distance. yes, she could have been out there, but it would have extended the illness

The realization is then that there's some need for creativity that functions in control of time, in service of the need to create discipline and aspire to more of who we want to be rather than what it is that we default to. I find that this is the most important part ot explore, hearing from oneself that there's something that we haven't encountered and that there is a torrent of voices that can come forth when you choose to slow down and pay attention to them, and that in these voices there is a collection of thoughts that underly one's actions and can be directed to, can be attended to and cared for, because they have been there and because they deserve to be there in the ways that they show up.

I've never been one to have discipline because I don't default to it, but I definitely aspire to it. If routine is that which speeds up time, there's a way to hack that routine into the exploration of the mind that slows down specific parts of the routine so that there is some liberty in the way that routine is adhered to - parts of what the routine can perform and what it is that it can do ahead of becoming something better than a repetitive function that creates sameness. That's not what writing does, that's not its service function, and it's not how I will ever pursue it.

However, how do I find myself tied to this goal? What's the real function of it? Is it to lock in and create a way for me to find bigger and better parts of myself? Do I want to explore bigger and better worlds that I've created? Do I want to increase my wpm just so that there's an easier transference of thought into the page? It's unclear.

the rain continues, the lake is invisible, she's destined to run on the treadmill today

Insights:

  1. Self-awareness and recognition of limitations:
    The writer acknowledges that they struggle with discipline and constraint.
  2. Catharsis as a driving force:
    Writing is motivated by the desire for emotional release and healing through their writing process.
  3. The struggle between spirit and reality:
    The writer grapples with finding balance between idealistic aspirations (spirit) and the practical realities of their life.

Actions

I'm going to go to the treadmill and run 5-10 miles. We'll see.

I'm going to come back and meditate.

I'm going to read some of the papers that were presented for this conference.

  • I didn't sign up for health insurance
  • I also didn't get to run the distance that I wanted to because I got sick. It was a much nicer day yesterday but my illness got in the way of being able to do anything, really.

item.title: Faith as a coordinating technology
item.description:
faith is a coordinating technology - it's well suited to the direction of huge groups of people because it is a conclusive and motivated set of traditions and actions that are well-connected to the utility of a common goal

this is the most interesting thing about coordination as rooted in faith, and it is indeed what is missing from the human species.

the act of believing some set of conditions will improve is based on a common ability to believe in the improvement of these conditions as exclusive of free will -- that is, faith is the act of believing that there will be a better outcome despite not knowing for certain that the outcome will happen.

faith is inimitably tied as well to hope, because hope is just as blind, while absolving itself of the lack of agency that faith inspires in some. if a sociological technology of faith is possible (and it is because we have evolved it in several directions as a species), then it's still possible to use that technology for the better; it's possible to use both faith and hope in the service of good things

this is in some ways what I think we have lost as a civilization: the inability to have faith in a collectively-held outcome that serves as many people as possible.

the effect of lacking an alternative executable collective coordination mechanism that efficiently orients humans in the same direction is that it results in a lack of commonly-desired outcomes: without an effective means through which to point all of us at something that all of us want, we each think that we want something different from our neighbor, either locally or on much larger scales. this results in coordination failure -- we don't move in the same direction, even when it could benefit all of us.

this is the danger of not having a meaningful coordination technology at the level of a species; now there is no way for us to meaningfully work together to solve collective problems.

this is why I think that we need to reconsider the social definition of faith and it's utility in how we approach collective problems.

item.title: On forgetting
item.description:
I want more people to talk about forgetting.

I want more people to think about the past and recognize that what they remember is only what was necessary, and that their lives are something that comes from the construction of a personal narrative, not from what we specifically chose to remember.

I think this is what troubles me the most - that at some point we conflated the idea of memory with the idea of permanence and because of this caught ourselves in the trap of remembering everything. Now, overloaded by the burden of this sort of rationalist thinking, we're trying to work our way back to a place that can make more sense of the world using heuristics rather than what we've been told to do - attempt to keep it all in our heads and then fault ourselves with the loss of what wasn't important.

A friend of mine sent me an article this morning about how it is that Gen Z people filter for information in the modern age, that it's no longer about the process of trying so hard to filter for truth and instead filter for what it is that their peers say about the subject1, because truth has become so maleable. It purports thats what we used to consider sources of truth are now so lacking in credibility that we've reached a point where an entire generation has essentially written off the idea of traditional journalism, making way instead for something that approximates relative truth, or what one could call 'truth by local consensus'.

Even the more current thinkers decry a state where this feels like something that should spurn concern rather than excitement - Klippenstein just wrote about it in his substack - but I find that there's something more fearful and less reasonable about taking this approach over, say, optimism.

In some ways, the trend toward truth by local consensus heartens me - it points toward a distrust of authority that feels more democratic rather than one explicitly oriented toward institutional credibility. When we step back to take it in, this says more about the lack of credibility in institutions as it stands2. There's some trepidation that can be had around the idea that local consensus can lead to disinformation as communities trend toward echo chambers that reflect back their own logic, but I have more optimism than this. I see those who participate in this form of truth-seeking as inoculating themselves against a firehose of institutionalized (mis)information - and it's this part that makes me think that maybe forgetting is something that we're supposed to do more of at the organismal level.

To me, forgetting does not mean that information is being lost and can't be retrieved - it's something more nuanced than this, instead its a process of pruning information for what is actually relevant. This is why it rhymes with the process of seeking truth, but more importantly it is how humans participate in making sense3 of the world around us. Forgetting is the process of taking what is relevant and allowing ourselves to settle into what the current of time pulls away from us - and I think there's something to embracing this as a natural process.

There are further implications to this that aren't so woo - thinking of forgetting in this way is valuable for practical application - and it's valuable to consider how this affects the landscape of logic that exists around how we create technology. Biomimicry was once (and should remain) a staple of forefront design, so there's no reason not to think about forgetting as an evolutionary process first and foremost (it literally is).

The present era is one that focuses so much on storing boundless amounts of information from even deeper wells of truth, and this is, broadly, a deviation from how information is managed in most natural systems. No one can tell me that every permutation of a tree was important to an oak, and no one can tell me that all the ways that a river can run are important to the way that one particular river flows. All information is local and adapted to circumstance, and the fidelity of that information is a product of its relevance to the environment it's a part of, not the entire body of possibility that precedes it - this would be immensely inefficient.

It's for this reason that I think forgetting is important - it's something that we need to learn how to do gracefully. Truth by local consensus is the human species adapting locally to the flow of information across the entirety of the internet. Zero-Knowledge Proofs are a mathematical repercussion of the same conclusion - a striving toward remembering only the truth that is relevant on the basis of the local information that proves it. Even the learning methodologies of the Machine Learning algorithms that support artificial intelligence depend on setting paths through knowledge4, regardless of how their datasets can be polluted.

It's not a question of doing so aimlessly - there's value in learning how to forget gracefully. Truth by local consensus is a form of adaptation, and on the landscape of an internet that by any measure of human history is still incredibly young5, humans are still figuring out how to adapt to consuming more information in a week than someone 100 years ago might have consumed in their entire lifetime. It stands to reason that we need to learn to trust the process of forgetting and to learn how to do it in a way that doesn't compromise our ability to reason.

There's also a finer point to put on this - I don't mean by any of my writing up to this point that you should throw caution to the wind and forget everything that you've learned. What I'm saying is that there's a significant cognitive burden in thinking that you have to remember it all, and this is not only unhealthy6 but is also something that you should release yourself from thinking you have to keep up with everything. We're not designed to think in terms of everything we've remembered, we're only meant to remember what is important to us based on the circumstances relevant to direct experience we have of living.

Forgetting is a process of accepting that access to boundless information does not mean maintaining access it all. More expansively, it also means treasuring that which you do remember, because it is likely that the natural course of things is to remember that which is most important to you.

  1. there's an irony in here mentioned in the article - that Google's technology called 'Perspective' filters these same comments for their own and stacks them against 'toxicity' - but this is a digression because truly what an abysmal reality we live in). ↩

  2. LM Sacasas speaks on this in his essays around 'Reading Ivan Illich' - particularly when speaking to the tendency for any institution to ossify and become an object that seeks to self-preserve rather than something that will always benefit those who created it. This thinking does find roots in scale free economics and the implications of network creation - but this is a subject for a wholly different post. ↩

  3. See sensemaking, or think about the process yourself! it's interesting to ponder how it is that humans create and congregate around truth. ↩

  4. Yes, yes, I know what you are going to say here, you can pollute the dataset. That's true! This is why I think that credible data is something that deserves to be talked about, but that, as well, is writing for another post. There is indeed a way to make this work. ↩

  5. Yes. The internet has been around like 70 years. Humans have been around as homo sapiens for like thiry-thousand years. We still have no idea what the internet will be for us in the future, so there's plenty of room to innovate. ↩

  6. Guess what, just like AI, your brain is an algorithm, so the information that you take in will inform the way that you think. Just look, there's even science on it - even though the point of this article is that humans seem to be able to come to these sorts of conclusions on their own. ↩

item.title: The Cruft · the first conversation between the Walker and the Figure
item.description:
"the distraction of knowing how time treats us, it is not unfair or cruel, it is observant, and in so being sees us in a Knowing that we can control the time we are allotted and the ways in which it is used."

the stories of this Earth are long past. they are memories, and as with most memories, they are incomplete. in the time where everything happened, The habit was to remember it all, the dream that what should be as a catalog of all that was - but we know - you know - that Wonder comes from incomplete things, from the open-ended questions that pour forth from mystery. they in their time obsessed over memory instead of giving value to the passage of time and the sheer magic of proving its existence. some knew this and built cultures and traditions of forgetting, and we can honor them as much as we can honor those who chose to remember it all. those who chose to forget allowed those few to move on - to know that which is valuable from the past and to move forward in its memory, but not in an exacting reflection of the past. you cannot replace that which is already happened, because now is a far more powerful message than then. even you know this, to take what you have learned and build the steps needed toward the future instead. it is a dream caught in the act of its own realization, and now you know you can be present for the event.

I cannot remember this place for you. even the memories I hold are fragmented, or somehow less than what was expected - but I am as well better for it. but I remember is harrowing and has crushed me, and the years have removed of it it's edges and the fear of its repetition - but the sun is still glorious. I still see it's light as something that gives back. I remember hope and time has given me an appreciation for that which I don't remember. what I don't remember is what makes the legend. what I've seen since then, and what I've retained - it told me that the most unstoppable of forces is this forward movement. I have found rust in appreciating its passage and reconfiguration. every moment can pour forth gifts."

Figure sat on nothing, breathing the facsimile of exhaustion from a shimmering blue of having taken in passing ages.

"but you can see all of this for yourself. there is meaning here, should you seek it. I cannot say that I think knowing the story as it occurred will be worth your effort, but it may be, maybe the story you learn will inspire you to seek out more. I hope this for you, I encourage you, and when you have gone and seen all that you can learn, come back to me, and I will tell you what I do remember, and I will tell you that it's beautiful, and I will tell you why I think it is beautiful."

item.title: Warman school - loneliness week 1
item.description:
How has your week been in loneliness?

Mostly I think that I've been seeing a yearning that was born from having faced my loneliness that has turned into a desire for solitude, which has made me feel particularly good about

What is your lonely place? What makes a place lonely? What places make you lonelier? What places make you less lonely? Why?

They do say 'it's lonely at the top', and my loneliest place is in leadership. It feels like a place?

Every time I've found myself in any workplace, I eventually get coursed toward leadership of some sort because I'm willing to take point on my thoughts or those of others and turn them into action, as though I'm a vehicle that people can use to get to where they desire to go.

It's a place that sometimes seems only I have access to and only I am qualified to take on, because as an executive who ended up here through nothing more than apparent will-to-do, I find myself so estranged from people who don't have this in them. When I do meet someone who has similar abilities, it's like meeting a ship in the night, we know that we can't actually possess the same space because we are not meant to. I have a desire to make change and to facilitate movement and I feel as though when I try to encourage others to take on this sort of self-engagement and self-motivation, I can't quite translate that it's not about garnering the necessary energy to do so from a perspective of positivity but rather that it's this relentlessness. There are pockets of this relentlessness that can be gestured toward contentment and even happiness, but it's a willingness to keep moving because if you are unhappy, at least you know your name.

I'm reminded of the speculative biology in Butler's 'Bloodborne' wherein there is a biological imperative toward leadership and motherhood over others, and that in meeting others who hold this imperative, you are destined not to occupy the same space because the imperative drives you toward separation from others, a near hostility that feels somewhat like needing to find others who understand, but knowing you can never really occupy that space together because your experience is altogether different in its own right.

I find that I can course away from the loneliness of leadership by experiencing glancing blows with other leaders in spaces where the guards are down and the parameters are temporary, where there is a penchant for sharing and collaboration instead, because while I am a leader, I don't want to be one, it's simply what keeps happening to me. I have had dinners with others who have guided teams toward the completion of projects, and understanding or navigating the social dynamics that come with leadership while interrogating them with others can make me feel less lonely - but these times always do have to end due to the nature of the act and the capacity is possesses within us.

I had my chart read a few days ago and what really stood out to me was that I am a leader, but I'm like an alien in being one; people follow me but they don't understand me. Knowing this makes me feel more lonely rather than less.

How do you know when you are lonely? How do you know when you are not lonely?

It hits me because I don't feel cared for, which answers both questions, when I have a harbored feeling of not having my needs met and not knowing how to meet them, and wanting/begging to go after them in a way that feels like healing. When I'm not lonely I don't feel this yearning, but when I am lonely, I want to solve for it.

What are your most lonely moments?

  • When Cherefawn broke up with me.

  • When Sara moved out and I realized I was going to have to do everything over again after Cherefawn and I split up.

    • There was a part of me that really wanted to live in aspace of thinking tha tI was going to end up with some sort of life partner, and I find that too often I fall into this feeling of thinking that the love of me life is a person instead of ths idea that they might be within me.

    The loneliness of this feeling is one of knowing that I have the ability to love someone, but that when I love someone in a way that is the most generative to how it is that I want to be as a person, I have come to experience a reality of those that I have tried to love pushing it away, revulsing from the idea that there is any way to think that far ahead and commit to a life that appears anything like devotion. This has been true enough that I've found myself thinking about whether or not I'll ever find someone who wants that sort of devotion and whether or not it's a devotion that is even logical, because so much of the way I love is tied up in trust and I've had to learn how not to trust people with my heart.

    Now that I'm an adult and I'm starting to feel more and more like my life is so much further down the track, I feel all manner of fearful between the moments where I feel the least lonely, because I can stare down the feeling of knowing that my loneliness isn't something that limits my life, and that no one can help me solve for that feeling better than I can.

    I started thinking about how when Sara and I split up, I was going to end up with the whole apartment and I'd have to pay all of the rent, and -- I didn't change this. I kept going, I kept paying the rent because the apartment is comfortable and I like it, but I let someone live with me because she needed somewhere to live and she hasn't left and I love her, but this apartment never feels like it's mine as a result, it never feels like a place where I can take complete ownership over how it makes me feel and why I'm living here by myself, I never really get to ask if this place is mine or not.

    When Sara moved out and I gave up the room to Tam I was glad for Tam because that's how you support your friends, but now I feel so estranged from everything because the group that used to tie us all together (Rage and Release) is no longer a safe place for us to be, so with that went all of my friendships that were tied up in what that web of connections had become and the effort I'd put into being with these people and holding them in my life, and then in January that fell apart and now I don't have them and I don't know what to do with their absence - it feels like a long sleep where I woke up and the world changed, and I didn't get to decide where it went.

    All of these times have tied themselves together around a feeling of needing to be desired or thinking that being desired is somehow what brings my life meaning, but then peeling back the layers and seeing that inside it's just some sort of collapsing star that deserved more attention than it got and should have felt better than it has, because look how far I made it on my own.

    If we live in an age of loneliness, it's because in the act of allowing everything to connect to everything else, we never stopped to ask which connections should be important, and we never developed the tools to navigate those questions without constantly trying to shift attention between the potentials that every connection could generate.

-

item.title: The bleeding hand on the train
item.description:
I watched a man's hand bleed on the train while wedging a book beneath his arm, the hand kept bleeding and he held an old T-shirt to it, and I kept thinking 'that shirt is ruined unless he gets it under cold water' while feeling waves if self-conscious fear just rampant coming from him, his bright red face when he got on because it had just happened and I'm sure it hurt but all of us hold back our pain when we feel as though we need to show others that we're capable of dealing with it.
I dropped the red-lead pencil I'd found on the side of the street right on its point and I kept thinking about how 'the core's probably broke now' so 'i'll just ride it out until the edges curl out' all the while listening to a woman caterwauling a version of a popular song that no one clapped to when she stopped, and the bare disgusting feet of a homeless man lain across the seats and no one sitting next to him, but he just wanted to sleep and I think that's fine and he should have been allowed to, but where are his shoes?

it is true that there is a dense sense of loneliness that all settles around being a transgender person who has assimilated sufficiently into the rest of society such that they no longer stand out for these parts of themselves. this can take the form of having to profoundly assimilate aspects of the self such as one's voice or mannerisms or dressing or the surgical alteration of the body to meet the standards of a society that would wish transgender people not to exist and yet somehow inside of this there is an understanding that there is profound loss in aspects of the self when reflected entirely off of a society that has not been made to apprehend any deviation from it's central norms.

I can feel the small sense of desperation that comes from realizing that there are some who have taken unto themselves a strong appreciation for that which makes them unique rather than tossing aside these aspects as though they are not something that makes them stand against the course of normalcy.

I deserve a love that sees me for who I am.

-

item.title: New York is becoming a rainy city
item.description:
New York is becoming a rainy city - a place that doesn't look like it used to, doesn't act like it used to, and won't be prepared for how it's going to be in the future - more like Seattle than what it used to be, no longer a biting temperature of winter closing and more of the form that seems to want to piss down constantly and that none of us are actually prepared to put up with.

it's funny because this is the time of year where I used to sit outside of coffeeshops for hours and hours in the mornings, somewhat reading books, somewhat reading my own mind - and this doesn't really seem possible anymore. I don't necessarily feel poorly about it, rather it's something to adapt to, something that is changing and that is going to have to lead to a new outcome.

being on vacation is it's own feeling, too - knowing full well that I don't actually need to do anything feels a little weird because it feels like admitting to myself that I don't actually need to do anything in the mean time of having decided not to do anything. I have to let myself acknowledge and let go of the feeling of thinking that I am required to come up with things that I have to do and that I need to be productive around. I don't - even if I go upstate with a guitar, a couple changes of clothes, food, books, and my notebooks and I come out of it not having done anything meaningful - that's actually fine, because that is somewhat the point of doing nothing: relaxing into a state of finding oneself in and among that which if makes us up. I'm excited by this prospect and it's something I want more of, to find peace in myself that I already have and to have that love for myself because this is something that I want out of the situation. I want to go up there and read and explore my own mind (should I bring mushrooms? maybe I should!) but the point can and will be to be with myself.

I never know who I am writing for, in fact - I used to write as though there was some audience that would read what I had to say, and I think I've moved away from that somehow, mostly out of a feeling that there is more to my own mind that deserves exploring and respecting, and I'm trying to start from this place rather than anywhere else.

Maybe at some point when you are writing for other people, you start to hear your own voice coming through whatever is sitting within it. When and if this is true, the deliberation placed into the words becomes apparent and there isn't really a reason to reject the notion of having to mean more to the words than you want to - of using the words as a form of practice rather than as a form of outward expression.

The question then becomes about crying, about feeling ripped from oneself and respecting the boundary condition that exist around the self and the expansion of the mind. Is the act of writing for others the act of telling people what you are thinking and feeling, or is it the act of arguing for a changed state of being?

If the latter, the writer has a responsibility to the reader not to tell a story, but for this story to change their mind - to present the truth as incontrovertible and then to controvert - because the Original Story is one that follows a known thread only to end up far away from it - un hilo guiando hacia otros caminos.

For the reader to come to the novel as their full selves is itself a sublime act, for a writer is required to reconcile that they arrive with the weight of their experiences and that this informa their response to what is written. As such that which is written and carried to the reader is a deeply vulnerable act of facing a stranger and telling them, earnestly

-

item.title: TSP - the religion of running
item.description:
What a trip.

Flying into Las Vegas with only the slightest understanding of what to expect, easing in to understand the dynamic, then feeling everything within me given to the road as a way of communing with the religion of running - i'm beyond astounded by what lives in us human beings.

We are capable of so much, of building out our bodies as vehicles for movement that seek only to commit to the outcomes that are necessary. In so doing, the act of movement becomes something that brings us up into ourselves and unfold us in the direction of a higher self, a transcendent state of committing to the ways we can push ourselves through the kindness of the relationship we build with our bodies.

I feel as though so much grew out of what we did out there. I've done things like this before but for some reason this really did feel different and was definitely born out of a need to grow in the direction of my own care and the love I have for the women that I run with. Even seeing that Julia had a really different attitude toward running as a result of this gave me a lot of grace around what I've built with them - not to mention that there's a shotgun of feelings I have about the people I did this with.

I want to sit with what Lauren said about Tam, but I don't know if I feel some strange sense of manipulation that sits around the edges of my feelings there, a desire to know and feel more about knowing if I'm actually holding Tam in my life in a way that is respectful of my boundaries and what I need for my wellbeing. I get the sense that it is and that for now it doesn't feel bad, but I do question what it's like to have my apartment back to myself, or have a roommate who actually pays rent, idk.

Beyond this I also question the fact that she helps in ways that are substantial but that I also know she really can't pay rent in the ways that she would like to. There's some martyred part of myself that flares up here around thinking that she's destined for something greater and that it's because of this that she's someone I want to harbor in my home. I don't know if this is a real feeling or if it's something that I need to look at with a degree of skepticism for my own well-being, because I'm actually not sure if I feel good about the way I'm giving myself to the situation. Some part of me would actually love to have the apartment back to myself, so I want to listen to that part and let it grow into whatever it needs to while also knowing that I appreciate the relationship we have for what it is and what we make from it, because I cannot believe that which we have made from it.

What Lauren said about feeling unthanked is valid, and I do at times feel as though she's someone with vision that deserves to be followed - however it is interesting the number of times someone has asked us why she is doing it and if it was for a cause, and it really wasn't, and probably won't be, but that simultaneously it is because it's her story of being able to exist in these spaces as someone who as of recent history didn't and doesn't have the liberty to have grown through privilege, but I don't know for sure how or why to feel anything about it because I'm just sort of allowing it to happen.

This last part feels like the crux, actually - I don't necessarily feel bad about the fact that I'm allowing it to happen and I do feel sufficiently checked in on this questions, at least as far as I can tell.

Separate from this, reading about Hunter Schafer is something that feels really grounding around the knowledge of how I approach being trans - because it's just not something I want to have to hold onto in the ways that I'm forced to. In the article she did for GQ she speaks to this idea by saying that:

there’s a meta quality at play here that we’re both aware of; of having to acknowledge the thing in plain language so that the thing might not have to be acknowledged one day.

which I find wildly true particularly because she is someone who has really made things happen for herself and doesn't want to be typecast into an identity that needs to encapsulate this as an experience. So many trans people allow themselves to end up in this pace that acts as a reverberating echo chamber of sadness and frustration, and I just can't sit in the feeling of knowing that it's something anyone should continue to have to live within in order to continue being.

Being trans is incidental, it's not something that people should have to continually face in their lives because they should be allowed to be complete humans beyond the point of self discovery, and what many cis people seem not to understand is that there's really a need for progressing beyond the trauma you had to move through in order to leave behind your experience and develop into a complete human. It can come off as being stunted, as being somehow connected only to this part of ourselves that happened to us, and as a result is absolutely an act of living in one's own trauma rather than developing beyond it.

My journey has absolutely been unfolding in the direction of something greater, so knowing that Hunter Schafer has been able to embody this same limitless energy is proof positive of how I'm approaching things, that I'm far more complicated than this single facet, even though it appears in my life over and over again and I am forced to give it attention. It doesn't define me, which is what makes it a separate experience from what I actually feel about who I am and what I want to do - that again, being trans is incidental, not a defining feature of who I am.

It doesn't mean I don't want to advocate for this part of myself or for others - I also know that I have an intense and willing attraction to other trans people at least in the regard of fearing that sort of connection - (most and foremost I think of the bartender at Rialto Grande who I always flirt with, which is refreshing because we both know and yet love to toe that line, just because it's the thing to do).

I think my relationship with running has made itself into something that lives on top of this, as well - that I'm a woman athlete and that there are parts of who I am that don't show up the same as for the experiences of cis women. However I actually find this to be something I hold a lot of promise around; mostly I feel as though I'm on par with the women that are a part of my cohort and who do the things that we do together, and mostly this is because I envision that there's something substantial to the reality that surrounds it - we're all similar and we gravitate toward one another because of the ways that we are similar, and yet somehow I do still see that we have our unique qualities that come to the fore around it. We are all impressive as hell as runners and this is something to be immensely proud of, and I think that the story of us as women who are doing these things makes this even more true.

This ties up my identity as a woman with that of other women athletes and the meaning that necessarily shows up around being in these spaces, because I remark so often on the fact that because I don't center my transness, I am not centered for my transness. The world responds in kind to that which you hope to seek from it, so if you choose to mute some part of yourself based on the way it makes you feel, this is fine, this is something deserved and that should be celebrated because I shouldn't have to live my life as though I'm required to take on these parts - in fact I know I don't.

That's why being in these spaces like the The Speed Project afterparty felt so magical - I no longer think or fear these things as being something that I have to defend, because I know that I don't have to. No one has a right to asking more from me with respect to the feeling that I hold around it, nor does it have to inform my interactions. It's entirely likely that I was the only trans person at that entire party, but I didn't even think about it, which frankly astounds me more than anything else.

My relationship with my womanhood is more important and more grounding than this, and most of the time I laugh at the fact that there's ever a part of the world that gets it wrong, largely due to the energy that I'm willing to put out and off and into to the world. I think this is magical because it's like transmuting elements - knowing so strongly something about myself that I don't need people to have to affirm it anymore (even though yes, 6 years in I still want that affirmation more often than not).

-

item.title: The Speed Project, Los Angeles → Las Vegas
item.description:
The desert gives us only a few times of year to run through it. Some of you know this for sure, as I do - I once wandered through northwestern New Mexico in late June, trying to prove I knew better, and almost gave my dog heat stroke instead. You should never argue with the sun in the summer in the desert. You'll never get a word in. The sun in the summer in the desert is too loud.

That's why running the desert in the spring is better; the Sun has not quite woken up. In March. the Sun still has a mouthful of sand and sleep-rimmed eyes. As a result, you can get in a few words before it rubs its eyes and beats down for the rest of the season like a beaming child unsullied by the anxiety of judgment.

If you want to run the desert, March in the Mojave is a good desert to test. You're more likely to survive its passage, and it will inspire you with the dreams of winter the sun has not yet shaken away. If you run the Mojave in March, you'll get to feel the weather that doesn't feel like the desert, a sideways wind that tests your core, a sleet that bounces off of a hat brim and into the shoulders of roads while you do your best to stay warm. If you run in the desert in March, at night the stars will feel as though they could swallow you whole just because they want to. You will let them, and you'll keep running over missing footsteps while chasing the flash of sky that might as well have been waiting for you to collide with it. If you run in the Mojave in March, you can look fifty miles away and run a good twenty of them and nothing will change.

If you do choose to run the Mojave in March, maybe one of those particular times you will come upon your best friend running 300 miles out of LA and you'll have to take her hand in yours to pull her 9 of those miles up a pass at the end of one of those fifty miles into a small town just outside of Vegas and the weather will lie to you the whole time as if it's the sun's favorite joke. Maybe while you walk and jog, she will fall asleep between footsteps, and you'll see faces in the mined-out cliffs you have to pass, and they will tell you stories through their layers about what the land has to offer you. You'll see those holes we make in the mountains in the chase for gold weeping out dust and chalk and you'll feel sorry for the mountains.

So you'll turn repeat the story to your friend that one of those faces in the mountain is snickering at you both for doing what you're doing. As you repeat it, the expression of that face will turn from a sneer to a grin while it reminds you both it has seen you--and any number of others--do this any number of times in the silly, long, winding story of its life. It will also remind you that you are built for grace in having chosen to take on the passage.

Maybe on this run, part of the way up the pass your friend will have to stop from all the tears that suddenly hug her old dog tight to her chest, where his memories fading are fading from her as she heals through the undertaking, while that dog in her heart put up one last defense between her and the venom an angry exit threatened to infuse in her before the escape you knew she needed. On that run, she'll live with you, the same way she lives with you, without question or sewn doubt - as though it was a calling, same as the brown of her skin choosing to commune with the dirt and to feel tired, just as tired as the dirt beneath, as though it's a form of prayer made just for this kind of motion. She will live with you in these moments as though the movement were made to remember our place in the dirt, aging downward, and your footsteps will cross Sandy Valley until you make it across the pass. Then the wind will keep screaming at you. Then the sleet will come, and the sun, and the discarded oranges that litter the side of the road.

22 miles later, when you and her and the other best friend who came to help share the ending run together toward the glass and flashing lights of the end, it might feel as though you have learned something new that wasn't there, but it may be something that lived within you since the beginning.

If running is meditation on the things that we humans leave behind (what is running, really), then running in the desert is specifically a form of communion with the things the earth has left behind. The sun leaves behind salt on the surface of a caked-out flat, and it is the same salt that gathers at the edges of our eyes. What little water reaches these places grasps onto hardy roots until they die and their skeletons litter the desert, just as our skeletons are all we leave. The wind and sun then bake it all into the to same whispered shades that lose their color, and our skin and our hair mimic this with our own passage into time.

Running in the desert is the act of choosing to bring into line aspects of the self that need changing with the time it takes to change. Relative to our lives, the changes of the desert can take an infinity - there are regions of the world where the land is only changed by the wind and the geological force of the earth moving. The desert chooses to change slowly, and running in the desert forces us to reckon with the pace at which we change. If in our short lives, we choose to sit with the change that comes over us as we move between the littered states of being, then the lessons we learn from respecting the rate of change are what running in the desert can teach us how to do. The desert is always willing to teach this lesson, but running through the desert in the spring is when you are most likely to hear it.

Having moved through that landscape will seek to place you like a seed within those layers of dirt. It will then wait patiently for a little rain and frost below a cold crust, and given the right conditions, might choose to sprout upward into the ancient explosive of crippled trees that dust the Mojave. Running in deserts feels like seeking a home in something desolate that does not care about your being there but is pleased when you are, and running through, alone, with friends, is listening for an eke of self-sufficiency in the self that seems to want to prove the possible. If you run through the desert in pursuit of yourself, it will feel like a rediscovery that over and over cracks open what you keep forgetting, and it will offer you the chance to leave behind these tawny layers with each forward footfall.

If you run through the Mojave in March, you might then share that end with so many others who sought the same end, and you might all have might have learned similar lessons. You'll laugh and share them, and these will be the friends you make in the desert. These will be the people who listened to the same whisper of sand they tried to keep out of their toes, and you'll commiserate over the experience of arguing with a sleepy sun and the weather that follows it. You'll laugh and share, and filled with the sunlight of early spring will make plans to do it again just so that you can see everyone do it again, and you'll all smile through the wrinkles the sun is offers as parting gifts - because yes, it really was better next year, and it was even better the year after.

item.title: The Path at L5
item.description:
Out at the edge of the L5 cluster, someone turned on an orbital zero-friction ion drive in just the right place and the Path was seen for the first time - a bright green flash that was hanging in orbit, then dimmed to a six-hundred-kilometer streak leading away from Earth. Science craft parked themselves around green light for a number of months, aiming to gather measurements of whatever it was that had been sparked into being around ignition, but any sensor type was only capable of detecting a 555 nanometer wavelength hanging in the air with no source - simply emerald green light floating in fixed orbit, without a source.
What made the beam more interesting than an immaculately conceived lightbeam sitting in space was that it changed direction with the orbit of earth around the planet, fixed on an unknown location off in the distance, wavering with the change of the L5's place in orbit.

The positioning of the beam relative to the earth's own orbit presented a problem. When the sun and the earth occluded the path, it showed up as a harmless 4-kilometer-wide beam that passed directly though anything in its path, inexplicably illuminating the insides of buildings as it passed through - but anything in the path would be cast in a fixed level of brightness that engulfed everything. Those who lived in its occlusion path would complain that they couldn't escape the light, but there was no getting around it - when the beam passed through the Earth, everything was green.
This lead to a divergence in responses - most populations sitting in the path of occlusion migrated away from this annoyance once the novelty had worn off - others thought that the beam was a sign from their god and that because of this, they should live directly in the path of the light. The science said nothing - it was harmless green light, but an annoyance, and there was nothing do be done about it, and no escaping the light if you were in its path - but green-light research centers as well built themselves into the occlusion path in order to better understand properties of the light.
About two years after the beam flashed into being, observers still paying attention noticed as well that the beam was slowly moving along its fixed trajectory, leading sages in Elysium City to plot the beam's trajectory out of our system, and to it's eventual name as 'The Path'. The movement of the beam was measurably slow - on the order of at less than a meter per year, but work put into measurement proved that this movement was accelerating over time - prompting sages to call for bigger investment from their parishes to study the phenomenon in the hopes that it would be understood before it accelerated out of our system. A number of probes were sent out ahead of its path as well - many-paneled stations built to either prepare for its passing, or in the assumed trajectory of its movement.

After ten years, the Path's movement had accelerated to a rate of two hundred meters per year with no sign of deceleration, and no progress had been made on the meaning of either the trajectory or of the beam itself - the rate of acceleration was too high for any meaningful propulsion mechanism to catch up once it was to reach high speed, and there was no telling if it would accelerate to the some unknown physical constant.

-

item.title: The Hidden Continent (excerpt)
item.description:
"Listen, I'm not really sure if this woman is on drugs or something, but we tested her and there's nothing in her system to indicate that she is."
"Ok - so what, you want me to talk to her? Why?"
"It's what she's talking about - she's acting like it's really urgent."
"George, it's LA. We have a lot of strung out people who believe a lot of this shit."
"That's what I thought too - but then she did something. I think you need to see it. It's not what you think. I didn't believe it either, but she did it a number of times and I'm not sure what to think. You have to talk to her."
"George, please be sure this isn't a waste of our time."
"Look, I would call a lot of the things that we've had to deal with in the last six months a waste of time, but I have a gut feeling about this. I don't think this is going to be a waste of time. Just talk to her. Just for a second. "

They unlocked the door to the interrogation room and there, sitting in the provided chair, was a slight woman, eyes a little bit cagey, but striking. Dark black hair, a strong, curved nose, dark skin in the way of leather heavy, driven eyes staring right through his own. Something about them - not quite a fire - more a question of knowing, something powerful that seemed to bely a knowledge. Wizened, but tired. He extended his hand.

"Well alright, hello, my name is Detective Harrow. I'm with the Federal Bureau of Investigations. I'm not sure how you were able to convince the people who called me, but I hear that you're here to talk about magic? What was your name?"
She looked back at him, her eyes sparking.
"My name is Leta."
"Ok, nice to meet you Leta. I apologize for all the formality to do with making you wait. However, you're quite persistent and you've been really patient, so I'm glad to make the time here. How can we help you?"
"My people are dying. No one knows, this needs to change."
He looked at her, pausing.
"Ma'am, have you had a drug test?"
She didn't react.
"Have you taken any medication today?"
A moment passed before she looked up at him, opening a mouth that didn't belong in cities and looked instead like someone who had spent years in the sun.
"My people are dying. I did not want to come here. I did not want to do this. I did not want to speak with you and show you what has happened but we cannot fix this on our own and we must fix it."

item.title: The Two Types of Internet
item.description:
a bit of a ramble on the direction I think the internet might be headed. I think we'll see two things. 1. Consumer internet most people will spend their time here, but generally speaking it will lack in much social depth. I think in part this will be the realm of the creator economy and adspace, where the goal is to make things that people want, or to find things that you want. It will mostly be a domain of parasocial interaction or direct consumerism, and will orient itself mostly around good user experiences and not much user input. It is generally not interoperable because it is a domain where platforms compete for market share, and the best way to do so will be to silo interactions into walled gardens. Users will generally not contribute their thoughts and opinions here, and the computer literacy will stay low in general. General examples: Instagram, TikTok, Pinterest, YouTube, Snapchat, etc. 2. Community internet These will be smaller corners of the internet where people who are literate in how to use all different manner of communication will create community across any number of platforms; the social layer will act (acts) as an interoperability mechanism since those who are in this space take their time to build relationships with one another, agnostic of medium. The barrier to access will be some degree of internet-native computer literacy, both socially and practically. Tech that is used here is a means to an end, and those involved will always be communities of intention. It's from these communities that new social coordination mechanisms will form that can operate on a digitally local level that does not care about the limitations of meatspace. More "interesting" things will be made here that generally will work to bring people closer to ideals Examples of this kind of internet are most of crypto and true FOSS, some science communities, Farcaster, Mastodon, and many subject area Discords and Subreddits, and will work best when they do not aim for popularity but rather functionality, since too large of anything becomes operatively diluted in utility. -- Both of these are ultimately good things, and characteristic of humans slowly evolving back toward tribal tendencies while using technologies that we made but did not have the social tools to adapt to. A consumer internet could result in people spending less time online, since they realize that they are not truly interacting with others and will spend more time interacting in meatspace, but it's equally likely people will doomscroll these environments. My hope is that socially we'll evolve past this, but that's just optimism. The countervailing force could be a heterogenous Community Internet, where select people who want to find their people can move with intention toward those who hold similar ideals, and will make meaningful things together. These communities will be small-bit-mighty, and will likely have enormous areas of effect on a Consumer Internet, since it will be a place for people to organize. I could also foresee competition between these internets, mostly due to a Consumer Internet wanting eyeballs and despising the organizational effects of there being spaces to organize online (this, I think, is actually what the purchase of X was about). -- Time will tell, but I think the greatest differentiating factor between the types of people that will occupy these internets will be based on the many forms on literacy, sociality, and collaborative tendencies. People will occupy both spaces in many cases, one out of obligation to a society that has integrated internet-as-media and the other out of a desire to find our tribes - but I hope that this works broadly in our favor. Generally, I think it will.

Crucial to this working is developing a sense of what online culture can look like in its many facets and how people can learn to navigate online spaces as either newcomers or as collaborators. Some communities will operate privately and only by invitation, while others will be inviting and places where others are attracted to feeling included - but I think all of this will evolve out of a human desire to create communities around mutually assured survival. I think there is a high potential that a good Community Internet might work toward better coordination despite individual differences in belief, in stark contrast to the feed-based internet that we had in the Social Media era that amplified discontent bringing us back to a time when humans simply dissociated from one another in situations of discontent. It will be difficult to determine whether or not it's working - tribes can still go to war with one another, after all - but maybe we'll have just a few less reasons to oppose those we're in community with than we do when faced with a feed of literally every other person on the planet.

item.title: On Seeking Utopias
item.description:
There's something to be said for the pull away from cynicism we’re beginning to see from the enabling effects of the new internet.

In some sense, the dystopian leanings of our predictions for humanity are starting to feel too prescient - we are living within these predictions rather than seeing them as some far-flung reality, and the experience is exhausting. It is a grueling existence made somehow more disheartening by the fact that the irrationality of humans rears its head again and again in face of what most would consider to be rational action.

So what can we do with the knowledge that we knew we would be living in the reality we are now experiencing, and that yes, indeed, it is our fault, and that yes, we also know what causes our course toward dystopia in the first place? All this in mind - extrapolations of our present into future, all the more far-flung and depressing as dystopian, must offer us pause. Do we want things to continue on course toward the fictional realities that we didn't expect to materialize? Do we let them? How much of it is under our control?

The last question I find the most urgent - if we know that present conditions are likely to keep us careening in the direction of disaster, and that we are here at our own hand - how much control are we willing to give up in the course toward a collective future, and what hand does any individual person have in ownership over control of this future?

Much of dystopian writing has us completely lacking in control - often because the faults that create a cause for dystopias have already happened, or the protagonists have little to no control over when or if they do. Any dystopia is written from an absence of control. Control is the protagonist in overcoming the conditions of being lacking thereof - admission to higher, more insidious or chaotically evil forces determine the setting. Hypercapitalist dystopias lead us into futures that elide control from individuals into a total obedience of market pressures and consumption, encouraging people to mean nothing but vectors for financial lifeblood. This is the extension of the present - capitalism alone in control, with individuals under its servitude - a financial market for every engagement and action in the material (and digital) world.

Disaster dystopias are not so different - where the bomb has already fallen, the plague has already destroyed society, the supervolcano has blotted out the sun. Here, hope can only take form in society, navigating the ashes, carving out control against the uncontrollable reality of disaster - and the solutions, paradises, or arcs for a story of exit all exist within the bounds of what is possible with disaster in control of the present. To find optimism against the face of disaster is to inspire hope in action - top take control of what little over which we can exert pressure. Optimism is a weapon against these stark realities, it is the only weapon through which to fight great improbabilities - the Hakagure's samurai facing off against certain death with no regard for their own life.

At the root of these inspired realities is a common theme - that we are not in control of the futures toward which we guided. Either we are led there by a blind and collective fault to which no individual holds blame, or there is a great external pressure over which our fates are stretched.

The most hopeful and the least human of these stories are seen as youthful fantasy - it's a hallmark of young adult fiction for a party of individuals or an individual to have sufficient control over the future that they might avoid, prove, or solve great calamity and thus save the world. That's why it's entertaining in the first place - it seems so improbable that any one group of people could both act enough in the best interest of humanity and have enough control to change the fate of the realities that we experience. It feels naïve, and it is. No one person could truly hold sufficient power to change the future, because no one person could ever hold so much control.

I think the greatest fear of humanity is to be in control and fail. It's a recurring theme in all aspects of improvement on societal and individual levels - that the hardest part of existing is giving up a desire for control when we don't have it. We hinge all aspiration on the illusion of control, and we learn to overcome frustration when we realize that we do not have control.

An Eightfold Path walks toward absolution along a tightrope of personal discipline (control) and willingness to allow existence to proceed without your influence (control). The opiate quality of a higher power, too, is thematic because the greatest situational grace for an individual is to relinquish control of their life to the determinism of a deity - to seek out calm in the recognition of a deterministic designer who can guide the present toward their intended future. Again - control of fate being handed off from the individual (or indeed the collective, with respect to the congregation) to something outside of the individual - because this makes a future that we could be in control of that much more palatable when it isn't in our favor, and puts us less at fault.

Optimism seems to sprout and grow when we take ownership over our direction - when an individual future is something toward which one person can steer, because the rudder is in their hand. There is hope in being called to action - there optimism in appreciating control as an enabling force. When we believe that we can guide fate, much more is possible. Problems feel smaller, more attainable, futures much more a vehicle for our hopes to arrive in, utopias all the more achievable.

When, then, does optimism have to do with sovereignty over control, and how does this apply to collectives, not individuals? Even blind optimism is giving oneself control over willingness to see things proceed in the most favorable direction, though not by our hand, instead by fate. But I am arguing for a more urgent sense of optimism, one that places control back in the hands of collectives, so that individuals feel that they can indeed have influence and guide collectives toward utopias.

The reason utopias feel naïve is due to an inspired sense that we are not in control - that we don't hold the keys to the future. What, then, if we allowed ourselves to believe that we did?

Dystopias do not exist when collectives are in control of the story and the futures being acted upon are in the interest of collectives. Agency is the greatest power we hold as individuals - the liberty to move freely and make choices. Dystopias sprout and fester around a lack of agency - we as individuals cannot move the path. The arc of success against dystopia is the defeat of the forces that impose dystopia and therefore maintain control.
