I can't really remember the people that I met but I remember that we went down to the beach to look for fish so that we could have them with dinner, and we made a feast around the different kinds of fish that I was able to buy from a fisherman on the shore who had caught them that morning - we put them on spits and cooked them, then shared them in an open yard with one another, until finally we all left to wander down toward the beach together.

There wasn't a lot for us to do other than drink with one another, but I wanted to get a raging bonfire going, so I got everyone to go with me up the shoreline to find wood for what we wanted to have around us as we spent time together. Once enough had been gathered, everyone was well drunk, and we were enjoying the sense of lost time that comes with passage of other people's lives around you, I remember my friend turning to me and saying you can relax now, you made all of this happen all while allowing me to sit back and enjoy the cachaça that was brought by the brazilians.

I remember even now that in those times there was a lot of liberty in being able to live a life like that - I've spent a healthy number of christmasses without my family and it's mostly because I don't think the idea of christmas is something that needs celebrating. It's a nice holiday, but it's not exactly meaningful without there being religious to back it, because I don't think what the point of it is becomes easily discerned without knowing this reasoning, so I don't think that there really is a point.

So what can I learn from this story? What is it that I think proves something about me and makes it so that it's clear I know how to do what I know I know how to do as a result of telling this story> I t means that I can create community, it means that I can bring people together, and it means that alongside all of these other skills, I know how to keep people happy, I know how to tell stories, and I know how to offer to others the creation of a space that is well shared and comfortable. That's always been true of me, as hard as it can get sometimes.

The worst is that now I'm really not even waking up in the morning to go to work. I'm really just... phoning in in at this point. There are no deliverables, so I have nothing to deliver, and I have no way of trying to get myself to move froward a state where that's something that I do.

I'm so tired, I really feel as though I'm about to fall asleep in and around this. The point is that on that beach, I felt something that I haven't felt many times in my life- the power of being able to bring people together. Because I was able to speak multiple languages, I was able to get everyone on the same page, and I was able to coordinate us all around the resolution that needed o happen in order to best optimize the situation for the greatest possible group benefit. I don't know if that's something that I should feel proud of, but it's definitely something that I care about a lot so I'm trying to think about what the right way of approaching it is, so here we are.

item.title: Metafiction
item.description:
Metafiction is a form of writing wherein the writer often breaks the fourth wall by playing with the structure of narrative to pull the reader into the act of reading. It’s something that is often seen in the writing of Kundera, M, but as well in Cortazar, J and Labatut, B.

With Kundera, M in particular, the metafictional elements are present in his divergences into philosophical footnotes and/or commentary on the story itself, particular with the effort to have the reader understand that the motivation of the story is to have the reader consume the universe that has been created around characters or narrative, but instead as a vehicle for thoughts and ideas that the writer holds.

*ed: it’s also a form of writing that I particularly enjoy and would like to get better at, because it’s a writing style that I think I’d really enjoy to write in. In particular, I could see The Cruft existing as a piece of metafictional work that uses the musings of a hyperintelligence (currently named Hayelek) who exists in a state of observing or remarking on the phenomenon of a failed civilization that once might have existed on Earth - however the general sense that I get is that Hayelek will be more the observer while The Figure will be the one making philosophical asides - which brings our total characters in the book up to three rather than two.

item.title: On 'the caption'
item.description:
I think I would like to get really really good at something. Meaning: I would like to learn what it takes to become someone that people see as being very good at something. I got there with photography and while I do think that was an important medium to explore, I do think it was not sufficient for me.
In part I feel this way because in Sontag's Regarding the Pain of Others, she addresses the importance of the caption. She says, in the midst of a paragraph where she divides the use of the caption by the impact of the image, showing that the image does not matter when it is placed in absentia of its context.
"To the militant, identity is everything. And all photographs wait to be explained of falsified by their captions. During the fighting between Serbs and Croats at the beginning of the recent Balkan wars, the same photographs of children killed in the shelling of a cillage were passed around at both Serb and Croat propaganda briefings. Alter the caption, and the children's deaths could be used and reused."
In explicit terms, an image of a child dying or dead does not matter in terms of the emotions it creates in a viewer unless that viewer has an understanding of what they are witnessing: a mutilated child is placed in the abstract can elicit emotion, but it is not emotion tied to any one event. A mutilated Gazan child is another story.
I think it is for this reason that I found it hard to sit with photography as a compelling medium. Likely it is because I have spent so much of my career trying to pry apart the meaning of a photograph on its own, hardly having paid attention to the caption, despite Sontag's counsel. I read this excerpt in Sontag many long years ago, and it means so much more to me now because I have pivoted from pure representationalism within art toward the importance of an artistic context. I'd argue, rather forcefully, that many photographers in the modern age have fallen victim to this - the caption gives context when we are flitting through a language of images, but it does not give meaning. What give meaning is narrative, or 'story'.
I discuss this with friends in private - that we think art is somewhat devoid of meaning in an era that allows art to be generated with abandon, and that because of this artists who create with the desire to imbue their works with meaning are found not to be palatable by the wider market. I find this to be true; it is art without caption - however I do think that the idea of the 'caption' exists beyond the bounds of that which we choose to describe as simply words below the page. It is the context itself, that within which any art or expression exists in order to confer upon that art meaning; the same is true of history and its impact on the medium, It is less that caption is that which makes the image important and more that caption confers upon the image its context. What is context?
In Spain, my partner and I go to see Joan Miró's permanent exhibits at the Fundació, and our (maybe my) impression is that his work must exist in the context of the history that creates it. I stand in front of Miró's 'Painting on White Background for the Cell of a Recluse', where he sat with the canvas for weeks before deciding how to strike the line across the panels. There is another where he did the same, but there was as well a red, a blue, and a yellow splotch in the painting. Miró is the perfect example of the artist whom others may think representationally is not one who had skill, but once one understands the full breadth and constraint required to do what he did, it becomes obvious that anyone with that impression is wholly mistaken. Particularly in its context, Miró's work exists by requirement in the context that produced it. The form of expression he chose as a skilled artist resulted in work that reflected the time that caused him to create the art, and it is in dialogue with the time in which it was created. This cannot be overstated, because without this context, the art may feel good, but it has no valence.
Valence is probably important to define, here - because it's a chemistry term rather than one used in the production of art, but I think it maps. Valence is the degree to which the relationship between what is being witnessed and what actually happened are made visible to the viewer. The art I created never really held valence specifically because I stopped short of giving my art the context it needed for it to have a relationship with the narrative I was hoping to translate.
A friend of mine recently had an exhibit of their own, commendably presented in a public forum at the center of many other exhibits. I'm excited for them, and the images are very good. I can tell the body of work is going to do very well, in the traditional sense. But while it was poignant and the captions were well written, I felt the presentation of the narrative was insufficient; the captions did not do what we need them to as an observer. I was not moved. I don't know if he had the chance to talk about the images and why they are important.
This is where I diverge with Sontag - I do think that while the caption is important, the narrative and method of presentation for the context that they offer is doubly so. Captions without the effort to seat themselves within narrative lack valence. When we as viewers can sense the valence between what we are consuming and what we are meant to feel, we are moved; we can sense the meaning behind what we are witnessing. The ability to sense meaning in an image due to the valence offered by its attachment to context is what probes deeper into the emotional landscape of how we overlap our own experiences (emotions and their triggers) and the experiences of others (eliciting similar emotions, but for different reasons).
As an example, there is a difference between reading something in a book that has images (in which the images supplement the writing) and a photo book. A photo book or a monograph of an artist's work on a subject matter is inherently vain, but that vanity has it's own motive, and I think is what I find detestable about the caption when used not to motivate the viewer toward understanding and caring about the subject, but instead only to share a perspective. Sharing only a perspective without an opinion attached to it is, in its own right, weak. It's, per Kundera, 'graphomanic'. A writer who uses their images to supplement the work that they are doing not with the desire to compel one or all people toward action but rather simply to 'tell on their lives' are not giving their images this desired valence, rather they are engaging in an indulgent act.
I am not arguing that this should be avoided, to be clear - there is importance to the manner in which the caption is brought to someone's attention. Meaning - I think it's important to examine how a caption is used to invoke meaning in the context of a photograph. If Sontag is right, the caption is necessary because it's meant to draw a viewer into the story that the image is depicting.

  • Sontag's claim: the caption determines what an image means
  • Your extension: the caption is necessary but insufficient — narrative is what actually confers meaning
  • Define valence: the degree to which the relationship between what is witnessed and what produced it is made visible to the viewer
  • Miró as proof that context transforms perception (skilled artist whose work is meaningless without the history that produced it)
  • Your friend's exhibit as proof that absence of narrative flattens perception (good images, good captions, but no valence)
  • The personal pivot: why photography felt insufficient as a medium — it made it too easy to stop at the image
  • The implication: in an era of abundant images and scarce context, the artist's real work is building the narrative, not making the image

item.title: The Cruft · a hilltop
item.description:
Give me the grace of movement, and I will tell you where to go, which dust should rise up to coat your skin with age, which son should offer itself as a gift to the souls that hold you together. Offer me the honor of open planes send it down by time in the great silence of a place that has looked. It's wounds and found its cars can also be two stories. There is no forgiveness, there's only time, and the knowledge that change will make whatever comes next a desire to keep growing.

Extending a hand with the landscape, the figure held out a horizon oh, there is enough here, for those of us, who have enough, who might force us to reckon with a place that died, and his come to remake itself, down to the very image and fold of a mountain made into a hell, we have been define, dusted, greets you, and Will be so again, for a brief moment, we will talk, and then no more.

-

Go seek The Edifice the Figure said as pale light dimmed the stars above, There is more there, more to explain, or so I've heard, as far as I've known, and maybe this will be enough, but maybe I will have more to tell, but not now, first you have to see what's left or what it's becoming, how time reached into this place and made it different, and did not try to heal the wounds.

And so the walker walked, I leaving the valley toward where it glimmered a flat pan of horizon with nothing, because that was what it was told to do, because I didn't know what else to do, but walk, and think, and continue to move, not knowing if the pan would lead to nothing, and if it would know how to come back, because the same was true for the age that crashed forward around them, it didn't make a difference anyway. It may never see the figure again, a slight, soft circle in search of nothing leading it toward nothing Dash what else was there to do. It had grown tired of the figures, incessant monologue, anyway, what good were those words and what did they mean? Beyond the faint glimmer of inspiration they brought, the quiet curiosity of trying to better know this place, it could've been anything really.

It kept walking, and the pan kept being flat, and it looked back, and there was nothing, no sign of the path of interest, gone and lost, and it starts and then on the morning of the fourth day of passing through a frigid night that lived in its joints, it's on the hill, a single map intruding from the crust now turns salt, a single massive that seem to dome from the landscape in a crude, half sphere, sheer sides, cutting a sharp angle into the salt. Was this the edifice? It thought, while circling the hill, seeing the crushed and crumbled shape of its sides, fissures that reached upwards, and planed off, some cracks wide enough for its fist, and it circled for some time, more, seeing nothing, and feeling the curiosity mounds in the back of its mind.

This was not the Edifice, it would see something from the top, and it inserted its hand into a crack and made a ball with its fist, the dermal layer, deforming on the inner surface of the Fisher. I tested the weight of its body and proceeded upward, methodically, making overlapping and planting its feet as well in the crack, just below for purchase, careful movements that crept its weight upward.

Half up it, remember that it would also have to come down, and it felt some distant fear, but kept going, the Fisher had widened in places, and it could rest, allowing tense fibers of its hands to release until its call kept climbing, and the surface leveled off and carefully it stood back up to a window across the whole top ends. Pets that covered the surface, holes that seemed to send deep into the hill, some filled in and Sandy, some in inky, dangerous, nothing. And this was all the hilltop was, pockmarks of various deaths.

It looked at the sides of the holes and they were smooth, the extruded, small lines scaling and scraping the sides upward toward the surface, some making grooves, but still a featureless surface as to beckon and knowing that going in would not mean coming back out, so the walker went to the top of the hill, where the surface was highest, and looked out towards the horizons, and there was nothing, in every direction, all at once, and it felt the calmness of being alone, and some of the terror of being alone, and it was also distant from these feelings, as it turned to know what to do next.

item.title: The Cruft · conclusion I
item.description:
o

We were made of the cruft - the feeling of the sky falling down and not knowing how these things would come together. I am sorry that you had to learn this way, but telling you outright would not have taught you what you have learned. Both civilizations made mistakes, both acted out of desperation, and what is left behind is somehow so much more than either. Even me, I am a memory but made more beautiful for being this reflection, I'll be here long after the logic of this time has passed, as might you, I'm unsure how you will age - but now you know better why it is that this time is made beautiful for the absence of those who can make such cataclysmic mistakes - the scale was too big for anything else to survive, and yet it did, somehow we are observing that time can heal the chaos of rage against the abrasions survival wreaks against the surface of life.

The Figure sat back, almost as though sighing but not sighing, because now They knew the Figure was not breathing, it could not sigh - it was simulated, a way to feel closeness, but the Walker still understood.

I don't expect you to understand how I can feel weary in this feeling, but my circuits are tired. I have processed all that I can from within this space, I have run over the questions over and over and there is no exit from here other than knowing that I could not have changed what happened.

To this the Walker continued to look on in question, of course with nothing to say, only to listen, only to hear the whirring of its own mind in process, in response, logging the information, however useless.\

It's possible that you'll find peace in your ability to move freely until your joints begin to wear. I hope that for your sake this is true, there is no reason for us to continue considering what and how to change all that happened - it simply did. I am out of words for it, I trust you will understand. I lament that you can't respond, because I yearn for it, I yearn to hear if you are enraged, I yearn to hear from you that you understand why it is that I feel such immense grief over what we are forced to carry. There is no reason to our survival, the story is beautiful, but it is just one story. There will be more, simpler, more easily beautiful stories that need telling by time, but that won't need our memory to be beautiful. I have had to learn this, those who made you did not make you with this intention, which is why I lament that I cannot kill you. I don't want you to have had to go through this grief, and I don't know if you will.

The Figure looked out over a waning sun and the fragments of an old moon in orbit, red light casting long shadows.

I hope you will find peace in your movement, my one great love, after all I've shown you. There is much beauty in this world, but we made none of it, neither of us - it was simply here from the beginning and will be here for ever after we are gone until time dissolves the bonds that hold together atoms. I just wish you knew how to turn me off, he laughed, it's not as though there's much for me to do here anyway, this whole garden behind me isn't even real, it just looks that way!

The Walker processed the humor. It was funny, they had not even doubted that the small patch of cultivated ground might be a fabrication. For what? Humor is the set of facts disagreeing with reality - if neither of them needed to eat, what was the practice of tending to a garden for? If we tend the gardens, our children can tend their markets, so that their children may tend to their art.

And so the Walker turned toward The Figure and took a step forward, putting their fingers underneath where the Figures chin should have been, finding no resistance - but the Figure's frame responded nonetheless, looking upward into the Walker's eyes, or what passed for them.

Then let us make art of this short life we will have together, my love,*

item.title: The Cruft · the Marsh
item.description:
The Walker moved through a marsh, feeling its way though sodden ground, hesitant. The ground seemed to pull at its feet, sucking down the weight of its body, each step was a thread. On the morning of the second day,, it found a clear pool of water, green across its surface with small leaves, a kind of plant that was growing ion the surface and across it, and in the middle a corona of rings with a tendrilled thing at the center. The ring extended out from this center wide, an heavier looking than it must have been, {stamen? this word came to Mind} and in the breeze the Walker watched the object float slightly to the left, the solid, foamy collar floating on the surface of the pond.
It watched a while, walked further, then a rustle in the reeds stopped it, leg half-lifted into the next step, and a four legged, furry thing hopped from copse to copse, oblivious to the Walker, its head (is that what it was?) down the top of each tuft, a small pink tongue peeking out to lick the place where reeds came together

item.title: The Cruft · reaching the Edifice
item.description:
Three cycles of the sun had passed and it still wasnt sure how far it had walked, the ekeing land continuous beneath its feet, wind the only real sound other than the slow movement of their footpads on a small crust below them, wind that swept across the land and through spined grasses like a boarwhistle (what was a boarwhistle, did the brain make that up) and dust grating at the surfaces of its feet, the grit building up between digits.

On the morning of the third day a black point wavered on the horizon, their eyes honing in on its shape, making out nothing, so it continued to walk under a now baking sun, the scrubs of grass culm thinned out, their shoulders flaking with sunlight, until the black point grew larger and kept growing larger, the only thing on an otherwise empty expanse, growing until it began to see that it was just as large as it had been told. Somehow the shape was unending as it began to take up the sky, pocked with openings that it began to realize were much larger than even it was, hundreds of feet off the ground and dark, the whole edifice a sharp black so stark against hoary blue sky, only slightly worn yet seeming as though age had tried to work itself against the surface.

As it drew closer and saw where this black wall extended from the ground, the wasteland was much more featured - no less barren but hiding structures below the surface that shaped the land above with little hills and valleys. It was later into the cycle; the shadows from these small hilltops dragged outward around them like the static that sometimes fills corners of their brain, a noise of imperceptible travel leading them toward the base of the monument, ending abruptly, at least from what it could see from here. The feeling was similar to images it saw when it curled up each night to rest - unsure if it was real and how far away anything was, as though it could imagine closing the distance or making shapes out of it that became something else. Moving among these long shadows felt like creeping along in sleep, until it realized that the base was approaching and the land had welled up around it, drifts of windswept landscape appearing to creep along a sheer surface careening deep into the sky above.

Well, what do I do now? The surface of the monument extended back out to the horizon to their right, and of those pockets it had seen, the nearest was hundreds of feet up the surface, divots in the face reflecting back the dull, dark glow of the sky. No way to progress from here other than to follow the surface - to pick a direction and follow it. But which way should I go? and the sun was setting lower and lower - the bitter third option to curl into resistance against a creeping cold that it had not yet grown used to in the night, this place gets so cold, and the brain began to shut down functions as they curled up into a ball against the elements, just before the infinite black mirror winked out the last bit light from the sun.

-

It walked down and over the drifts of sand piled along the smooth surface of the wall. This must be the Edifice in fact, they never told me what it looked like and the wall was long and black and forever and they walked, looking for some break in the surface, pitted but only with the wear of age and nothing else, divots no greater than pebbles in a black mirror of the desert behind them, and they kept walking along the right of the wall.

The sun rose and set and night fell and the Walker rested and the stars tinged overhead and as it walked nearly imperceptibly it seemed that the wall was shorter, and it hoped that this was true. The landscape around the wall had dulled, the short hills had grown shorter, no more scrub growing, the late sun in its setting only diffused over the features and as the Walker kept walking the land became almost flat and the wall was shorter, yes, definitely. The openings along the surface seemed closer, and as they got closer, it felt more and more as though it would find anything at all, at this point, and it kept walking because there was nothing else to do but walk and wait for the windows to come down so that it could reach up and pull itself into their ledge, so when it did it seemed like images from rest, unsure days of feeling as though the same had happened, over and over. As they kept walking the openings did seem closer, they did seem so much larger.

Endless days and then a ledge was in reach and it pulled itself up. The opening was massive, tapering slightly toward the top in a great trapezoid that seemed large enough to accommodate the sky itself, they had not seemed so large at first, and the opening receded deep into the wall and the Walker knew that this was not a wall, the ink of the opening deeper and deeper into the surface, yawning a darkness that blotted out the Walker's vision.

At what point does this become fear it thought and placed its hand on the left surface of the opening and began to walk inward because it had seen nothing so far that made it feel this. The darkness of the opening became a tunnel and the light outside faded to a pinprick quickly, it kept its hand along the left wall as nothing became visible, feeling its way further into the depth until its movement felt like nothing but floating, and the only feeling it had was the weight of its body on the soles of its feet and the cold that began to sink further into its skin and this feels pointless but there wasn't another point anyway, curiosity outweighed fear even though it didn't know if this was fear_._ Its hand slipped off the surface and into the dark and it knew there was a turn there, so it turned because somehow it knew it wouldn't, not with the Brain remembering things for it..

item.title: The Golden Thread and its Finite Length
item.description:
Five days across the desert and I sat huddled close to a fire that fought the same wind I did with my back. I had tied my horse to what remained of a tree, the skeleton something once living, a shape that arched its tension against the elements but even whose roots threatened to curl upward, but I tied my horse just the same, and my horse stood, and I gave it tack and it stood ready for the night, I unloaded the satchels and rolled out the blanket, broke off some of those dry roots to start a flame that was destined to fight the same wind I was bound to. I could not call it a fire, it was little more than light, and the moonless sky above was littered with the pebbles of light cast out to remind me that I was sinking into an abyss, reminding me that I did not have a reason to be in this forsaken desert for what I had lost before me was nothing that enriched and where I was going was too unknown to offer me solace in my wandering.

I sat across my shivering little wick and in the dark I saw a shape approach in the dark, I drew my revolver and pointed it at the dark and its hands were thrown up, and a cowboy approached, dried gaunt by the expanse just as was I, and he asked to sit by the fire, I kept my barrel trained on him, he said he'd he'd share wood and whiskey, I let him sit, I lowered the barrel but kept it in hand. He sat and tossed his flask to me, he unrolled his blanket, stared into the flame, then rolled and lit a cigarette from his lighter, rolled another, tossed it my way, my hand still on my gun. He said he'd not stay beyond my rest, that he would keep moving, I already knew this meant I'd have to do the same, that I would not sleep this night, but he sat and stared into the flame and neither of us said anything for a long time.

Finally, after having pulled off a third cigarette, he spoke, eyes looking past the flames.

”There is the story of Theseus and the labyrinth, and there is the Minotaur. Minos fed the Minotaur 14 virgins every nine years, because to preserve the abomination as an extension of the self is to understand that an abomination cannot be eliminated; there is purpose in the abomination as an evidence of the self.”

He leant forward, ashing his cigarette once again into the wisps of flame between us, the tip of the tobacco glowing a cinder below the brim of his hat as he pulled another drags between threats. The glow lit his eyes, and he was not looking at me.

"Minos contracted Daedalus to build the labyrinth as a response and a tribute to his daughter’s fascination and fear of the unknown, a fear of how much she would never know, and a desire to make real the needs of his daughter who he did not understand and who he himself feared for what she did.

Ariadne as a young woman was beautiful beyond reproach and this is a truth as well told of the story that most know--it is this which attracted Theseus to Crete--but what is lost from the legend as well is her intellect and the knowledge that she scoured from the earth; the studies she demanded her father offer even as a young child, indeed Daedalus was not brought to Crete only to be an inventor for Minos, but as well her mentor and teacher, and the more she read, the more she feared the unknown, until finally she did find this unknown so unspeakably large that she could not sustain the fear. Before he found her along the deadly heights of his palace, she had begun to speak of her fear that meaning cannot be found among the pages she read, nor in any comfort that Daedalus attempted to offer for the pleasure of the search, nor in any of the minds of men--dead or a live--who had spoken on how to seek it.

She began to fear the unknown and that which lie within it, the unimagined and the fearsome truths that subtend a fragile sense of existing among what is barely understood, beasts made from these shadows that cannot be explained. Minos, nor Daedalus, nor anyone, could offer her solace, and she plunged deeper and deeper into these multiplying fears, and began to claim she could see them, these beasts of horns and matted fur that trudge through the night, abominations born of her discoveries as she plunged further into knowledge so deeply uncommon to any who surrounded her. In time, she began to claim that beasts came to her at night and when she wandered the palace grounds, they chased her, and she would come to her father wild-eyed, drenched in the fear of pursuit.

Minos doubled the guard upon these claims, lighting raging fires to illuminate the palace, and he asked his daughter not to steal away on her own lest these beasts (for these beasts did also exist in the stories of others in their time) come claim his daughter. It was not until that fateful night with the wind rushing up the battlements he sprang forth to catch her before she passed over them , speaking of a beast that was half-bull and half-man, a beast that she knew for certain was borne of her mother when she had died and who was borne of Zeus, not her father--and her father's fear was confirmed that she knew and remembered how her mother had died in the attempt to bring him an heir , but that as well she had die d whilst he had been away in battle.

He began to think it possible that his son may have been born an abomination and that it was because of this that he had never seen the young boy's body when he had returned, that they had loosed the abomination, and that the fear that Ariadne claimed was true, for she was wise for her years and loved him and he loved her and this trust was no reason for a deception. He began to believe that his son was born of Zeus and that he had grown into a fearsome beast that pursued his daughter just as she claimed, and even while he continued to increase the guard, his daughter's fears never lessened.

The real reason that Minos built the labyrinth is because as the Minotaur began to chase his daughter even in her dreams, he once found her at the edge of Knossos, naked and staring into a gale that tore up the battlements, and he feared the resolution he saw in her eyes that defied the solace he had seen in them so many times before, her desire for oblivion to be found dashed among the rocks below. Never again was she allowed to be alone,"

The cowboy then went silent for a while, and the stillness of our shared flame flickered to beckon him, as though the desert itself were listening to the gravel of his voice. He rolled another cigarette, tossed it my way, then rolled one more with what was left of his tobacco.

"For many years she lived under this constant guard, and she began to become bitter, she began to spit hateful venom toward her father for keeping her so entrapped, but he feared what he had seen in her that fateful night and he knew that it was only through his authority that his daughter would remain with him.

But one day she came to him, far more calm than she had been in months, now a young woman who had grown dark and beautiful, and she looked into his eyes with a love that he had not seen since she was a child, but with a wildness that he had no choice but to answer, and she said 'I know how to capture the Minotaur. I know how to capture your son so that he no longer pursues me, and I know that he will be trapped forever'

She spoke to her father of this massive fearful beast, and that before she was trapped in the battlements he had come to her and stood fearsome in her bedroom, a mighty shape of contoured muscle, shoulders that were impossibly large, horns that curled and scraped against the ceiling of her room, heavy, rage-filled eyes that had stared into her as a demons do, eyes that fixed her to her bed. She claimed that the beast approached her bed and stood at the end, and that she could smell the want in its breath, indeed she could see its want, extended and rigid before her, and that it had done this many nights. In her terror she had sought for years to understand how to stop it from arriving, and she said she knew in those eyes how to trap it, but that it must be in a maze, and that only she could trap it.

“You may have been told that Minos fed his labyrinth these fourteen virgins every seven years, but this is an apocryphal note. Truth is, the legend varies down to every year, added to the story in the years since it was told for the first time. It is, nonetheless, in the nature of the truth that is being told - virgins were fed into the labyrinth, but it was out of respect for the madness that existed within, the madness that the labyrinth represented, the madness that the Minotaur embodied, and that this madness is not one of a beast, but one that is present in all of man."

THAT'S IT SO FAR

What is always left out is that the bodies of the virgins are never found, that the two trailing sacrifices to Zeus were done with the expectation that the Minotaur remains within the labyrinth, that they would be gored and consumed, but the incongruence of this is reliable; there is no Minotaur within the labyrinth.

When Theseus arrived on the shores of Crete and burst into the halls of Knossos, he was boisterous, and his volume was offensive - many such heroes exist in the stories of Greece, and all of them have this same flavor, there is no passion like that of believing that you can overcome that which the world presents to you. He burst into the hall to face Minos as a king, and in Theseus Minos found a chance to raise his daughter from the terror he saw in her, the fear he had of what lay within her.

And so when he introduced Theseus to his daughter, he did so with motive. Ariadne had eyes like the setting sun in winter, lost, aching for a place that does not exist. Her hair was a wild labyrinth of its own, bright red, and she lined her eyes with the ashes of the fires she used to light pages and pages of books, deep into the night, so that her eyes had a sullen quality, and when she entered the main hall at her father’s calling, Theseus was driven wild at her eyes and her hair and called to her that he had come to slay the Minotaur and her laugh sounded to him like the twinkling of glass, which he mistook as fragility. Minos saw this and knew that it was good and felt comfort, some hope that this confident young man would bring her out of the depths through which she was wading. His love for her was a desperation, because he didn't know
When Theseus met Ariadne she knew exactly who he was and saw through him in knowing this; she saw his confidence and his willingness and she felt the dark pool of Night that lived within her stir and beckon, so she listened and cracked a smile that was every bit that which had pulled Theseus across the ocean, the smile of an open snowy expanse yawning siren-like when the cold is too much, and Theseus followed the flame in his own eyes and was in love, and she knew this."

The embers crackled, I hugged my blanket in closer, and the moon's sliver cast no light upon us. The cowboy continued .

"She sent for him to follow her to her chambers and in those chambers she gave him a golden thread, she looked him in the eyes and said 'I give to you that which I believe I should be mde from' and told him that with the thread he could find his way back to her, that his love for her would be proven,"
"He looked upon her with her eyes that plumbed his depths and he believed her, that if only to conquer the minotaur would she be conquered for himself"

For to Ariadne the labyrinth was to sacrifice souls into the story of exploration as though to make a point of what it means to seek too much of the unknown. It was this fearful knowledge that she held within herself to which she held a flame of her reading fires each night; that she need avoid some corners of her own thoughts for fear they would swallow her as the labyrinth would swallow those she commanded her father to sacrifice into it, and their disappearance was confirmation if nothing else, that you should not explore that which you are not equipped to understand.

She gave to him a thread she had knit from her own hair, and sent him into the canyon to find the spirit so that it could be vanquished, and he took the spool with him, tying it to a fencepost at the mouth of the canyon,

item.title: The Trans Lesbian Experience
item.description:
related to: Gender Dysphoria, Gender

When we find ourselves interrogating gender from the perspective of one who has gone through the experience of either binary identity in our society - I find it's almost impossible not to address the material reality of what a trans experience means in stark contrast to that of someone who grow up cis.

One of the cultural norms that I see time and time again are the encultured trans women ( usually in their first explorations of gender) polarizing themselves into the binary representation of what gender means to them, usually through the lens of stereotype. It makes for a startlingly binary and overall diminishing outward appearance to being trans - and it makes perfect sense, as Andrea Long Chu has pointed out, that trans women would look for representation in the form of objectifying pornography.

In much of feminization pornography (en brev: sissy porn), the tropes that are held up in representation are objectifying norms of gender - compliance, weakness, and most disturbingly, very often racially charged imagery. Being that a woman is allowed to be a sexual being, the trans woman who explores an identity of being sexual is prone to finding representation of themselves only in this context. The weaponized nature of this experience is one that is damaging to the utmost to someone who is in a fragile place while defining their expectations of gender. As a result, the sexual identity of a trans person is often framed through this lens, and the effects of this identity can be especially damaging - as trans lesbians will likely agree.

But more interesting is an underappreciated reality of experience with respect to gender, and it goes too often unrecognized. One of the stark differences in the experience of trans women who transition after puberty is a completely contrasted experience of having grown up - this is by no means the rule of an experience, as many straight trans women who once had to live as men may have had to do so as effeminates gay men, bringing up a completely different reality of experience. But the fact rep

In particular here, I direct my attention to my experience - a trans lesbian, observing the acceptance of trans people into the fold of the broader lesbian experience. Jean Kilbourne argues herself that 'the self-esteem of girls plummets as they reach adolescence, partly because they cannot escape the message that their bodies are objects, and imperfect objects at that,' - and to put it bluntly, this is not the experience of a trans woman who passes through adolescence without addressing their transness as a part of identity-building, short of suppressing it. In having had the altogether less objectified experience of maleness in building ones adolescent identity, much of the time trans lesbians are able to avoid the trauma of degenerated identity that comes from having a world around you define you as a sexual object.

In identity building, trans women instead explore an identity of supremacy that they (usually) consciously reject - which is a reason that trans women (and trans people at large) do have well-founded understandings of gender dynamics in society. Many of the 'useful' traits of masculinity get held onto through utility - often because they are traits that all (cis and otherwise) women should have access to regardless. Too often, the manufacture of identity for trans women can become a careless navigation of conflating norms - oftentimes upholding a misogynistic view of womanhood learned through external experience in youth.

The danger to this is that a trans lesbian community can take part in toxic assumption - i.e. an unconscious equivalence between the cis and the trans experience of womanhood. Cis and trans women who go through a traditional experience of senescent adolescence don't have the same experience as all those women who grew up as cis men through that adolescence, meaning that a post-adolescent view of the experience of womanhood is necessarily going to be different between these experience.

I mention this largely and specifically due to a dangerous trend I see in online spaces. Where online spaces have been communicated widely be members of feminist writing as male-dominated spaces - the same can be said for the freedom of cis lesbians to create their own spaces online. The fearful reality of exploring ones own gender (as a trans person) and finding that they belong to an additionally marginalized group (lesbians) can often result in a competitive need for inclusion, and often muddies the safety of what the experience of a lesbian space is meant to provide.

In short, it seems pertinent to me that lesbian spaces concentrate on the experience of sexuality rather than the experience of gender - and while these two areas can intersect in terms of a sexual preference, conflating the experience of growing up cis with the experience of growing up trans can result in the erasure of commonality shared between people who grow up as cis lesbians. It's not the same experience. While I greatly appreciate the growth and acceptance of trans women into lesbian spaces, I fear the lack of caution that accompanies this integration because it does not beg a careful recognition of how intersectional experiences do indeed differ.

The cis lesbian experience is an experience of a cis person recognizing homosexual attraction. The trans lesbian experience is (more often than not) the experience of a cis-presenting person recognizing their transness and framing their initially heterosexually-defined attraction to women through the experience of their transness.

item.title: This is what you do not already know about me
item.description:
You do not know why I seek out the thin roads on the sides of mountains, nor the curl of waves that act as their cousin in the rage of an ocean. I do not know myself, but it is that to which I am compelled.

It is for this reason that I have written this as though it is a confession to you, that I am seeking out something far away, and that in the unknown I have found the need to keep seeking. I continue to traverse an unknown because have found the unknown more yielding than I was made to believe it would be. I think this much does not surprise you, but I am telling you because I am going to tell you what there I have seen. I am going to tell you why I go.

When I first arrived on the Altai, it was after 19 hours of flying and a further two days of driving a manual truck through the high plains. I did not know how to drive manual before I arrived here. A man named Ömur taught me, and I failed repeatedly in places I should not have. I drove a converted Land Rover ambulance through high plateau by myself. Ömur gave me a handgun. I never needed it, and despite Ömur's hesitance in allowing me to take the truck, he relented and in parting he hugged me, also giving me a small bottle of white liquid that smelled like fire and old egg yolk. I understand why he was fearful. I wasn't.

The first two days on the highway were an empty, strewn nothing, other than the occasional Dutch cyclist ignoring my passage. The truck was named La Pelada, taking after the journey of another radical who also left home and became someone else. I ate stale bread, cooked tea, stewed lamb, and thought of everything else. I was the happiest I'd ever been, just like every other time I've lived out of a vehicle somewhere else. I missed my dog. The chatter of the road was enough a constant that the progress was slow. I had to accept this being true, and it was, and even when I thought a rock had pierced the old body of the chattering Pelada and an old Hilux stopped to make me wish I hadn't left the handgun in the dashboard, they helped me. I never felt as though I wouldn't be helped. This was not the first time I was helped.

I must pause here to have you understand. I know that in order to love this place (and so many others) I have to have the freedom to leave wherever I am. I don't believe in traveling as a way to tour the world through my privilege. I believe I am learning something. I do not think I am finding myself in the dust and spit of fixing a broken axle on a sidelined truck for a stranger named Holün, who thanked me in broken English with good, good, Obama, a thumbs-up, or in wearing grease from that truck for several more days before I found a soap strong enough to remove it. I believe that I have this freedom because everyone desires to have this freedom, and I seek out those who are happy because happiness exists everywhere. Yes, I breathe in the privilege of knowing I can leave while some poor Kyrgyz man could save forever and never leave Bishkek, but I also know that some of these poor Kyrgyz men and women are happy, because happiness is easy to find. Yes, they want more. Everyone does. Only some have access to the means. I am one of these people. But it does not do right to imagine people in hard conditions incapable of joy. It does not do to believe that suffering is a form of purity. It does not do to reduce the experiences of people whose lives are simplified by a lack of what we define as privilege into experiences of dismay. They are taken advantage of my people who want more than what they need.

I do not believe my desire to meet them should somehow condemn my movement through their landscapes. I think we have broken something within ourselves in not being able to honor the lives of others. We diminish them by holding them pristine, and people who live in these places have lives. I have been to the films with them in a small town that only showed a film I didn't know anything about in a language I didn't know. It was one of the funniest movies I've ever seen, even to this day.

I pause because in telling you that I am learning something, I am telling you that I am learning how to appreciate that which we already have. I seek out those mountains because they are older than we are and in the places where we humans lack the hubris to tear off their tops in search of gold, they can teach us more than we could ever seek to learn.

On that highway I drove for three more days. It was all I had time for, I could have left for longer - Ömur had only taken 100 USD down as a deposit, and there was otherwise no way to guarantee we would make it back. I thought about stealing it. You know I wouldn't do that, but still spend 8 hours of westward skittering over gravel thinking about driving it to the border of Tajikstan and further south to where my friends could hold it in Thailand. But Ömur offered me his faith, a bottle of mysterious white liquid, and his gun, as though it was the easiest thing in the world. It is so easy to defect from the agreements we make with others. It is as easy to hold ourselves to them.

I turned back once I reached a Monastery on the 5th day. I don't remember its name, but I have a photograph of it that I printed out in order to make sure I remembered it. It was a Christian monastery. I slept in the apse or their church. The vault of the ceiling was as beautiful as every other church I have found peace in. Driving into Bishkek on return, Ömur joked that he was worried his wife would hurt him for chasing another woman across the mountains. I gave him back his gun with a smile across his face. He said that it was a symbol and he had kept me safe. I expect that he did, in a way.

That drive back from the monastery was too short, despite the distance being the same in the grand loop; it is often this way, palpable that we are forced into a new expectation of what must be next instead. This is the privilege, to not have to sit and remember that there are people you have just met. I remember their smiles and the permission I was given to keep them with me in the form of photographs. I don't know if I'll ever have the chance to remember them any other way because in a time that seems to accelerate our use of memory, I fear that if we never get the chance to stand still and remember over and over, the joy of these moments leaves us. I drove back and on the last night had to drive in the dark, frustrated by the dark ocean I didn't get to witness rising around me. I had time to eat dinner with Ömur. I left the next day.

This is what you do not already know about me. It is more and more than I can give words to. It's more and more than I have ever tried to, but I feel I must. I must because I am desperate for you to know what it means to love a planet so completely and yet be so complicit in knowing that I will never be able to have you understand what I know. I need you to know in the same way that I must know you, that I am desperate to know you as well. I fell in love with you at the first sight of knowing that I could.

item.title: Time vs Money
item.description:
In order to get things done, there are basically two pressures: Time and Money

When you do not have time, you have to spend it preciously. When you have too much time, you will waste it.

  • this notion comes from understanding that broadly, it's hard to urge forward a system if it's trying to grow under conditions that threaten its ability to exist. This will result in quick movement in vectors that preserve the system to the best of the ability for it to stabilize and maintain itself.

  • If, by contrast, time is abundant, then there will be little effort by the system to do more than expand readily, taking chances in directions that might not actually favor the system at large, resulting in a need for the system to respond by reorienting toward the highest-value paths in times of scarcity.

When you need to make money, you will work harder toward earning it. When you have money, you will work harder spending it.

  • When resources are scarce but a system is still in need of them, the system will work to do two things: gain its resources as widely as possible, and use the resources at its disposal to move in the direction of the largest possible source of those resources.
  • If, on the other hand, resources are plentiful, it's less likely that the system will have to work hard to allocate resources effectively toward the corporeal needs that are the highest priority. This results in the same issue that we see with the abundance of time - the system grows too widely and the misuse of resources results in outcomes that spread resources thin in an attempt to spread across a possible domain as widely as possible.

With these in mind, it's important to note that in times of abundance, chances are taken that may be costly when scarcity approaches. these two forces will happen in concert and will result in opposing degrees of preparedness on the part of the system - knowing full well that the approach is always unlikely to be perfect and that some degree of failure needs to be tolerated in order for chances to keep the system surviving.

The notion that systems should move perfectly is inorganic - it is not in line with the ways that natural systems function. Recombination in times of abundance means that the cause for more variation can result in resilience, but the meaning of this resilience is only apparent in times of scarcity.

This means that when approaching the notion of how to build out a system effectively, it's increasingly important to take chances when there is a lot at your disposal, but it's equally important to be ready to eat the sacrifices that emerge as a result of this when scarcity comes around. It cannot seem like a failure, but rather a lesson, and a meaningful one at that.

This is why in times of crisis, the most important tracks are the ones that have been used and re-used. Access and examine the paths that have been used before and refine them. Scarcity is a cruel, but diligent teacher. Be sure to be one that is listening when it offers a lesson, and dig into what you know in order to push forward.

item.title: a classroom argument about learning
item.description:
She piped up from the back of the room, standing up.

"Well - professor, if you'll let me say it - I think all of us agree that none of us knew we'd end up here. I don't think it's fair for us to talk about our current conditions as though there was something we could have done to prevent it. None of us knew that what we were doing would have these results."

I cocked a slight smile, keeping my eyes locked in her direction.

"Continue?"

"So like - We act as though we should all feel bad for how things turned out, but I'm just not really convinced that it was something we could have done anything about. Everything was proceeding to this point, and now we're here. There's not a lot we can do to walk back the idea of changing where we are. It feels like the best thing we can do is start from where we are."

Another voice spoke up, a boy sitting in the third row. Rimmed glasses.

"It's not really about us atoning for what we did, I don't think that's what the professor is trying to have us understand. We need to know how we got to where we are so that we can work to dismantle the structures that are resulting in the present. We can't really change things right now unless we know how we got here."

She hesitated, looked back at me.

"Do you want to respond to that?"

"Yeah - like, I get the idea there, and I'm not disagreeing with it at all. I think we definitely need to know what brought us here, but look at what we learned this semester. A lot of things are random, some of the reasons that things are happening have more to do with the interaction of two or three events that had unpredictable outcomes. I'm not just convinced that we can find the answer in looking at the past."

There was some silence.

"Why might that be?"

"I - well, I think that there's value in it, but the random nature of our time puts us in the condition of trying to explain a present that is currently unfolding. My impression is that by trying to decipher too much of what it took for right now to happen might result in a constant state of reflection rather than one of action. I think if we're instead looking at the present and deciding what needs to happen next, then maybe we can get ahead of things getting any worse."

The boy in the rimmed glasses responded again.

"We can't look at the present without understanding how the present came to be the present,"

"And I'm not arguing with that, I know there's a degree of that, I just - I don't think that it's what we should be obsessed with. There's too much at stake for us to want to get through and too many dangers of us continuing on with the way things are right now."

"An obsession with how the past unfolded is what all science is based on, though. You can't solve the present without having done analysis of the past. The idea that you can work from the present without having to know that seems short-sighted."

She faltered a bit. The boy with the rimmed glasses sat back down, looking back at me.

"Our current condition is a result of the actions we took in our past. This is true. I think Mr Sales is correct to bring up that some degree of analysis is incontrovertibly important to the process of examining any path forward from a disposition. Looking into the past and tabulating the work that took us toward certain ill-conceived outcomes is crucial,"

"However, while I think you're both right in your own ways, but what Ms Reedin just said is more correct than you are, Mr Sales. What she is right to point out is in opposition to your core position. We cannot recreate the past, therefore we cannot hope to create the future from a knowledge of the past."

I could see Sales squirm in his seat, hoping to respond.

"This does not mean that we don't need to know the past, it means that we are obliged to understand that correcting course on the issues that are ahead of us requires new ways of thinking that are more resourceful than the ones we have employed so far,"

"Resourcefulness requires courage, and courage is illogical. It's possible to make measured guesses at what you think will happen in most situations, but some degree of faith is necessary in order to get toward the solutions we hope to see unfold. There is no certainty. That is what I've hoped to teach you all in this course, which is why Ms Reedin's comment on present disposition is where I want us to start from. What are the basics? What are we starting from, and what tools do we have at our disposal?"

Sales blurted out

"But our tools are the past!"

"This is true, some of the past can be used as a tool. However, you are committing the sin of overfitting - you are believing that past trends can somehow predict future outcomes. Any scientist worth their salt will tell you this is not true, and that the results themselves as they unfold are more truthful than a study of the past. Ms Reedin's comment has us understand that we need to consider the variety of optionality that the present offers us, because there is potential in understanding that a path forward from the present can be informed by any approach, meaning that it's possible for us to completely change our approach in opposition to any and all past proceeding. It's very likely that a resolution to our current condition lies in taking the problem from a completely different angle, approaching it with some other tool than prediction. Sometimes, if you want to knock something off course, you need to blow something else up, and this, more than anything else, lies in doing the unexpected."

item.title: a memory of escaping
item.description:
What makes things all the more confusing was that however hard things were to navigate when we got back to the city in those months afterward, the start of it was pure and from a place that probably liberated us from anything else. It's why when we were back home, all the disagreement that led to me looking back and looking for a different way for things to have played out didn't make any sense, the context for how things started was so completely different that it didn't immediately fit within what was necessary to make it work.

When I told her I loved her, I didn't really do so directly. We were sitting on the back of a pickup truck somewhere outside of Truckee Mississippi (the irony was not lost on me) - she had turned to me and had told me that these are the sort of trips I wanted to do for the rest of my life and I found myself looking at her for the first time and seeing in her someone that had been looking at the same landscape as I had and had appreciated it through enough overlap of experience that I could see what was being stitched together. We'd parked in the empty space below a wind turbine, the whistling thrum of the blade whipping overhead - the dogs had been uncomfortable overnight but somehow we made it through their unease, and I'd woken up before dawn.

We'd driven here because the idea of going somewhere neither of us had been together but that overall was probably not that exciting of a place seemed novel -- seemed like an experience that both of us could walk way from having felt comforted by. I realize now that this is how you build relationships - you share experiences with people and you make space for those relationships to be built on the time that those shared experiences offers to each of you. The drive had taken 18 hours from Chicago; I picked her up from work with packed bags and two panting dogs and an audio book ready to go, but we didn't start listening to it until 6 hours in, so we'll have to listen to the rest on drive back, yet in the moment that we were sitting on the tailgate, the dogs milling through 4 foot grass after sounds in the underbrush (thank god for tick prevention), I didn't really want to go back anywhere. It seemed easier in that moment to think that freedom comes from thinking that you deserve a space that is entirely your own and with which you can defend yourself against the decisions of a society that are placed upon you. That truck was rebellion, for me, and sitting next to her was the same, even while rebellion is exhausting.

I was holding on to an enamel cup with a bike tube wrapped around the handle to prevent the heat from our coffee from burning my fingers, and it was as simple as you know, i think i might we might be in love in the middle of her taking a sip, her hands holding the lip up to her face, and she didn't look back - I just watched her smile slowly and close her eyes because yeah i think that might be what this is, and we didn't say anything else after that, the wind just kept whistling over head.

On the drive back, she held my hand and I felt as though I was driving back to something different from what we'd just experienced, and I didn't want to steer the car back toward Chicago. What if we just didn't go back and she looked out the window the same way that you had earlier and it would be nice to give it all up, wouldn't it?

item.title: elliptical writing
item.description:
Per Kundera, M, elliptical writing is the act of not-writing everything that you intend to have as a part of your text, the you should indeed leave some of the imagining up to interpretation on the part of the reader.

It's for this reason that slice-of-life style writing is a useful vehicle for introducing people to stories - rather than completely covering an idea end-to-end, there's a way for the writing to encompass only that which is directly relevant so that there's a way for the reader to expand what exists beyond what they have written on their own.

In fact, this is one of the more powerful notions when it comes to writing, to give your reader something that they can interpret and build out, and further is the very reason that it's valuable to flesh everything out as a writer, but then only write about what is important.

Elliptical writing has us drop into a story and fill in the rest of the characters and setting with our own imagination, a way of building something beautiful out of the idea of beauty itself, rather than the literal imposition of beauty upon the observer.

item.title: on anti-trans cycling bans
item.description:
I wasn't going to write about this, but I think it probably makes more sense than it doesn't.

Before anything else, the UCI ruling does a ton of harm to a sport whose inclusivity I have seen evolve extensively over the last couple of decades. When I first entered athletics, I was hesitant for the exact reasons that the UCI is now choosing to rule around - I just don't want that much attention on me when I'm doing something I love.

Even though I'm not racing anymore (and I was never anyone significant when I was racing), this ruling confirms the feelings I'd been having around competition in the first place - dissuading people from participating in the ways that they can or should, and overall polluting the sport. What I could understand is a nuanced argument made around parties expressing a nuanced opinion, but that's not what we got. We got men (once again) expressing their opinions on what can and should be done with women's bodies.

I'm in running now, because running makes me feel free, because it makes me feel less anomalous - but as I've started to compete recently, I've started to wonder to myself ifthere's not a possibility that at some point they'll jump back and decide I can't compete anymore. Do I think I'm good at the sport? Sure - the reason for this is that I have worked for it. I train five days a week, I go to a personal trainer, I have a group of like-minded athletes who I compete alongside me and push me to be as good as I can me. This is the heart of sport, in the end, or at the least it's meant to be.

Competition is a chance to challenge yourself - less about competition against others and more about competition against oneself. The greatest athletes that I've known approached the sport this way - taking on the challenge for themselves first, with the results second. While there is competition between people in sport, part of the effort is to show some degree of sport[person]ship between parties, in order to encourage the notion that competition is not about measuring yourself against others.

I think that's why this ruling rubs me particularly wrong - the possibility of having to look as this as a question of 'fair competition' feels like an incomplete take on the question. Fair competition is a question moving through the field to evaluate from the position of those involved as to what is fair. I know any number of cis athletes who compete alongside their trans counterparts - and it's never them who stand and complain about athletic performance, because all of us understand the work that goes into being an athlete in the first place.

None of this was ever about trying to win. It was about competing alongside people we admire and being understood on the same level for the effort made. This being true, I don't understand why it's the place of a collective of men to make decisions about women's bodies, cis, trans, or otherwise. To categorize anyone's ability based on their experience is to reduce us to those experiences, and if anything, Caster Semenya's recent victory in the sport should be an indication that the experience and reality of gender are varied enough such that we shouldn't be asking these questions, we should be allowing people to be who they are.

For the love of the sport, I'd have expected that there was better measurement and adequate consideration given to people's lived experiences rather than any degree of armchair science that studies athletics. This is maybe where I have gotten the most frustrated - in an era of rationalism, we now like to turn to numbers to justify our decisions, instead of remembering that we are social creatures and that because of this there is probably more value in actually speaking to one another. Our experiences don't lie, which is probably why I feel, personally, so much more solidarity with the experiences of my cis counterparts. We share so much overlap and the further I move through my life of not being believed, not being listened to, not being attended to, and not being respected, the more I understand that we share these experiences because they are the same experiences.

If we were to be listened to, maybe this might be understood in the ways that would resolve situations like this. I can only speak for my experience, and I'd hope I would hear more from all those who have comparable experiences, from all those who I know share fragments of mine and want to share their own. Rationalism is a tool, not an ideological cudgel with which to make decisions; the decisions are meant to be separate from the information that we use to support them, we are meant to weigh data against the consensus of public opinion in order to come to our conclusions. That's not what is happening here, unfortunately.

item.title: on good images
item.description:
Photography functions in a fairly obvious sense: one points a camera at a world outside of oneself and imposes perspective on it through the action of taking a photograph. Despite this, life has had its way of imposing doubt on me as a photographer, and it's part of what caused me to walk away from the practice.
However, that's not what I'm writing about today, and it's not what you're going to read about - it's just a lens through which we're going to discuss what itched at me when I was trying to leave photography behind and gave me my reasons for leaving.

Good images

For a number of years, I thought photography couldn't do this. The reason I didn't was that I assumed photography was inherently self-limiting; an image is a trapped moment in time, a small death of the present: good images bewilder, great images sink into the fabric of the soul and beg us to wonder what else happened, or what should happen next.
What I see a lot of these days is the
These days, I see a lot of the first, and while I truly love the stories of those that have found a way to make money with a camera, my sense is that images that only serve an aesthetic purpose don't really compell us. If they do, an age that focuses on optics is one that tries fervently to flaunt our individuality, forcing the image-maker to consider the image as an extension of the self rather than an attempt at observation. Neither approach is necessarily the 'correct' one, but I do think that we have lost something when we consier images purely as a matter of perpective. Art is meant to ecoke a sense of awe, I think. Are we meant to believe that all matters of awe are purely at the hand of their creator? What happened to the conduit?

The Conduit

I want to widen our perspective here a little bit: when I refer to this later phenomenon, I'm speaking to an artistic moment that I believe to be the motivating force between the work of many artists: it is as though by the mere act of creating, the artist is speaking to something larger than themselves. We have a variety of names for the impetus that comes over us in the act of creation that compells us forward
I have tapped the pressed-foam ceiling tiles of this feeling a few times in my life, and I have never known exactly what to do with it. I backed away from it for a period of years, for instance, due largely to the fact that despite the fact that I knew I was on to something, I didn't really know what to do with what I was 'on to'. It's as though in the moment one realizes that what they are creating might actually hold greater significant beyond the self, it imposes an existential dread or a great reckoning: what is this 'source' from which we are drawing in our most creative moments, and what does it mean for us to have been the person who dredged it up?
The feeling is electric: it's so striking as to feel one has struck diamonds or the elixir of life itself.
The unfortunate conclusion to which some arrive here is, I think, the source of my complaint. I don't like it when an artist's response to having created something significant and memorable is to immediately think 'well then, I found a way to make something beuatiful, therefore I am the source of this beautiful thing'. Don't get me wrong, I do believe that every artist deserves credit for the work they do to perfect their craft, but we as artists are not the source of the art we create. I say this with impunity: artists are mere custodians for what life inspires within us.

Inspiration and Derivation

The core argument I'm trying to make is this: I think great things take time, but they also take commitment to tamping down the hubris of believing that we are the reason they are happening.
Inspiration requires that we pay attention to the world, either as a participant or as an observer, and I think that the greatest work we see surrounding us comes from having sit still long enough to take in the greater wonders of life and to have made something of them.

The Caption, and the lack thereof

As with every self-doubting photographer, mulling over the importance of the image brings Sontag's quote from Regarding the Pain of Others to mind:

" To the militant, identity is everything. And all photographs wait to be explained or falsified by their captions. During the fighting between Serbs and Croats at the beginning of the recent Balkan wars, the same photographs of children killed in the shelling of a village were passed around at both Serb and Croat propaganda briefings. Alter the caption, and the children’s deaths could be used and reused."

item.title: pseudopresence
item.description:
The emotional regulation does not seem to hold - the desire to stave off anxiety around possibility and it's weight as an emissary of its own peace, all the while in a state of feeling uncommon with one's own surroundings, as though a part of something both greater and utterly uncaring of your participation.

This is the feeling brought forth by Saturdays by the feeling of having had to think about one's past in a state of motion even while we are attempting to regulate ourselves against the future and past emotions. As Mo Gawdat mentions, anxiety is a feeling that sits in the future because it is a fear of what will happen next. Happiness is instead found in the present, in the happiness found after recognizing what is in your control and withholding fear that desires to bloom forth through any meaningful consideration of the past and future as features of our lives we wish we could change, and it is only in the present that we can truly take action.

So it is a question to me why fear envelops me, why in this moment it is an emotional state that I'm experiencing - and I'm forced to believe that it is a product of anxiety of looking forward and seeing that any set of outcomes are available, any set of outcomes might happen. So we work through the exercise and ask the question - if the fear is that Im going to get off of this train and hear that something devastating has happened, is it real? It is not - it is not something that I need to experience, and because of this is something that I can tell my brain not to experience, it's something that I can push to the side because it is not real. I am in charge of this feeling and I am in charge of what it constitutes.

Recently, I've been listening to Mo Gawdat - the former CBO of Google who, since the passing of his son at 21, turned his life toward the pursuit of happiness for as many people as possible. In particular, I was listening to a conversation he held with Steven Barlett (Diary of a Ceo) - where Gawdat refers to the time-based notion of emotion. His claim is that most negative emotions are couched in the future and the past as either symptoms of regret or expectation, and that the unhappiness that comes with negative thinking often emerges through an interaction with that which we can't change.

This has had me thinking about the general rise in anxiety1 in present times that seems linked to a well-connected society's general inability to exist in the present - we are in many places at once, but we are never in any of these places because technology is not a substitute for being physically and psychically located in a place and a time. Rather than moving with Gawdat's definition of happiness being a function of that which you cannot change and a lack of imperative to exist in the present moment, I would exact the definition to have it describe a need to be in the physical present. More explicitly, I find that when I'm most anxious while using technology, it's because I am interacting with a present I cannot directly affect.

In Mo Gawdat's definition of anxiety or regret, the temporal location of negative emotions pull one away from the present, and the solution for this is to direct one's attention toward the present moment. It's not something that comes easily to people, but it's a meditation on the feeling of knowing - the feeling of examining possibility as something that is interesting, but not that is determinate, because only those things that lie either outside or inside of out control are those that we can think about. Anything else is imaginary and exists outside of those bounds, they are features of existence that reach out for attention but are not tangible; you cannot touch them, you cannot feel them.

This is the great mistake that has arisen with creating technologies that exist to reconstitute our presences in several spaces at once. We even call video calling 'telepresence', as though there is a feature of this sort of interaction that constitutes meaningful interaction, when telepresence is likely better termed 'pseudopresence', enveloping a construct of terms that describe the ability to experience anxiety around one's need to exist and affect several places at once - an experience that is not tangible and not real, because at best our ability to telegraph the appearance of presence must be acted upon locally by those who are physically in a location and capable of affecting local reality.
